items.descriptionOriginal: Δεν μπορείς να εγκαθιστάς μια τεχνολογία και να την παρατάς στη μοίρα της, δήλωσε στην εκπομπή UPDATE του ΕΡΤnews , ο Διοικητής της Εθνικής Αρχής Κυβερνοασφάλειας , Μιχάλης Μπλέτσας , σχολιάζοντας τις τελευταίες κυβερνοεπιθέσεις στην Ευρώπη και δη αυτές στα ψυγεία των σούπερ μάρκετ και των τραπεζών αίματος. Στο συγκεκριμένο σημείο, ο κ. Μπλέτσας έκανε λόγο για αμέλεια εκ μέρους αυτών που εγκαθιστούν την τεχνολογία, αναφέροντας ως παράδειγμα ψυγείο μεγάλης εγκατάστασης στην Ελλάδα που μετά από όσα έχουν συμβεί στην Ευρώπη «είναι ακόμα ανοιχτό και μπορεί ο οποιοσδήποτε να μπει από οπουδήποτε στο διαδίκτυο και να το ελέγξει». Εξήγησε μάλιστα ότι οι κυβερνοεπιθέσεις γίνονται προγραμματιστικά και ότι αυτός που τις κάνει δεν γνωρίζει απαραίτητα ότι πίσω από ένα ψυγείο που θα χτυπήσει κρύβεται π.χ. το ψυγείο μιας τράπεζας αίματος. «Δηλαδή δεν υπάρχει κάποιος που λέει “πήγαινε εκεί, πήγαινε εκεί, πήγαινε εκεί”. Λέει “πήγαινε σε αυτές τις διευθύνσεις του διαδικτύου, σε αυτή την περιοχή και ψάξε για τέτοια ψυγεία και κλείστα”. Τώρα αν αυτά είναι σε σούπερ μάρκετ ή σε τράπεζα αίματος ή οπουδήποτε αλλού, δεν νομίζω ότι δίνουν ιδιαίτερη σημασία», ανέφερε ο κ. Μπλέτσας, συμπληρώνοντας πάντως ότι αυτή είναι «μία εικασία που βασίζεται στις δικές μου γνώσεις και στις δικές μου εκτιμήσεις». Επανερχόμενος ωστόσο στο θέμα, ξεκαθάρισε ότι «από τη στιγμή που αφήνετε τη συσκευή εκτεθειμένη, κάποιος θα της επιτεθεί αργά ή γρήγορα». Ερωτηθείς τι είναι αυτό που τον ανησυχεί περισσότερο με τον «εφιάλτη» των χάκερ, ο κ. Μπλέτσας προσπάθησε να γίνει καθησυχαστικός υπενθυμίζοντας ότι οι ηλεκτρονικές υπηρεσίες μάς απαλάσσουν από μετακινήσεις οι οποίες πάντα ενέχουν μεγαλύτερο φυσικό κίνδυνο. «Οταν δεν κάνουμε μετακινήσεις, εκτιθέμεθα πολύ λιγότερο στο φυσικό κίνδυνο, ο οποίος είναι πολύ μεγαλύτερος από τον ηλεκτρονικό αυτή τη στιγμή. Η πιθανότητα ότι θα σας επιτεθεί κάποιος χάκερ και θα σας κάνει φυσικά κακό είναι ελάχιστη. Η πιθανότητα ότι θα σας χτυπήσει κεραυνός είναι πολύ μεγαλύτερη αυτή τη στιγμή», είπε χαρακτηριστικά ο κ. Μπλέτσας , συστήνοντας ψυχραιμία η οποία «θα μας βοηθήσει στη συγκεκριμένη περίπτωση για να δούμε τι πρέπει να κάνουμε». Κληθείς τέλος να τοποθετηθεί στο αν οι τράπεζες διατρέχουν κάποιον κίνδυνο, ο κ. Μπλέτσας ήταν και πάλι καθησυχαστικός λέγοντας ότι «τα χρήματά μας στις τράπεζες, στις ελληνικές τράπεζες τουλάχιστον για τις οποίες έχουμε εικόνα, είναι απόλυτα ασφαλή». «Το χειρότερο που μπορεί να γίνει σε κάποιον είναι να μην μπορέσει να κάνει κάποια συναλλαγή για κάποια ώρα και να την κάνει λίγο αργότερα. Κανένας δεν έχει χάσει τα χρήματά του στις ελληνικές τράπεζες, τα οποία έχουν γίνει και πολύ περισσότερο ηλεκτρονικά τον τελευταίο καιρό. Το περισσότερο χρήμα αυτή τη στιγμή είναι άυλο και ηλεκτρονικό. Επομένως, γιατί να ανησυχούμε για κάτι το οποίο έχει γίνει πιο ασφαλές από παλιότερα;», διερωτήθηκε ο κ. Μπλέτσας συμπληρώνοντας ότι κατανοεί το κλίμα που έχει δημιουργηθεί και εκφράζοντας την εκτίμηση πως απ΄ ότι φαίνεται «υπάρχει κάποιο σχέδιο να δημιουργηθεί φόβος στους πολίτες των ευρωπαϊκών χωρών». www.ertnews.gr

Οι τεχνολογίες γονιδιακής επεξεργασίας προσφέρουν μια πιθανή εναλλακτική λύση στα φάρμακα που μειώνουν τα λιπίδια. Σε ένα νέο πείραμα CRISPR, μια μόνο έγχυση μιας θεραπείας γονιδιακής επεξεργασίας διατήρησε χαμηλά επίπεδα τριγλυκεριδίων σε πιθήκους…
items.descriptionOriginal: High levels of LDL cholesterol and triglycerides, which are types of blood fats, are major contributors to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Gene-editing technologies offer a potential alternative to lipid-lowering medications. In a new CRISPR experiment, a single infusion of a gene-editing treatment kept triglyceride levels low in monkeys for three years. The findings support the possibility of controlling blood fats with a lasting DNA change, potentially replacing daily doses of medication.

items.descriptionOriginal: Brewers in China used red mold and bast-fiber textiles to filter rice-based alcoholic beverages approximately 5,000 years ago, according to a new study. University of Arizona researchers examined 16 pottery vessels and five specialized filters from the Wayaoli archaeological site in China’s Zhejiang Province. Using microscopic residue analysis, they identified starch grains, phytoliths, fungi, and microfibers preserved on the pottery. These residues indicated that the vessels were used to produce rice-based alcoholic beverages, including red-colored alcohol made with Monascus mold. Ancient brewers used red mold to ferment rice Archaeologists first found five unusual pottery filters with connected upper and lower bowls. Based on their design, they suspected they might have been used to produce alcohol, although it appeared they could also have supported other processes, including grain processing and water purification. However, residue analysis revealed rice starch and traces of Monascus mold, which is associated with traditional red rice brewing, on all five filters. Its enzymes break down rice starch into sugars that can then be fermented, the study reported . Additionally, the mold produces red pigments, suggesting that the Ancient Chinese drank red alcohol. Some starch grains showed damage consistent with cooking and fermentation, providing further evidence that the vessels were used in alcohol production. Researchers also discovered several starchy plant fibers, including foxnut, Job’s tears, and underground storage organs. The residue evidence aligns with an earlier study conducted at the Shangshan archaeological site in Zhejiang Province, dating back 10,000–9,000 years, which indicated that Monascus was used to ferment rice-based beverages. Another processing technique Researchers found traces of microscopic fibers identified as bast-fibers, which stem from the inner bark of plant stems and can be used to manufacture textiles. That suggests ancient brewers placed woven fabric inside the upper bowls of the pottery filters to separate the liquid from solid material. “These bast fibers were likely woven into textiles and placed on the upper filter bowl to improve alcohol filtration,” said researchers. The study states that bast-fiber textiles were used for filtration, improving both the taste and clarity of alcoholic beverages. However, researchers found no intact cloth at the archaeological site. Alcohol held ritual significance According to the study, most of these pottery filters came from burials excavated at the site. These vessels frequently appeared alongside other pottery associated with household activities, including jars, plates, and cooking pots. The researchers interpreted the presence of filters in burials as evidence of alcohol’s importance in the community’s social and ritual traditions. Late Neolithic societies in the Lower Yangzi River region were known for their intensive rice agriculture, technological innovation that increased social complexity, and elaborate ritual practices. Rice fermentation played a role in advancing culture and manufacturing techniques. By analyzing the microscopic residues on ancient pottery, researchers uncovered a major feature of these cultures. They identified evidence of both fermentation and filtration techniques used about five millennia ago. The study findings demonstrated the production of rice-based fermented beverages using Monascus molds and bast-fiber textiles. It suggested the significance of alcohol during the social and rituals during the Late Songze and Early Liangzhu periods.

items.title: Η ασυνήθιστη οικογενειακή παράδοση της μητέρας της Κεράλα
items.titleOriginal: Kerala’s Unusual Mother-Side Family Tradition
items.description: Στην Κεράλα, η περιουσία του πατέρα σας θα μπορούσε να ανήκει στα παιδιά της θείας σας! Όπως και στη νέα σειρά AKKA, για αιώνες, πολλές οικογένειες Nair ακολούθησαν ένα μοναδικό μητρογραμμικό σύστημα που ονομάζεται Marumakkathayam, όπου η οικογενειακή ταυτότητα και η κληρονομιά περνούσαν από την πλευρά της μητέρας. Ακόμη και ο γιος ενός βασιλιά δεν μπορούσε να κληρονομήσει τον θρόνο. Πήγε στον γιο της αδερφής του!…
items.descriptionOriginal: In Kerala, your father’s property could belong to your aunt’s children! Just like in the new series AKKA, for centuries, many Nair families followed a unique matrilineal system called Marumakkathayam, where family identity and inheritance passed through the mother’s side. Even a king’s son could not inherit the throne. It went to his sister’s son! But here’s the twist: women passed down the family name, while men, especially the eldest maternal uncle, held the power. The system was abolished in 1975, but matrilineal traditions continue in parts of India. items.descriptionOriginal: Μια πρωτότυπη, αλλά και ιδιαίτερα αμφιλεγόμενη ιδέα επιστρατεύει η Κίρσα Κέκελε, γνωστή ως η «πρώτη κυρία» του Μουσείου Παλαιάς και Νέας Τέχνης (MONA) στην Τασμανία , για την προστασία των αρχαίων δασών της περιοχής. Δημιούργησε το OnlyFerns, μια πλατφόρμα τύπου OnlyFans, όπου οι συνδρομητές πληρώνουν για να παρακολουθήσουν ερωτικά βίντεο με θεματολογία εμπνευσμένη από τα δάση και τη βιομηχανία ξυλείας. Το σχέδιο έχει έναν φιλόδοξο στόχο: τα έσοδα από το περιεχόμενο να χρηματοδοτήσουν εναλλακτικές δραστηριότητες για τους εργαζόμενους στην υλοτομία, ώστε να προστατευτούν πολύτιμες δασικές εκτάσεις χωρίς να χάσουν οι ίδιοι τις δουλειές τους. Ερωτικές σκηνές μέσα σε δάση και πριονιστήρια Ήταν απλώς αξιολάτρευτοι»: Οι furries συγκεντρώνονται στα γυρίσματα ομαδικής ερωτικής σκηνής για το OnlyFerns.Φωτογραφία: MONA Το OnlyFerns περιλαμβάνει 12 βίντεο, τα οποία γυρίστηκαν σε ιδιωτικές δασικές εκτάσεις και πριονιστήρια της Τασμανίας. Στην παραγωγή συμμετείχαν περίπου 20 δημιουργοί περιεχομένου του OnlyFans, οι οποίοι ταξίδεψαν στην περιοχή για τα γυρίσματα. Ανάμεσα στις σκηνές βρίσκονται ιδιαίτερες ερωτικές περφόρμανς, με πρωταγωνιστές ανθρώπους ντυμένους με στολές ζώων, καλλιτέχνες και performers που υποδύονται υλοτόμους ή ακτιβιστές. Η ίδια η Κέκελε εμφανίζεται σε ρόλο τηλεφωνήτριας ερωτικής γραμμής σε πριονιστήριο, συνδέοντας τους ενδιαφερόμενους με τις ιδιαίτερες φαντασιώσεις τους. «Ήταν απλώς αξιολάτρευτοι. Ακόμη και όταν συμμετέχουν σε σκηνές για ενήλικες, εξακολουθούν να δείχνουν πολύ χαριτωμένοι και σχεδόν αθώοι», σχολίασε η καλλιτέχνις για τους performers με τις στολές ζώων. Το Μουσείο MONA και η Κέκελε κάλυψαν το κόστος της παραγωγής, τις αμοιβές των δημιουργών και του συνεργείου, καθώς και τη δημιουργία ενός ντοκιμαντέρ και ενός βιβλίου που συνοδεύουν το εγχείρημα. Διαβάστε ακόμα Πώς συνδέεται το OnlyFans με την προστασία των δασών Οι περισσότερες περιβαλλοντικές εκστρατείες δημιουργούν ένα δίπολο “εμείς εναντίον αυτών”, αφήνοντας τους εργαζόμενους έξω από την προσπάθεια προστασίας. Αυτό δεν είναι πρακτικό», λέει η Κέκελε, η οποία απεικονίζεται στη φωτογραφία. Φωτογραφία: MONA Η ιδέα δεν περιορίζεται στη συγκέντρωση χρημάτων. Το σχέδιο προβλέπει ότι οι εργαζόμενοι της δασικής βιομηχανίας θα μπορούν να απασχοληθούν στην κατασκευή ξύλινων διαδρόμων και έργων τέχνης σε περιοχές παλαιών δασών, αντί να συνεχίσουν να κόβουν δέντρα στις συγκεκριμένες εκτάσεις. Η Κέκελε θεωρεί απαραίτητο να μη βρεθούν οι υλοτόμοι αντιμέτωποι με την περιβαλλοντική προστασία και να μη χάσουν το εισόδημά τους εξαιτίας της αλλαγής στη διαχείριση των δασών. «Είναι κρίσιμο για την επιτυχία του σχεδίου να διασφαλίσουμε ότι δεν θα χαθούν ώρες εργασίας», τονίζει, υποστηρίζοντας ότι πολλές περιβαλλοντικές εκστρατείες δημιουργούν ένα δίπολο ανάμεσα στους ακτιβιστές και τους εργαζόμενους, αποκλείοντας τους τελευταίους από τις λύσεις. Η κρατική εταιρεία Sustainable Timber Tasmania, η οποία δραστηριοποιείται στη διαχείριση των δασών και την παραγωγή ξυλείας, δήλωσε ότι βρίσκεται σε συζητήσεις με το MONA σχετικά με τις φιλοδοξίες του εγχειρήματος. Παράλληλα, χαρακτήρισε την πρωτοβουλία σημαντική, καθώς έφερε διαφορετικούς ενδιαφερόμενους στο ίδιο τραπέζι και δημιούργησε χώρο για συζήτηση γύρω από τη δασική διαχείριση. Το ακριβές ποσό που θα συγκεντρωθεί από τις συνδρομές παραμένει άγνωστο. Όπως παραδέχεται η Κέκελε, η έκταση των έργων θα εξαρτηθεί από την ανταπόκριση του κοινού, αλλά και από την πιθανή οικονομική στήριξη του συζύγου της, Ντέιβιντ Γουόλς, και άλλων εύπορων υποστηρικτών. Οι περιβαλλοντικές οργανώσεις αντιδρούν Η Έμμα Μέι Γκίμπσον, γνωστή και ως Μπέτι Γκράμπλ, είναι μία από τις performers που συμμετέχουν στο OnlyFerns. Φωτογραφία: MONA Παρά τις φιλοδοξίες της δημιουργού του, το OnlyFerns έχει προκαλέσει έντονες αντιδράσεις σε περιβαλλοντικές οργανώσεις, κυρίως λόγω της συνεργασίας με τη βιομηχανία υλοτομίας. Η Κέκελε είχε ιδρύσει το 2023 το Forest Congress, με σκοπό να φέρει σε διάλογο περιβαλλοντικές οργανώσεις, επιστήμονες, εκπροσώπους των αυτόχθονων Palawa και ανθρώπους της δασικής βιομηχανίας. Ωστόσο, η προσπάθεια συνεννόησης δεν βρήκε σύμφωνες όλες τις πλευρές. Τον Ιούλιο, η Wilderness Society αποχώρησε από το συνέδριο, καταγγέλλοντας ότι η βιομηχανία υλοτομίας δεν έχει κάνει ουσιαστικά βήματα για να διορθώσει τις επιβαρυντικές πρακτικές της. Από την πλευρά του, το Bob Brown Foundation, που είχε μποϊκοτάρει εξαρχής τη διαδικασία, χαρακτήρισε το σχέδιο υπέρ της υλοτομίας. Η οργάνωση υποστήριξε ότι η προστασία μόλις του 3% ή 4% των δασών, με βάση τον χαρακτηρισμό των παλαιών δασικών εκτάσεων από τη βιομηχανία, αφήνει το υπόλοιπο 96% εκτεθειμένο στην αποψίλωση και την καταστροφή της άγριας ζωής. «Το να τερματιστεί αυτή η τραγωδία δεν είναι περφόρμανς τέχνης», ανέφερε χαρακτηριστικά σε ανακοίνωσή της, επισημαίνοντας ότι η προστασία των δασών αποτελεί μια τεράστια πρόκληση για την Τασμανία και την Αυστραλία. Η «ριζοσπαστική διπλωματία» της Κίρσα Κέκελε Η Κέλι Πάνθερ υποδύεται μια χίπισσα ακτιβίστρια στο βίντεό της για το OnlyFerns. Στο παρελθόν εργάστηκε ως στρίπερ για να χρηματοδοτήσει τις σπουδές της στην περιβαλλοντική επιστήμη και δηλώνει ενθουσιασμένη που συμμετείχε στο εγχείρημα. Φωτογραφία: MONA Η Κέκελε υπερασπίζεται τη συνεργασία με τους υλοτόμους, υποστηρίζοντας ότι η προστασία των αρχαίων δασών μπορεί να αποτελέσει κοινό στόχο. Όπως εξηγεί, το σχέδιο επικεντρώνεται σε εκτάσεις για τις οποίες υπάρχει ευρύτερη συμφωνία ότι πρέπει να διατηρηθούν, καθώς αποτελούν αναντικατάστατα οικοσυστήματα. Η ίδια περιγράφει τη φιλοσοφία της ως «ριζοσπαστική διπλωματία» και δηλώνει ότι επιδιώκει να βρεθεί ανάμεσα σε αντίπαλες πλευρές, αναζητώντας σημεία συνεννόησης. «Μου αρέσει να βλέπω τις πεποιθήσεις μου να ανατρέπονται», αναφέρει χαρακτηριστικά. Η καλλιτέχνις δεν είναι άγνωστη στο κοινό του MONA. Είναι σύζυγος του ιδρυτή του μουσείου, Ντέιβιντ Γουόλς, και είχε βρεθεί στο επίκεντρο της δημοσιότητας το 2024, εξαιτίας της δικαστικής διαμάχης για το έργο Ladies Lounge, έναν χώρο του μουσείου στον οποίο απαγορευόταν η είσοδος στους άνδρες. Το OnlyFerns αποτελεί πλέον μία ακόμη προσπάθειά της να συνδυάσει την τέχνη με κοινωνικά και περιβαλλοντικά ζητήματα. Το αν η ασυνήθιστη αυτή ιδέα θα καταφέρει να συγκεντρώσει αρκετούς πόρους και να συμβάλει ουσιαστικά στη διάσωση των δασών της Τασμανίας, μένει να αποδειχθεί. items.descriptionOriginal: In Bajaura, in Himachal Pradesh's Kullu district, farmers have had to rethink their orchards twice. As changing weather made apple cultivation harder, they turned to pomegranates. Then plant viruses began affecting those orchards too. Now, persimmons are offering another possibility. For anyone who associates Himachal with bags of apples brought home after a holiday, that change may be surprising. For the people tending these orchards, it comes down to a pressing question: what can they grow to keep earning from their land? Rising temperatures, declining snowfall and unpredictable rainfall are making familiar crops harder to rely on. Farmers are responding by trying different fruits, growing crops together and changing how they care for their soil. Their efforts feature in a study by the Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW), supported by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD). Released on 31 October 2026, it draws on experiences across 12 gram panchayats in Mandi, Kullu, Sirmaur and Shimla . The study identifies 25 ways communities can prepare for climate risks. Among them are practices villagers have already begun putting to work, shaped by what they see happening in their fields and around their homes. What do you plant when the familiar crop struggles? Bajaura's move towards persimmons shows how much adjustment farming now demands. Replacing apples with pomegranates did not end the uncertainty. Farmers had to look for another option when disease affected the replacement crop. Growing a mix of crops can help spread the risk of a poor harvest, though poor transport and limited cold storage still constrain farmers' earnings. Photograph: (Himachal Watcher) And choosing a fruit is only part of making an orchard viable. Farmers need water to grow it and roads to get the harvest to buyers. In Bajaura, dwindling irrigation water and roads damaged during disasters continue to make both difficult. In Parara, Sirmaur, growers face a related problem. Residents report that changing rainfall and rising temperatures have altered planting schedules and increased diseases affecting tomatoes and garlic. Some farmers are combining garlic cultivation with specialised apple varieties . The village's efforts also include natural farming and rainwater harvesting. Growing a mix of crops can help spread the risk of a poor harvest, though poor transport and limited cold storage still constrain farmers' earnings. For a farming household, finding something that grows is the beginning. Being able to sell it is what helps pay the bills. In Sandhu, change begins with the soil In Sandhu, Shimla, farmers are reconsidering how they grow their crops. Community members report that prolonged chemical fertiliser use has affected soil quality and fertility. Local women have responded by taking up natural farming, which avoids synthetic fertilisers and pesticides and uses resources available on the farm. The aim is to nurture the soil while reducing reliance on purchased chemical inputs . According to community accounts documented in the study, the practice has spread to more than 20 families after residents found it profitable and better able to withstand extreme weather. That experience gives neighbours something practical to consider: a different way of farming already being tried close to home. Yet even healthier soil and a different crop need water. In nearby Sirmaur district, that has brought women's groups back to the traditional sources their villages once relied on. Bringing water back to village life Thana Kashoga once had 35 perennial baoris, traditional spring-fed water structures that supplied households throughout the year. According to the study, only 10 remain. Residents report declining rainfall and rising temperatures , putting increasing pressure on these sources. The shortage reaches into everyday life, affecting drinking water, irrigation and livestock. Fodder scarcity and forest fires have also made pastoral livelihoods harder to sustain. Local women have responded by taking up natural farming, which avoids synthetic fertilisers and pesticides and uses resources available on the farm. The aim is to nurture the soil while reducing reliance on purchased chemical inputs. Photograph: (Triya Gulati via The Print) Women's groups have taken on the work of maintaining and restoring the baoris. Their efforts connect directly to what farmers are trying to do: keep village life possible as the conditions supporting it change. These communities still need dependable irrigation, transport and support to carry their work forward. A new crop cannot fix a damaged road, and a restored water source needs continued care. But in Thana Kashoga, there is a tangible reason to keep going. Women's groups clean the baoris monthly. Five springs have been revived, with work on another five or six under way. Sources: 'Villages in Himachal adapting climate change with new crops, revived springs' : By Shailee Dogra, Published on 1 November 2026 'How can Himalayan communities anticipate risks and adapt to a changing climate? Evidence from 12 Gram Panchayats of Himachal Pradesh' : By Ahana Chatterjee, Meet Kumar, Srishti Mandal, Taveri Rajkhowa, and Shreya Wadhawan, Published on 31 October, 2026

items.title: Η συζήτηση Μητσοτάκη με την ιδρύτρια του οργανισμού «It’s just period» για τη μείωση του ΦΠΑ στα προϊόντα περιόδου – Δείτε βίντεο
items.titleOriginal: Η συζήτηση Μητσοτάκη με την ιδρύτρια του οργανισμού «It’s just period» για τη μείωση του ΦΠΑ στα προϊόντα περιόδου – Δείτε βίντεο
items.description: Τη σημασία της στοχευμένης μείωσης του ΦΠΑ στα προϊόντα περιόδου και της συνδρομής της κοινωνίας των πολιτών στην απόφαση αυτή ανέδειξε ο Πρωθυπουργός Κυριάκος Μητσοτάκης σε συζήτηση που είχε, στο Μέγαρο Μαξίμου, με την Ισμήνη Δροσοφορίδη, ιδρύτρια του οργανισμού «It’s just period». «Θέλω να σας συγχαρώ για τη δουλειά την οποία έχετε κάνει και για τον τρόπο με τον οποίο αναδείξατε ένα θέμα το…
items.descriptionOriginal: Τη σημασία της στοχευμένης μείωσης του ΦΠΑ στα προϊόντα περιόδου και της συνδρομής της κοινωνίας των πολιτών στην απόφαση αυτή ανέδειξε ο Πρωθυπουργός Κυριάκος Μητσοτάκης σε συζήτηση που είχε, στο Μέγαρο Μαξίμου, με την Ισμήνη Δροσοφορίδη, ιδρύτρια του οργανισμού «It’s just period». «Θέλω να σας συγχαρώ για τη δουλειά την οποία έχετε κάνει και για τον τρόπο με τον οποίο αναδείξατε ένα θέμα το οποίο είναι υπαρκτό, το αυξημένο κόστος για τα προϊόντα περιόδου για όλες τις γυναίκες», σημείωσε ο Πρωθυπουργός. «Γι’ αυτό και πήρα -ευαισθητοποιημένος και από τη δουλειά την οποία κάνατε και από τις μελέτες τις οποίες δρομολογήσατε- την απόφαση από 1η Ιανουαρίου 2027 να μειώσουμε τον ΦΠΑ στα προϊόντα περιόδου, από το 24% στο 13%», συνέχισε ο Κυριάκος Μητσοτάκης. Δείτε αυτή τη δημοσίευση στο Instagram. Η δημοσίευση κοινοποιήθηκε από το χρήστη Ismini Drosoforidi (@ismini_d) Η μετάταξη των προϊόντων περιόδου, αλλά και των ειδών ακράτειας ενηλίκων, στον μειωμένο συντελεστή ΦΠΑ, όπου ήδη βρίσκονται οι βρεφικές πάνες, περιελήφθη στο ψηφισθέν νομοσχέδιο του Υπουργείου Εθνικής Οικονομίας και Οικονομικών για την υλοποίηση των φοροελαφρύνσεων και των μέτρων ενίσχυσης του εισοδήματος που ανακοινώθηκαν από τον Πρωθυπουργό στη ΔΕΘ. «Το γεγονός το οποίο αναδείξατε πράγματι με ευαισθητοποίησε και εμένα ιδιαίτερα, ότι μπορεί να υπάρχει έστω κι ένα κορίτσι το οποίο δεν χρησιμοποιεί προϊόντα περιόδου, χάνει ημέρες σχολείου γιατί πολύ απλά δεν μπορεί να αντέξει το κόστος αυτής της δαπάνης, είναι κάτι το οποίο πρέπει να το αντιμετωπίσουμε», τόνισε ο Πρωθυπουργός, αναφερόμενος στη θετική επίδραση που θα έχει η μείωση του φόρου στην καθημερινότητα των γυναικών και των κοριτσιών. «Ζήτησα από το Υπουργείο να προσθέσει και τις πάνες ακράτειας στη μείωση του ΦΠΑ από το 24% στο 13% -θα τεθεί σε εφαρμογή από 1η Ιανουαρίου 2027. Έχουμε πολλούς πιο ηλικιωμένους συμπολίτες μας οι οποίοι αντιμετωπίζουν και αυτοί ένα ιατρικό ζήτημα. Χρειάζονται τα προϊόντα αυτά», προσέθεσε. Ο Κυριάκος Μητσοτάκης στάθηκε, επίσης, στη σημασία της μετακύλισης του μειωμένου ΦΠΑ στα προϊόντα περιόδου στο ράφι. «Επειδή ακριβώς αφορά μια συγκεκριμένη κατηγορία προϊόντων, τα οποία παράγονται από έναν μικρό αριθμό εταιρειών, είναι και αρκετά εύκολο για την πολιτεία να εξασφαλίσει ότι αυτή η μείωση θα περάσει αυτούσια στον τελικό καταναλωτή», επισήμανε. «Μακάρι και να μπορούμε να έρθουμε και σε μία συνεννόηση και με τις εταιρείες αυτές, να βάλουν και αυτές λίγο πλάτη, ώστε να μειώσουν και την τιμή προ ΦΠΑ, έτσι ώστε η τελική ελάφρυνση που θα δει η γυναίκα που θα αγοράσει αυτό το προϊόν, το κορίτσι που θα αγοράσει αυτό το προϊόν, να είναι μεγαλύτερη από τη μείωση αυτή καθαυτή του ΦΠΑ», συμπλήρωσε ο Πρωθυπουργός, προσθέτοντας ότι μέσω της πλατφόρμας PosoKanei οι καταναλωτές έχουν τη δυνατότητα να κάνουν σύγκριση των τιμών των προϊόντων περιόδου σε πραγματικό χρόνο. Κατά τη διάρκεια της συζήτησης τέθηκαν οι προτάσεις του «It’s just period» σχετικά με την περαιτέρω υποστήριξη των γυναικών και των κοριτσιών ως προς τα προϊόντα περιόδου . «Αναγνωρίζω απόλυτα ότι προφανώς δεν λύνουμε το πρόβλημα, ότι είναι ένα πρώτο βήμα. Αλλά είναι ένα πρώτο βήμα ευαισθητοποίησης της πολιτείας για ένα πρόβλημα το οποίο, δυστυχώς, δεν το είχαμε συζητήσει και δεν το είχαμε μελετήσει στη λεπτομέρεια που του αρμόζει», ανέφερε ο Κυριάκος Μητσοτάκης. Ειδήσεις σήμερα 400.000 νοικοκυριά καλύπτουν από την τσέπη τους τις δαπάνες υγείας – Πόσα πληρώνουν οι ασθενείς σε φάρμακα «Να μην γίνει ο διαβήτης εμπόδιο στα όνειρά της»: Ένας πατέρας μιλά για την 13χρονη κόρη του και τη ζωή της με τη νόσο Η Ελλάδα από τις πρώτες χώρες με πρόσβαση στην ευρωπαϊκή πλατφόρμα Epi+ για την ανίχνευση απειλών υγείας

Οι ερευνητές διαπίστωσαν ότι ένα πρόγραμμα αποκατάστασης τεσσάρων μηνών υπό επίβλεψη βελτίωσε τον πόνο, τη μυϊκή δύναμη και την ποιότητα ζωής χωρίς να καταστρέψει τον χόνδρο του γόνατος. items.descriptionOriginal: A new study suggests that the right kind of exercise could help protect young adults from early knee osteoarthritis following ACL surgery. Researchers found that a four-month supervised rehabilitation program improved pain, muscle strength, and quality of life without damaging knee cartilage. The findings challenge fears that exercise worsens injured knees and could transform how patients recover from ACL reconstruction.

Τέσσερις μήνες αφότου η κόρη της μετακόμισε σε ένα νέο σχολείο, η Shivani Tyagi αποφάσισε να ξαναδείτε την εμπειρία της με ένα…
items.descriptionOriginal: For a five-year-old, changing schools can mean more than walking into a new classroom or learning a different routine. It can also mean leaving behind familiar faces, favourite teachers and friends who have been part of their everyday lives. Four months after her daughter moved to a new school, Shivani Tyagi decided to revisit the experience with a simple question: "When we changed your school, how did you feel?" Her daughter's answer caught her attention. "It was very upsetting," she said, explaining that the hardest part was leaving her friends behind. She hadn't wanted to do that. Even after settling into a new school, children may need time and space to process the emotions of leaving old friends behind. Rather than brushing aside the response or reassuring her that everything was fine, Shivani chose to listen and ask her daughter more about how she had managed the change. Making room for difficult feelings Shivani, a certified nutritionist, parent coach and NLP coach, believes that children do not always express what they are feeling immediately. Sometimes, they need time, reassurance and a comfortable space to put their emotions into words. Her daughter had settled into the new school, made friends and appeared to be adjusting well. But Shivani wanted to understand what the transition had felt like from her daughter's perspective. When she asked how she had managed the move despite finding it upsetting, her daughter explained that she was willing to try. Having the space to express what she was feeling made it easier for her to navigate the change. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Shivani Tyagi - Parent coach, Nutritionist, NLP practitioner (@parenting_with_shivani) For Shivani, that was a moment of pride. She was happy to see her daughter acknowledge that something had been difficult while still finding the courage to give a new environment a chance. She also understood that making new friends did not mean forgetting the old ones. They could still stay in touch with their previous classmates while gradually building new friendships. Keep asking, even after they seem settled School transitions can bring a mix of emotions for young children. Excitement about a new classroom may exist alongside sadness about leaving familiar surroundings. And just because a child appears comfortable after a few weeks does not necessarily mean they have processed everything. This is why Shivani makes it a habit to have open conversations with her daughter about everyday experiences, whether big or small. For parents navigating a similar transition, the approach need not be complicated. A simple conversation over dinner, during a bedtime routine or on the way back from school can create an opportunity for children to share what is on their minds. Simple everyday conversations can help children feel safe expressing emotions they may otherwise struggle to put into words. Instead of immediately offering solutions, parents can begin by asking what they miss, what they enjoy about the new school or whether anything has been difficult. The idea is not to have all the answers but to let children know that their feelings are welcome. Sometimes, a child does not need to be told that everything will be fine. They simply need to know that they can talk about what isn't. All images courtesy of Shivani Tyagi Source: 'Helping Kids Handle Change at School' by PBS Kids, Published on 11 January 2022.

items.descriptionOriginal: In South Sudan in 2024, just out of high school, Nyakangba Nelson Luka Poyo asked himself what kind of life a kid born in 2021 in Tambura would have apart from killing, hatred, bloodshed, and living in a camp. Amid tears, that question gave him his life’s purpose. He thought if young people had opportunities to learn and communicate, and the space in which to express themselves, they could realize alternatives to violence. He called it a “Peace Voice.” Young people make up an estimated 70% of South Sudan’s population, yet they have no voice. They are swept up into conflict at a shockingly young age. In a Peace Journey program, Nyakangba learned about Laddership, and how to become a “ladder” for others lifting them up through support and opportunities. Now, through Peace Voices to Vision, he helps young people “develop a common understanding of how to live together peacefully. Everyone deserves peace.”

items.descriptionOriginal: This article is published in partnership with Museum of Solutions For a child who has never used a computer independently, the first lesson in artificial intelligence isn't about algorithms. It's about a cursor. For one Grade 6 student from a government school in Maharashtra's Raigad district, that lesson began inside a 10-storey children's museum in Mumbai's Lower Parel, tucked into the old Kamala Mills compound: the Museum of Solutions (MuSo). When the student joined an immersive artificial intelligence (AI) learning programme there, computers were still unfamiliar territory. Even using a laptop touchpad and typing basic commands were challenges. But over the next few sessions, that began to change. By the end of the programme, the student had created an email account, learnt to use Microsoft Word and OneDrive, and taken part in coding challenges through Minecraft Education. What started with the basics of operating a computer had opened a door to exploring artificial intelligence, experimenting with technology and understanding how it works. "From day one, it was pretty interesting. The AI workshop at the Museum of Solutions brought teachers and students together to learn about technology, explore AI and understand how it can be used to find solutions to different problems, from those in our classrooms to challenges at a global level," says Meera, a student, who attended the workshop at MuSo. For thousands of children from underserved communities across Maharashtra, such opportunities are becoming a first introduction to the technology that is increasingly shaping the world around them. Students experiment with machine learning by training models to recognise objects and understanding how the information they receive shapes their results. Through AI Explorers, an initiative at MuSo, children are learning about AI through interactive games, experiments, creative exercises and coding activities. The programme, supported by Microsoft Philanthropies India and implemented by JSW Foundation, aims to make AI education more accessible to children who may have limited opportunities to engage with digital learning. Between July 2025 and June 2026, the initiative reached 9,087 children through foundational AI workshops, while another 313 students took part in a more intensive 10-hour learning pilot. It also trained 80 teachers and worked with 36 schools and 17 NGO and community partners across six districts of Maharashtra. But the numbers tell only part of the story. At its heart, the initiative is about making sure that a child's access to emerging technologies is not decided by the circumstances they grow up in. Bringing AI education beyond privileged classrooms AI is already influencing how children interact with the world, from the content they watch to the apps they use. But knowing how to use a digital device and understanding the technology behind it are two very different things. For children from underserved communities, opportunities to explore AI, experiment with coding or even use a computer independently can be limited. The data bears this out. According to the Ministry of Education's UDISE+ 2024-25 data, only 57.9% of schools in India have computers that work for teaching, and in government schools the figure falls to 52.7%. In Maharashtra, more than 25,000 of the state's 1.08 lakh schools, nearly one in four, had no functional computer. Children explore how AI works through interactive activities, learning to question its outputs rather than simply accept them. At home, the gap is wider still. The ASER 2023 'Beyond Basics' survey of rural youth aged 14 to 18 found that while about 90% of households had a smartphone, only 9% had a computer or laptop. Those with a computer at home were far more likely to know how to use one (85%) than those without (33.9%). Meanwhile, AI is arriving in classrooms. From the 2026-27 academic year, the Ministry of Education is introducing AI and computational thinking in schools from Class 3 onwards. This gap led MuSo to conceptualise AI Explorers. It's a natural fit for a museum whose very name is a mission statement. Opened in November 2023 by the JSW Group and founded by Tanvi Jindal Shete, a former Teach For India fellow, the not-for-profit museum aims to empower children to find solutions to India's most pressing problems. Within a year, it was named on TIME's list of the World's Greatest Places of 2024 and became the first Indian museum to win the international Hands On! Children in Museums Award, competing against 32 museums from 17 countries. "AI already shapes children's lives through the phones in their homes, the apps they use and the content they are shown. Yet children from underserved communities rarely get the chance to understand how it works, let alone question it," says Susan Vaidyan, Head of Education MuSo. The programme introduces students from Classes 5 to 10 to foundational AI concepts, machine learning, prompt engineering, digital literacy, coding and responsible technology use. Rather than beginning with technical explanations, the sessions use familiar examples and hands-on activities. In one activity, students use a teachable machine to train a machine-learning model to recognise different objects or images. They experiment with the data being fed into the system, and then do something unexpected: they deliberately train it incorrectly to see what happens. When the model begins producing inaccurate results, the children grasp an important truth about AI: its outputs depend on the information it learns from. The programme also introduces students to AI-generated creativity, prompt-based exercises and community problem-solving challenges, allowing them to explore how the technology can be applied to everyday situations. Microsoft's involvement brings technology platforms, learning resources and expertise in responsible AI to the programme. The programme introduces children to responsible AI use, including online privacy, misinformation, bias and cyber safety. "An inclusive AI economy cannot begin at college or the workplace; it has to begin in the classroom," says Kishore Kumar Thangavelu, CSR Lead, Microsoft Corporation India Private Limited. Through Microsoft 365, students learn to create email accounts, organise their work using OneDrive, write documents in Word and use Excel to organise information. They also explore Copilot to improve sentences, summarise information and help with everyday tasks. Minecraft Education and MakeCode introduce coding through play. Students programme a virtual agent to chop trees, build walls and construct structures using instructions, loops and conditional statements. The programme also uses Minecraft's CyberSafe world to introduce online safety through games and practical challenges. That matters: ASER 2023 found that nearly half of rural young people on social media didn't know basic safety features, such as blocking or reporting a profile. But the learning isn't limited to how these tools work. Children are also encouraged to question the technology, recognise its limits and consider when it should or shouldn't be used. AI Explorers began as a two-hour introductory workshop. But the team soon realised that children needed more time to move beyond demonstrations and engage with the concepts themselves. "It's important for children to not just use AI tools but to question their outputs and understand their limitations," says Susan. The 10-hour programme, spread across three days, gives children the time to do just that. They begin by exploring how AI and machine learning work, including the exercise where they deliberately train a model with incorrect information. On the second day, they explore agentic AI through block coding and a game that shows how AI agents observe their surroundings and make decisions. The final day focuses on responsible AI, covering privacy, transparency and bias, with examples such as deepfakes, phishing and voice assistants that struggle with different accents. Coding activities through Minecraft Education help students understand instructions, loops and conditional statements while learning through play. For Susan, the aim is to move children beyond watching demonstrations to experimenting, asking questions and recognising that a machine's answers are not always right. "They stopped watching and started doing: trying things, getting wrong results and working out why," she says. Their questions began changing too, from what AI could do to how it arrived at an answer, and when its outputs should be questioned. What changes when children get access? Over the course of a year, AI Explorers reached 9,087 children through its foundational workshops. Another 313 students spent more time with the subject through the 10-hour immersive pilot. The programme travelled across six Maharashtra districts (Mumbai, Mumbai Suburban, Thane, Raigad, Ahilyanagar and Pune), reaching children through 36 government and aided schools and 17 NGO and community partners. There was also an effort to ensure girls were part of this learning experience. Of the 7,398 student records collected, 54% were girls. That matters in a country where, ASER 2023 found, rural boys were more than twice as likely as girls to own a smartphone, and half the boys surveyed had an email ID, compared with under 30% of girls. But what did the children take away from these sessions? Between July 2025 and June 2026, AI Explorers reached 9,087 children through foundational workshops across six districts of Maharashtra. The assessments offer some clues. In the foundational workshops, 81% of the students assessed showed greater interest in AI, while 61% showed an improvement in AI literacy. Among the 126 students assessed in the immersive pilot, 80% demonstrated an understanding of AI and machine learning. Around 75% showed awareness of coding and cyber safety, while the same proportion had set up an email ID and accessed Microsoft 365, in some cases for the first time. For some children, the change was also visible in how they began to look at technology. At a Marathi-medium school in Mumbai, a group of girls initially felt that technology and AI were too difficult for them. But as they experimented with AI games and prompt engineering, they began creating AI-generated content, discussing ethical questions and using digital tools to explore sustainability challenges. What had once seemed out of reach had become something they could try, question and create with. From first steps to future dreams The Raigad student's journey offers a glimpse of what this access can make possible. At the start of the immersive programme, using a touchpad and typing basic commands were challenges. By the end, the student had independently navigated several digital tools, created an email account and taken part in coding activities. For Meera, it was a fun, experience-oriented way of learning, where she learnt about AI in depth through games and interactive activities. For children with limited access to computers, the programme offers an opportunity to explore technology, build digital skills and imagine new possibilities. "What I found interesting was that we were not just learning about technology, but also understanding how to use it safely and think about things like online privacy, fake information and bias," she adds. As Susan puts it, success is not simply about children learning to use AI tools. It is about seeing them experiment, doubt what a machine tells them and ask questions of their own. As AI becomes part of more aspects of everyday life, the ability to question it may prove just as important as knowing how to use it. And that is a lesson these children are beginning to learn early. All images courtesy of Museum of Solutions team

Their analysis of 51 studies could transform how scientists evaluate anti-aging treatments, although whether these biological changes actually extend life remains uncertain.

Η σκληρή δουλειά του οδήγησε σε μια ασυνήθιστη καινοτομία…
items.descriptionOriginal: Every year, tonnes of paddy stubble are set on fire across Punjab, adding to the air pollution choking North India. But what if this farm waste could become something useful? For eight years, Gurdaspur-based innovator Parminder Singh experimented with paddy waste in his garage, even when people mocked his idea. His hard work led to an unusual innovation: drop-down ceiling tiles made using paddy stubble. Designed to provide heat and cold insulation, these tiles are also waterproof and fire-resistant. Through his startup, Agro Stubble Management, Parminder hopes to give farmers a reason to earn from crop residue instead of burning it. His vision is to establish production plants across Punjab, where discarded stubble can become a valuable raw material. It’s an idea that could turn agricultural waste into a resource, create livelihood opportunities and offer another way to tackle stubble burning. #StubbleBurning #Punjab #SustainableInnovation #ClimateAction #AgriTech

items.descriptionOriginal: For 560 children at New Life School in Dharavi, Mumbai, the future of their education depends on one question: will their school continue to exist where it stands today? The preschool has been educating children in the neighbourhood for four decades. Yet, throughout its 40-year history, it has never owned the land on which it operates. Now, as Dharavi undergoes redevelopment, securing that land has become central to ensuring the school's future. An effort to help the institution do so has brought together an unlikely group: a 19-year-old college student, his friends and a community determined to preserve access to education for the neighbourhood's children. Taking on a fundraising campaign of this scale meant Daniel had to understand several areas beyond his college curriculum, including corporate social responsibility (CSR) funding, institutional philanthropy and campaign strategy. Daniel Gupta, a third-year advertising and media student at Mumbai University, is leading the effort through an initiative called Dharavi Rising. After raising Rs 22 lakh against an initial target of Rs 20 lakh for the school's expansion, the team has now set its sights on a much larger goal: Rs 1.5 crore to help the school secure its land and continue serving children in the neighbourhood. For Daniel, the initiative is about more than keeping a school open. It is also an attempt to change how people see Dharavi, a neighbourhood often discussed through the lens of overcrowding, poverty and redevelopment, rather than through the lives, aspirations and institutions of the people who call it home. And he is learning to take on this challenge while still attending college, without any prior fundraising experience or an established professional network. Building a movement around a school Daniel's connection with New Life School began through a friend whose parents run the institution. Learning about the school's four-decade-long journey also brought him face to face with a pressing question: how could an institution that had served generations of children secure a future for the next ones? "People are often surprised when they learn that this school has been running for 40 years without owning its land. We want more people to know that it exists and understand why securing its future matters," Daniel says. What began as an effort to support the school gradually took shape as Dharavi Rising, an initiative that brings together young people and the wider community to address the institution's long-standing challenges. For the teachers, the campaign offers an opportunity to draw attention to a school that has continued to serve children despite the uncertainty surrounding its future. "We wholeheartedly support Daniel's mission to secure the future of our school in Dharavi. We want to do everything we can to ensure that the children's education continues without disruption," say teachers Kelsi Rani Raja and D. Packia Hincy. For the teachers, the campaign offers an opportunity to draw attention to a school that has continued to serve children despite the uncertainty surrounding its future. Their support also reflects a practical concern for families who depend on accessible schooling. The team wants to preserve an institution that parents can afford, rather than see its future compromised by the changes taking place around it. From Rs 20 lakh to Rs 1.5 crore When Daniel and his college friends began working on Dharavi Rising in November 2025, the idea was to find creative ways for young people to contribute to a cause. Daniel was just 19 when he took on the responsibility of building the initiative. With no previous experience in fundraising or social-impact work , he had to learn how to approach potential donors, understand funding mechanisms and communicate the school's needs. The team's first fundraising effort set a target of Rs 20 lakh for the school's expansion. They eventually raised Rs 22 lakh, marking an important milestone for a student-led initiative. However, the initial achievement was only a starting point. The larger challenge of securing the land on which the school stands remained. View this post on Instagram A post shared by New Life School | Dharavi Rising (@new_life_school_dharavi) This prompted the team to launch Dharavi Rising 1.5, with a fundraising target of Rs 1.5 crore to help secure the school's future. The new campaign takes on a more ambitious, long-term challenge: ensuring that an institution that has educated generations of children can continue to do so. Learning to navigate an unfamiliar challenge Taking on a fundraising campaign of this scale meant Daniel had to understand several areas beyond his college curriculum, including corporate social responsibility (CSR) funding, institutional philanthropy and campaign strategy. "I had absolutely no prior experience in any of this, so I needed guidance. I realised there would genuinely be no better tool than ChatGPT," he says. Daniel had been using the AI tool even before starting Dharavi Rising. Like many students, he initially turned to it for help with college presentations and assignments. But as the initiative took shape, his questions became more specific. How does CSR funding work? What policies should he understand? How could he explain the initiative to potential supporters? What would a fundraising campaign need to communicate to people who knew little about the school? ChatGPT became one of the tools he used to work through these questions. "I used it to explore naming and branding ideas, work on campaign strategy , understand broad fundraising and CSR concepts, and develop outreach material. I also used it to identify website requirements and organise my thinking about how to present Dharavi Rising to prospective donors," he tells The Better India . The tool helped him break down an unfamiliar and complex task into smaller, more manageable steps. He also used AI-generated text in donor communications. View this post on Instagram A post shared by New Life School | Dharavi Rising (@new_life_school_dharavi) Daniel estimates that ChatGPT saves him two to three hours a day, helping him balance college with the demands of organising the campaign and communicating with potential donors. However, he recognises that AI cannot replace the judgement and effort required to run an initiative of this nature. He says he rejects suggestions that do not align with Dharavi Rising's objectives and is careful about the information he shares with the tool. He also acknowledges that he has not followed a systematic process to independently verify all the guidance generated by ChatGPT. Ultimately, the campaign continues to depend on people: the school staff who understand its needs, the families whose children attend it, the friends supporting the initiative and the donors willing to contribute. Keeping education within reach For New Life School's teachers, the central concern remains the children. The campaign is not simply about raising money for a building or an expansion. It is about helping secure the future of an educational institution that has remained accessible to families in the neighbourhood for four decades. The challenge now is to build on the team's initial achievement and reach enough people to support the school's longer-term needs. The challenge now is to build on that initial achievement and reach enough people to support the school's longer-term needs. For Daniel, the effort also carries a larger purpose: changing perceptions of Dharavi and highlighting the aspirations, initiatives and community institutions that exist within the neighbourhood. "My work with Dharavi Rising began with a desire to change perceptions of a neighbourhood. It has since developed into a concrete effort to help protect one of its educational institutions . Yes, AI has helped me navigate some of that unfamiliar territory, but the purpose of all our work remains rooted in the school and the children it serves," Daniel says, pointing at the colourful artwork-laden boards in the classroom where he was sitting during a conversation with The Better India . For the 560 children who attend New Life School, the goal is simple: to ensure that a school that has been part of their neighbourhood for decades can continue to be part of their future. This Children's Day, those who wish to support Daniel's efforts to secure the future of New Life School and its 560 children can contribute by visiting dharavirising.com and making a donation.

items.description: Η Peggy Scott (την οποία υποδύεται η Denée Benton) πέρασε μεγάλο μέρος της Χρυσής Εποχής για να ανακαλύψει τι είδους συγγραφέας θέλει να γίνει. items.descriptionOriginal: Peggy Scott (played by Denée Benton) has spent much of The Gilded Age figuring out what kind of writer she wants to be. As a Black woman in the early 1900s …the journey hasn’t been an easy one. When a white newspaper offers to publish her work, Peggy discovers that the editor wants her to use a pen name and change her Black protagonist to a white character. This prompts Peggy to write for a Black newspaper instead. Now in Season 4 , that question has become even more important as her literary career takes off and she prepares to marry Dr. William Kirkland (played by Jordan Donica). Her ambitions have put her at odds with people who have their own ideas about what her future should look like. This storyline might be fictional, but the world Peggy was navigating was very real Erica Armstrong Dunbar , the show’s historical consultant and co-executive producer, has explained that Peggy is a composite character inspired by several Black women of the era who were creating professional opportunities for themselves, including journalists Ida B. Wells and Gertrude Bustill Mossell, as well as novelist Julia C. Collins. Mossell is a particularly fascinating person to discover. Gertrude Mossell’s writing ambitions also took her into the Black press Born in Philadelphia in 1855, Mossell came from a prominent Black family with a strong tradition of education and civic involvement. Though her mother died when she was very young, her father encouraged Mossell and her sister to read. By the time she was a teenager, she was already writing. Her commencement speech on “influence,” arguably her first work of note, was published in the Christian Recorder after she graduated. As an adult, Mossell worked as a teacher before becoming a journalist in the early 1870s. She eventually wrote for numerous Black newspapers and periodicals, as well as publications serving predominantly white audiences. Then, in 1885, she took on a new role at the New York Freeman , a Black-owned weekly newspaper published in New York City from 1884 to 1887. Founded and edited by journalist and activist T. Thomas Fortune, the paper covered politics, education, civil rights, and other issues affecting Black Americans. It also gave Black writers a place to address their communities directly and shape the conversation around their lives and ambitions. Mossell became the writer behind “Our Woman’s Department,” a column devoted to the interests of Black women, including education, women’s rights, and the challenges facing Black girls and women. We can still read some of what Mossell wrote. In one surviving column , she explained that the department would focus on the “success, progress or needs” of Black women. She encouraged readers to engage with debates about women’s rights and education and invited them to contribute material that could benefit other women. Like Peggy, Mossell wasn’t simply trying to find a place to publish her work. She was helping create a space where Black women’s experiences and accomplishments could be discussed on their own terms. Mossell continued that work beyond her newspaper columns In 1894, she published The Work of the Afro-American Woman , a book documenting the accomplishments of Black women in areas including literature, education, suffrage, temperance, and abolition. She was also active outside journalism. After marrying physician Nathaniel F. Mossell, she helped raise $30,000 for the Frederick Douglass Memorial Hospital and Training School in Philadelphia. She also organized a local branch of the National Afro-American Council. The Gilded Age creators drew on several women when creating the resilient and ambitious Peggy, but Mossell, in particular, shows why Peggy’s ambitions were completely historically plausible. The post Peggy Scott’s writing career on ‘The Gilded Age’ echoes a Black journalist who made her own rules appeared first on Upworthy .

items.description: Η νόσος Lafora είναι μια σπάνια γενετική πάθηση που συνήθως επηρεάζει παιδιά και εφήβους, προκαλώντας συχνές κρίσεις και σταδιακή απώλεια της γνωστικής λειτουργίας. items.descriptionOriginal: Lafora disease is a rare genetic condition that typically affects kids and adolescents, causing frequent seizures and the gradual loss of cognitive function. There is no cure, so the focus for many parents inevitably turns to quality of life. That’s something Detroit mom Azeza Kasham was struggling to maintain for her 17-year-old son, Gigi Breadiy, earlier this year. He was diagnosed in 2019, just days after his older brother died of the disease. Kasham’s husband has his own health problems and isn’t able to work, and the couple has two younger boys as well, so she took on multiple jobs to pay off medical debt. Breadiy uses a wheelchair, and the family home wasn’t fully accessible, so caring for him was becoming increasingly difficult. She’d tried fundraising on social media, but still felt like she was drowning. A stranger she connected with online would be her rescue buoy. Josh Liljenquist is a Minnesota content creator with over 23 million followers. Many of his videos fall into the somewhat controversial random-acts-of-kindness genre, but the 28-year-old’s main focus is rallying tangible support for people in need. After learning about Breadiy, he posted footage of himself meeting mother and son in February. Less than two months later, a GoFundMe he launched for them had raised nearly $600,000. “It’s just completely changed my life, you know?” Kasham shared during a recent phone call with Nice News. “It’s enabled me to give Gigi everything he needs, but that’s not all [Josh] did. And that isn’t even the most important thing. He restored my faith in humanity.” In the nearly seven months since meeting, Liljenquist and Kasham have become extremely close. “She’s literally like my second mom,” he said, adding: “She keeps saying that I changed her life, but I think she changed my life more than I changed hers.” His own mother also speaks to her often, and even flew out to Michigan to spend time with the family. The women connected so strongly because they both know what it’s like to care for a sick child, and the financial toll it can take. For the first six years of Liljenquist’s life, he was in and out of the hospital. He has a genetic disorder called alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency as well as eosinophilic esophagitis, a chronic inflammatory disease of the esophagus. That background has led him to direct more energy into helping families experiencing similar situations. “I want other parents to not have to deal with the same thing that my parents dealt with,” he said. But his fundraising has benefited people in all sorts of circumstances: a man in need of a new roof, a couple facing homelessness, a woman hoping to open a permanent pay-what-you-can cafe. For Kasham, the support from Liljenquist’s felt like God had answered her prayers. He, too, felt a divine hand in their meeting. The fact that they belong to different religions was a moot point. “She kept asking me, ‘Well, you know, you’re a Christian person. I’m Muslim. Does that matter?’ And I’m like, ‘Oh my gosh, no, not at all,’” he recounted. “That’s the first thing she would ask me. And I said, ‘Why would that matter?’” Before the GoFundMe, Kasham had to bathe Breadiy in the garage because the shower wasn’t accessible. Now, the family has paid down debt and made upgrades to their home, including a roll-in shower, that allow him dignity and privacy. “He has his good days. He has his bad days,” she said, noting that his seizures have worsened in recent months. “But one thing he has that puts the biggest smile on his face is he has his own space.” You can donate to Lafora disease research through Chelsea’s Hope .

Άλλες φορές, όχι τόσο. κοινωνικός επιστήμονας…
items.descriptionOriginal: Chemistry doesn’t have to be romantic. You can have friendly chemistry and professional chemistry. Of course, romantic chemistry is always great, too. It’s often believed to be one of those things that two people either have or don’t. There’s no way to define it or force it. Sometimes, you just hit it off. Other times, not so much. Social scientists, however, might disagree with that notion. A team at Dartmouth College has been hard at work analyzing thousands of conversations to define the indefinable: what makes for a good conversation? Analyzing thousands of conversations reveals conversational patterns Psychologists at Dartmouth College were not content with the idea that a good conversation is something that’s “difficult to define, but we know it when we see it.” So they set out to find a way to measure what makes a conversation enjoyable. They’re not the first to study good conversations. Previous research has shown that people with high similarity in the words they use and the topics they talk about score higher on romantic interest, group cohesion, and other metrics. But the authors of this study astutely pointed out that most existing research treats these attributes as an overall average—for example, for how much of the conversation were the participants aligned? Instead, they argue that similarity is a “dynamic signal.” Conversations have a give-and-take. There will be places where people agree, where they’re similar, and where they diverge. That was the data the team really wanted to dig into. After studying thousands of conversations between random strangers, friends, podcast hosts, and even speed-dating encounters, a few patterns emerged and were published in the journal Science Advances . Borrowing terms from signal processing , they described conversations that bounce all over the place quickly with no rhythm or pattern as “white noise.” “Red noise” came up when “partners are closely aligned; they remain aligned for long stretches, continuing to repeat, elaborate, or restate the same ideas. When they diverge, they remain apart, with limited reconnection.” Pink noise conversations, or the ‘Goldilocks zone’ If white noise was too chaotic and red noise was too boring, then it was a pattern called “pink noise” that was just right. Hence, the researchers called it the “Goldilocks zone.” Pink noise happens when conversation partners slip in and out of agreement and similarity at a comfortable pace. They can enjoy some common ground for a while before someone introduces something new, something that might cause them to diverge. But they find their way back to common ground and similarity in due time. It’s not overly rigid and boring, nor too random and chaotic. It’s just right . When pink noise levels were high, conversation partners rated enjoyment, connection, and engagement highly. To a lesser degree, they were even more memorable. What’s fascinating about the research is that whether a conversation featured white noise, red noise, or pink noise had nothing to do with how similar two people were overall. It was a study of the conversation’s pacing and rhythm: how often and how quickly they aligned and diverged throughout. The findings held whether people were strangers or old friends. The researchers even found that measuring pink noise in speed dating encounters could predict how likely participants were to want to see each other again. How pink noise can improve chemistry The full study on pink noise in semantic spaces is quite complex, full of rigorous data analysis and scientific concepts. But that doesn’t mean it does not apply to our real-life interactions. First, it’s a good reminder that conversational rhythm is everything. Even if you have a lot of common interests with someone, moving through them too fast or chaotically can make the conversation less enjoyable. Similarly, staying in the comfort zone of agreement for too long is a snooze. Try to find the Goldilocks zone. Productive tension in a conversation is good. People on the red noise scale had a lot in common, but didn’t explore those similarities in an engaging, memorable way. Segueing the conversation into new territory, perhaps with a “That reminds me of…” is a pro move, especially when you’re not sure the other person can relate. Exploring the dissimilarities and then finding your way back to common ground is a big part of the chemistry recipe. Chemistry can improve with practice . The study found that podcast co-hosts dramatically increased their pink noise levels over their first 50 episodes. The more you get to know someone, the better you understand how to find that perfect rhythm. The exciting new study proves that good conversation, chemistry, or whatever we want to call it, can not only be defined, but also measured, predicted, and even improved over time. But great conversations are still a two-player game, and you can’t do it all on your own. Meeting someone who really gets it, and gets you, is still an exciting find. The post Scientists studied thousands of conversations and found the repeatable pattern behind ‘chemistry’ appeared first on Upworthy .

items.description: Η ηθοποιός Goldie Hawn, 80, είναι παθιασμένη με την ψυχική υγεία και είναι ανοιχτή για τις δικές της μάχες με την κατάθλιψη και το άγχος για δεκαετίες. Το 2003, ίδρυσε την MindUP, μια πρόληψη…
items.descriptionOriginal: Actress Goldie Hawn , 80, is passionate about mental health and has been open about her own struggles with depression and anxiety for decades. Hawn’s mental health challenges began in her 20s when she was new to fame. She sought help and has continued to encourage others to do so by openly sharing her story. In 2003, she founded MindUP , a preventive mental health program to support students, educators, and their families. In a recent interview on The Jennifer Hudson Show , Hawn shared an easy trick she often uses to boost her happiness. Goldie Hawn’s happiness trick Hawn also shared her happiness trick in an exclusive interview with PEOPLE . “I smile at everybody,” she told the publication. “I’m on the street and I have a smile on my face. And you do receive back because people actually return that.” She went on to explain that acknowledging others and connecting with them is more than “an act of kindness—it’s a state of mind.” One place where she looks to acknowledge people is the elevator in her apartment. “You’re in an elevator: ‘How are you today?’ ‘Oh, I’m feeling pretty good.’ ‘Oh, that’s good. I’m happy to hear that,'” she told PEOPLE . “I do that when I’m in New York in my elevator in the apartment. And people are so sweet. And then when they get in the elevator again, ‘Oh, I got to see you again!'” In another interview on Khloe Kardashian’s podcast, Khloe in Wonderland , Hawn added that making herself smile is an instant happiness booster. “If you are sad, but you make yourself smile—I don’t know, sometimes I walk down the street, and I kind of have a half-smile on my face—it changes your brain completely,” she explained. “Your brain thinks you’re happier…it shows you how connected our body is [to] our brain.” View this post on Instagram Goldie Hawn’s depression battle During a 2021 interview with Good Morning Britain , Hawn explained more about her struggles with depression and anxiety. “When I was young, I became depressed. I was 21, and I was rising to success,” she said. “I was very depressed, and I had a lot of these issues where I couldn’t even go outside in public.” In a 2024 interview on the Making Space with Hoda Kotb podcast, she added that her anxiety also came with panic attacks after she landed a role on her first television sitcom called Good Morning World in 1967. “They said they wrote a part in for me, and I called home and I said, ‘Mom, you’re not going to believe this,'” Hawn shared. “And then I became anxious, and I had little panic attacks, and then I realized that every time I’d go into a restaurant or a place, I’d get dizzy, and I would want to go home.” Although she had never struggled with happiness before (she noted that her childhood was “joyful”), things changed. “I didn’t know what happened to my joy. I mean, I lost my—I tried to fake my smile. I’ll never forget that. It’s the scariest thing that has ever happened to me,” she explained. How Hawn treated her depression and anxiety To help her cope, Hawn sought professional help from a psychologist. “I went to a doctor, and I spent nine years with him,” she noted on Making Space with Hoda Kotb . “Why? Because I was learning about myself. I was learning about how to forgive, and I was learning, as I grew extremely successful, how to be able to manage other people’s perception of me because they didn’t know me.” Hawn continues to make it her mission to be honest about her own mental health struggles to help others. “We can’t live in the dark and wonder what’s going on with me. We have to know that people do experience this,” she said. “And it’s really important to acknowledge it. Because only until you acknowledge it can you fix it.” The post Goldie Hawn says this simple happiness habit helps keep her depression at bay appeared first on Upworthy .

Moore expertly impersonated not one, not two, but 19 of the 21 soloists from the original. Justin J. Moore recreated 19 voices from ‘We Are the World ‘ We’re talking male and female voices, from Michael Jackson and Bruce Springsteen to Tina Turner and Diana Ross. In fact, the impersonation that got the most compliments was Moore’s rendition of Cyndi Lauper. Produced by Quincy Jones and written by Michael Jackson and Lionel Richie, “ We Are the World ” brought together some of the biggest voices in American music at the time. Each soloist gets only a short featured passage, but those snippets are so distinctive that listeners can often identify the singer almost instantly. In other words, the song is practically a vocal-impression obstacle course. Here’s the full lineup Moore covered: Lionel Richie Stevie Wonder Paul Simon Kenny Rogers James Ingram Tina Turner Billy Joel Michael Jackson Diana Ross Dionne Warwick Willie Nelson Al Jarreau Bruce Springsteen Kenny Loggins Steve Perry Daryl Hall Huey Lewis Cyndi Lauper Kim Carnes The only original soloists missing were Bob Dylan and Ray Charles. Lauper may have been one of the trickier voices in the lineup to reproduce. Her 1980s sound combines a bright, piercing quality with expressive vibrato and playful, almost cartoonish inflections. She’s also a master mimicker herself. As a child, she practiced by imitating characters from Broadway albums like My Fair Lady and West Side Story , shifting her pitch to develop unusual tonal flexibility and control. How Justin J. Moore creates his singer impressions Moore grew up learning the fundamentals of singing from his Juilliard-trained, opera-singing parents . That classical foundation taught him to pay close attention to the mechanics of singing, giving him a strong foundation for understanding what makes one voice sound different from another. He later studied a wide range of singing styles, including rock and pop, giving him an even bigger palette of sounds and techniques to draw from. Now, he teaches those skills through courses on vocal impressions, breaking down the techniques that make a singer’s voice recognizable. In one YouTube video, Moore breaks down how he impersonates singers like Adam Levine . For that impression, he explains that Levine keeps his voice toward the back of his throat while using a relatively wide-open mouth for vowels. Ed Sheeran , conversely, puts the sound farther forward and keeps the mouth relatively small when producing vowel sounds. That makes it clear that a convincing vocal impression involves much more than simply changing your pitch. Moore pays attention to where a singer places the sound, how open the mouth is, the shape of the vowels, and the physical habits that accompany a particular vocal style. Those small changes can make two singers with similar ranges sound completely different. Moore imagines famous singers performing other hit songs He also has videos that are just as educational and entertaining, where he imagines different artists singing other iconic songs. For instance, there’s Radiohead’s “ Creep ,” sung by Michael Bublé, and Green Day’s “ Boulevard of Broken Dreams ,” sung by Brendon Urie of Panic! At the Disco. What’s fascinating about watching these videos isn’t just Moore’s singing ability. It’s how thoroughly he seems to analyze what makes each singer sound like themselves, then recreate those details in his own voice. And that’s certainly part of what makes the “We Are the World” performance so much fun to watch. It’s a pretty remarkable demonstration of just how much goes into a great vocal impression. The post From Cyndi Lauper to Michael Jackson, talented singer impersonates nearly ‘We Are the World’ artist appeared first on Upworthy .
