items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Top Phoenix Wholesale Cabinet Suppliers Compared by Price and Material Quality and Sustainability Reading Time: 5 minutes Top Phoenix Wholesale Cabinet Suppliers Compared by Price and Material Quality and Sustainability Contractors and remodelers working in Phoenix face the same problem: too many cabinet suppliers, too little transparency on what “wholesale pricing” actually means. This guide breaks down the top Phoenix wholesale cabinet suppliers compared by price and material quality so buyers can pick a source that fits their project volume, timeline, and budget without guessing. Finding quality wholesale cabinets in Phoenix without overpaying Phoenix’s construction market runs fast. Builders and flippers need cabinets in days, not weeks, and the difference between a supplier with real inventory and one that drop-ships on a six-week lead time shows up hard when a project stalls. The five suppliers below represent the range of options available, from local custom shops to national manufacturers, evaluated on product quality, service model, and fit for trade buyers. 1. Highland Cabinetry Best for: Builders, contractors, remodelers, and investors buying at volume Location: 3011 E Broadway Rd, Phoenix, AZ 85040; also serves Mesa, Chandler, Scottsdale, Glendale, and surrounding cities Products: Shaker, Euro, and Nano style all-wood cabinets; soft-close doors and drawers; dovetail construction throughout Standout: 20,000-plus kitchens in stock restocked bi-weekly; tiered pricing delivers 10% to 20% savings as volume increases Highland Cabinetry launched in 2018 specifically to serve trade professionals – builders, general contractors, handymen, and restoration companies – who need quality RTA cabinets without retail markups or long delays. Contractors sourcing wholesale cabinets in Phoenix from HCI get manufacturer-direct pricing, dedicated account management, and included 3D design renderings that speed up quoting. Delivery options cover job site drop, client delivery, and warehouse pickup. The tiered pricing model rewards repeat buyers, so per-unit cost drops as project volume grows, a real advantage for anyone running multiple flips or builds at once. 2. Premium Wholesale Cabinets Best for: Homeowners and trade clients seeking full-service design and installation in the Phoenix metro Location: Serves Chandler, Gilbert, Glendale, Mesa, Paradise Valley, Peoria, Queen Creek, Scottsdale, and Tempe Products: Custom kitchen and bath cabinets; also covers offices, wet bars, pantries, closets, and outdoor kitchens Standout: Over 100 years of combined design experience across staff; full consultation, hardware selection, countertops, and lighting available Premium Wholesale Cabinets is locally owned and has run operations across the Phoenix area for more than a decade. Their model leans full-service: clients work with an in-house design team – Eric Skinner leads ownership, backed by designers and installation specialists – moving from concept through install under one roof. Highlighted projects include the Dove Valley Kitchen Remodel, Harris Kitchen & Bar, and Brown New Build Scottsdale. Reviews consistently mention responsive communication and a team that listens before making any recommendations. It’s a stronger fit for clients who want guidance through the whole process rather than buyers looking to pull from existing stock. 3. Hardware Resources Best for: Custom cabinet makers, OEMs, and dealers sourcing hardware and functional components at scale Location: Headquartered in Bossier City, Louisiana; distributes nationally Products: Decorative and functional hardware, dovetail drawer boxes, vanities, cabinet hinges, drawer slides, organizers, LED lighting, sinks, and linear moulding Standout: 140 patents filed; part of Dimora Brands, operating across cabinet hardware, door hardware, faucets, and accessories Hardware Resources has been in business since 1990 and employs around 201 people. It doesn’t sell finished cabinets. The company’s focus is the components and hardware that cabinet makers and dealers build around, so it fills a different need than full-cabinet suppliers. Trade buyers who fabricate their own boxes, or who need a consistent hardware supplier across multiple projects, will find the product catalog deep. Acquired by Harbour Group in 2010, it now operates under the Dimora Brands umbrella, which spans several related product categories. 4. Decore-ative Specialties Best for: Cabinetmakers and industry professionals sourcing custom doors, drawer fronts, and RTA components in volume Location: Monrovia, CA headquarters; manufacturing in Irwindale, CA; Elk Grove, CA; and Monroe, NC Products: RTA cabinets, doors, drawer fronts, drawer boxes, moldings, accessories, finishing, and hardware in wood, plywood, 3D laminate, and melamine Standout: Founded 1965; ranked 68th on the FDMC 300 list of top North American wood products producers; fast ordering software Decore-ative Specialties has manufactured cabinet components since 1965 and employs between 501 and 1,000 people across three production facilities. Their ordering platform lets cabinetmakers spec and order ready-to-assemble frameless components with a six-working-day ship window, faster than most made-to-order competitors. The company holds U.S. Green Building Council membership and won a WMIA Wooden Globe Award for Innovator of the Year in 2016 for a CNC sander shaper capable of producing 500 doors per day. Shipping from California adds lead time for Phoenix-area buyers, but the component depth and production scale make it worth considering for larger orders. 5. Premium Wholesale Cabinets of Arizona Best for: Phoenix metro homeowners and contractors who want custom cabinetry with financing options Location: Serves Phoenix metro including Chandler, Gilbert, Mesa, Scottsdale, Tempe, Glendale, Peoria, and Queen Creek Products: Custom kitchen and bath cabinets, closets, wet bars, outdoor kitchens, pantries, and offices; countertops and hardware included Standout: Featured in Phoenix Home & Garden and LUX Magazine; financing available; over 100 years of combined team design experience Premium Wholesale Cabinets of Arizona is locally owned and operated, with a decade-plus track record in the Phoenix market. The team – owner Eric Skinner, designers Michael and Brianna, and installation specialists Ralph and Billy – takes projects from design consultation through final install. Case studies on their site include the Mountain Residence and Harris Kitchen & Bar builds. The financing option sets this company apart from most wholesale suppliers, making it accessible to homeowners who aren’t paying fully out of pocket. Coverage across nine Phoenix-area cities means most metro projects fall within their service footprint. What separates cheap from quality in wholesale cabinet suppliers Price alone doesn’t tell the full story when comparing Phoenix wholesale cabinet suppliers by price and material quality. The construction matters more than the finish. All-wood boxes with dovetail joinery and soft-close hardware hold up through years of daily use; particleboard carcasses with stapled corners don’t, regardless of how good the door looks. Lead time is the second variable most buyers underweight. It matters. A supplier quoting an attractive per-unit price on a six-week lead can cost more in carrying costs and delayed closeouts than a slightly pricier source with stock already on the shelf. Phoenix’s build pace is fast, and inventory availability is a real differentiator. And the service model matters. Trade buyers running multiple projects benefit from dedicated account management and volume pricing, both of which reduce administrative overhead across the board. Full-service shops suit homeowners who need design help and one point of contact. Knowing which model fits the buyer’s workflow before committing to a supplier saves friction later. Sustainability and material choices in wholesale cabinets Sustainability is becoming an increasingly important consideration for contractors, builders, and homeowners comparing wholesale cabinet suppliers in Phoenix. Beyond appearance and price, buyers should consider where cabinet materials come from, how they are manufactured, and how long the finished products are expected to last. Cabinets made with durable materials can reduce the need for premature replacements, helping minimize material waste over time. Material selection plays a major role in a cabinet’s environmental impact. Solid wood, responsibly sourced plywood, and composite materials with low formaldehyde emissions are worth considering. Buyers can also ask suppliers whether their products meet recognized environmental standards, such as FSC certification for responsibly sourced wood or GREENGUARD certification for low chemical emissions. These credentials provide additional insight into material sourcing and indoor air quality. For trade buyers managing multiple renovation or construction projects , durability is another important part of sustainable sourcing. Features such as dovetail drawer construction, soft-close hardware, and sturdy cabinet boxes can extend product lifespan and reduce replacement needs. Choosing suppliers that maintain consistent inventory and offer reliable delivery can also help limit unnecessary transportation and project-related waste. When evaluating wholesale cabinet suppliers, contractors should look beyond claims of being eco-friendly and ask for specific information about material composition, manufacturing practices, certifications, and product durability. A supplier offering a combination of responsible material choices and long-lasting construction can provide better long-term value while supporting more sustainable building practices. Bottom Line The top Phoenix wholesale cabinet suppliers compared by price and material quality serve meaningfully different buyers. Volume-focused contractors benefit most from sources with real inventory, tiered pricing, and fast turnaround. Custom shops and full-service providers fit homeowners or smaller projects where design support and installation coordination matter more than unit cost. Hardware and component specialists like Hardware Resources and Decore-ative Specialties serve fabricators rather than end buyers. Match the supplier model to the project type, and pricing usually works itself out. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Algae Could Be Nature’s Secret to Energy Efficient Solar Panels Reading Time: 4 minutes How Algae Could Be Nature’s Secret to Energy Efficient Solar Panels With global temperatures hitting record highs, and energy demand continuing to increase, the need for cleaner, more renewable power generation has never been more urgent. Investment in solar was greater than all other power generation technologies combined. But despite this high level of investment, solar power still faces challenges in real world applications. The most notable are efficiency and stability issues, especially in low light conditions. While commercial silicon solar panels convert roughly 15-20% of the sunlight they are exposed to, and recent record-breaking perovskite research having led to energy efficiencies surpassing the 30%-mark, nature has spent billions of years perfecting a far superior alternative. Algae, Natures 95% Efficiency Secret When we think of solar power, we usually think of traditional silicon-based panels baking upon suburban rooftops, yet some of the most groundbreaking advancements are happening at an intersection between materials science and biology. Researchers are looking towards nature, specifically algae, to unlock the future of clean energy. Microalgae and cyanobacteria have evolved over billions of years to become the planet’s most efficient solar harvesters, these photosynthetic organisms can process 95% of the sunlight they absorb even in low-light, underwater, or filtered light environments. Researchers are now looking toward these organisms and asking, “Could they hold answers to how solar panels can be more efficient?” Photosynthesis is an important chemical reaction in which plants, algae, and certain bacteria convert solar energy into chemical energy, that is then used by the living cells. Researchers are using this framework to study bio-photovoltaics (BPVs), devices that harvest electrical currents directly from the photosynthetic activity of living microorganisms. Microalgae, namely cyanobacteria and red algae, use a unique geometric protein arrangement, their surface is made from a mass of light harvesting antenna called phycobilisomes in a way that mimics a funnel. This outward-facing geometry vastly increases the cell’s surface area for light absorption. A major cause of energy loss in standard solar photovoltaics is photon scattering, in algae’s case the geometric rods catch photons from multiple angles and funnel them inward toward a single, central reaction center. It is important to note that compared to the land environment, which typical solar panels would be located, light intensity decreases underwater and becomes unstable as it is refracted or absorbed by the water. Yet cyanobacteria and red algae can live in water as deep as 100m because they have evolved sophisticated light harvesting antennae allowing them to harvest a much more diverse range of wavelengths, most notably short-wave light (blue-green light). Additionally, some freshwater alga can absorb far-red light, typically out of the optimal range for chlorophyll to absorb, by rearranging chlorophyll molecules into larger clusters within its photosynthetic antenna. Decoding Nature with Spectroscopy Researchers use benchtop spectrofluorometers to run highly sensitive fluorescence extraction and emission measurements. Image Gemini Spectroscopy is an invaluable technique used to study the interaction between radiative energy and matter, or in this case how light of varying wavelengths interacts with algae. To translate the characteristics of algae into scalable technology, researchers must first precisely map how these organisms handle photons. This requires analyzing the organisms’ internal pigment-protein complexes for a range of metrics: Light Absorption – The process in which light is absorbed by matter and converted into energy. Energy Transfer – The process by which energy is passed between one ion to another ion, vital to the development of efficient luminescent materials. Fluorescence Emissions – The process where a substance absorbs light or other electromagnetic radiation and immediately re-emits it as light of a longer wavelength. To achieve this level of precision, modern research laboratories rely on advanced spectroscopic equipment. Researchers use benchtop spectrofluorometers to run highly sensitive fluorescence extraction and emission measurements. Fluorescence Emission Spectra: Researchers shine a fixed wavelength of light into the algal culture to capture the exact fingerprint of the re-emitted light. This reveals how energy is distributed across different pigment groups (i.e. Chlorophylls and Phycobiliproteins). Fluorescence Extraction Spectra: Researchers can pinpoint exactly which specific colors of light are most effective at driving energy transfer within the organism. This is achieved by sweeping across a broad spectrum of light wavelengths and measuring resulting emission at a target wavelength. How Can Algae Impact the Future of Solar? The long-term vision of this research stretches far beyond boosting power metrics. Algae are part of a paradigm shift in renewable energy by serving as the blueprint and living engines for next-generation “Bio-Solar Cells,” also known as biophotovoltaics (BPVs). Bio-solar cells leverage living, self-repairing photosynthetic microorganisms like microalgae and cyanobacteria to convert sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide directly into electrical current. Traditional silicon-based photovoltaic panels require resource-intensive, toxic manufacturing which relies heavily on rare earth metals, and when they reach the end of their lifespans, recycling them creates a large electronic waste challenge. In comparison, BPV solar units offer a circular alternative with potential future iterations that could function as disposable, compostable solar elements. BPV power output is currently low (around 0.345 mW/m², which is much lower than standard silicon panels), making them unviable for whole-home power, though suitable for low-voltage sensors or trickling light. Another avenue sees specialized algae being integrated into traditional solar panels, not as a living organism but by using diatom shells. Diatoms are a unicellular phytoplankton that naturally build porous, glass-like silica shells to aid in the capturing of light during photosynthesis, even in murky water. Researchers have found that when these shells are applied as an antireflective coating or integrated into the panel’s encapsulant layer, their nano structures trap and scatter visible light effectively, which has been found to boost silicon solar panel efficiency by at least 4%. The use of diatom shells has also led to reduced panel degradation and extended panel lifespans as the material naturally blocks UV light. UV exposure degrades materials and reduces performance over time, which is unfortunate for devices that, by design, are exposed to it consistently. While scalability and long-term performance remain as the biggest challenges for energy efficient solar panels. By using precision spectroscopic research to take a closer look at our natural world and using spectroscopy tools to uncover its “secrets”, researchers are proving that the greenest future for solar energy might come from the very planet we are trying to protect, in one of nature oldest organisms. The post How Algae Could Be Nature’s Secret to Energy Efficient Solar Panels appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News What to Look for in a Long-Term RV Campground: Examining Sustainability, Facilities and More Reading Time: 4 minutes What to Look for in a Long-Term RV Campground: Examining Sustainability, Facilities and More Choosing a long-term recreational vehicle (RV) campground brings everyday comfort and environmental care onto the same checklist. Over several weeks or months, you’ll want suitable hookups and a site that makes settling in straightforward. Recycling and water conservation deserve attention, too. The right base should suit your daily routine while giving you practical ways to camp responsibly at an affordable rate. Look for Flat Sites and Flexible RV Hookups Knowing what to look for in a long-term RV campground starts with your vehicle’s size and the room you’ll need to maneuver. Flat, wide sites should provide enough clearance to enter and leave comfortably. Ask about dimensions and whether a pull-through or back-in layout suits your setup. An RV-friendly description may still leave you with questions, so give the campground your vehicle’s measurements when discussing available site types. Full hookups provide water and sewer connections with electrical service. Confirm that the available electrical supply matches your RV, and clarify whether wastewater disposal is via a site connection or a shared dump station. You’ll also want to know where the bathrooms and laundry facilities sit relative to the RV camping area. Ask which holding-tank products the campground’s wastewater system accepts. The Environmental Protection Agency warns that some deodorizer chemicals can contaminate groundwater if dumped improperly , while formaldehyde-containing products can disrupt septic treatment. Its guidance identifies biodegradable enzyme- and citrus-based alternatives. Follow the product’s dosage instructions and the campground’s disposal procedures. Check the Campground’s Sustainability Efforts Recycling facilities and clear conservation guidance provide practical details for evaluation. Your own habits also shape how you use those shared resources. 1. Conservation and Site Upkeep Practices Clearly labeled recycling containers are a useful starting point, although you’ll want to ask what happens after collection. Find out which materials the campground accepts and where guests should take them. Recycling ranked as the most important sustainable practice to campers in the 2025 Camping and Outdoor Hospitality Report, with 53% of respondents selecting it. Water conservation and wildlife conservation each received 45%, while roughly one in five campers valued electric vehicle charging stations. Those findings can help you choose questions that match your plans. A campground should be able to explain how guests report leaking taps and follow its wildlife guidance. If you travel with an electric vehicle, confirm that a suitable charging station will be available during your visit. 2. Low-Impact Camping Habits Leave No Trace campground guidelines recommend using durable surfaces , including established trails and paved paths, to reach shared facilities. Leave No Trace also advises keeping trash out of fire rings and collecting overlooked belongings before departure. During your stay, keep equipment within your site boundaries so neighboring campers and shared paths have their own space. Leave bathrooms and other communal areas ready for the next person. Before you leave, make one final walk around your site to pick up any trash and forgotten tent stakes. Compare Long-Term Rates and Overall Value Monthly or seasonal pricing may offer better value than paying nightly. Request a quote for your specific dates, including any minimum-stay requirement, before comparing campgrounds. Your quote should show whether the rate covers water and sewer service, as well as electricity. Laundry or visitor charges may need a separate line in your comparison. Ask which facilities will operate during your visit, especially if you’re planning a winter stay. Confirm availability for the whole reservation, including any dates when services change. A useful comparison connects the price to your routine. If laundry access matters every week, establish its cost and availability while reviewing the rate. The same principle applies to optional activities. Give the facilities you expect to use more weight than extras you’re unlikely to try. RVing also has a substantial economic footprint. The Bureau of Economic Analysis puts its 2024 contribution at $27.5 billion , using current-dollar value added. RVing ranked second among conventional outdoor recreation activities nationally and first in nine states. That figure measures industry activity, while your campground quote gives you the information to assess your own costs. Consider Top Long-Term RV Campground Providers These providers offer starting points for an extended stay. Check availability and environmental practices at the individual campground you’re considering. 1. Kampgrounds of America KOA provides the largest system of independently owned and operated campgrounds. With over 500 locations across North America, KOA offers a broad range of options for an extended stay. Level sites and full-hookup options complement clean bathrooms and consistent service standards. Select campgrounds offer KampK9® dog parks, while knowledgeable staff can help you discuss extended-stay availability and rates. Key Features Full hookups Extended stay options Pet-friendly sites 2. Equity LifeStyle Properties Equity LifeStyle Properties operates RV resorts and campgrounds through Thousand Trails and Encore. Both brands offer longer-stay options, with full-hookup RV sites available through Encore. The portfolio includes lakeside and coastal settings, as well as inland destinations, offering varied surroundings to consider. Its properties also host activities and events, which may appeal if you’d like opportunities to meet fellow campers. Key Features Extended stays Varied destinations Organized activities 3. Sun Outdoors If you prefer a resort-style base, Sun Outdoors offers seasonal and annual stay options. Amenities vary by property, with pools and organized events among the possibilities. Check how the resort’s operating season aligns with its agreement length, since the months you can use the site may differ. That distinction matters when choosing between an occasional getaway base and a longer, continuous visit. Key Features Seasonal stays Resort amenities Organized events Frequently Asked Questions Site suitability and environmental practices deserve attention alongside the full cost of your stay. Q: What should I look for in a long-term RV campground? A: Prioritize level ground with enough clearance for your vehicle and utility connections that match your setup. Confirm wastewater disposal arrangements, then check where you’ll find bathrooms and laundry facilities. Q: How can you tell if an RV campground prioritizes sustainability? A: Clearly explained recycling and water conservation practices provide specific measures for evaluation. Ask how those systems work during your visit and what guidance the campground provides for protecting wildlife. Q: Do long-term RV rates offer better value than nightly rates? A: Monthly or seasonal rates may offer better value, depending on your dates and the services included. Evaluate the full quote, including any additional charges and the facilities available during your stay. Find the Right Long-Term RV Home Base for You A comfortable extended stay starts with a campground that fits your vehicle and makes daily routines manageable. Clear conservation practices give you ways to care for the place while you’re there. With your dates and priorities in hand, contact the providers that interest you. Their campground-specific details can help you choose a base that suits your budget and aligns with your environmental values. items.descriptionOriginal: Episode Description: Los Angeles tried to ban oil drilling once before, in 2022, and the oil companies won in court. This time, neighbors who had spent more than a decade living beside the wells came back with new state law on their side, and LA became the first major US city to end oil extraction for good. Arielle and Karissa also cover a record night of governor firsts, electric ferries that lift themselves out of the water, a tutoring program born in a Zimbabwe refugee camp, and a dermatologist-approved case for skipping the occasional shower. Support TWEENS on GlobalGiving: https://www.globalgiving.org/projects/transformative-education-for-refugees-in-zimbabwe/ If you have questions, comments, feedback, suggestions, or just want to say hi, send a message to: podcast@optimistdaily.com . Want to be part of the Optimism Movement? Become an Emissary . Subscribe to our FREE Daily/Weekly Newsletter and follow us on Instagram , X , and Blue Sky . The Optimist Daily is a project of the World Business Academy. Donate link: https://www.optimistdaily.com/donate-to-support-the-optimist-daily/?lsc=41ef528d Theme and all original music by Marvin Lanes Transcript: Karissa: Hello everyone, I’m Karissa Arielle: I’m Arielle Karissa: And welcome back to The Optimist Daily’s weekly roundup Arielle: Yes. What an eventful time that’s been in the States. Uh, how are you feeling, Karissa? Karissa: Yeah. An eventful week, I would say. Yeah. Um, I am feeling pretty optimistic. I know last week’s podcast episode we didn’t talk about the midterms results, but there were a lot of great election turnouts from last week that we’ll talk a little bit about in the podcast, and I feel just very hopeful. Arielle: Yeah, definitely a week full of optimism, and it’s been big news also here on the other side of the pond. So we try to keep it not so politically charged with The Optimist Daily, because there’s already so much tension when it comes to politics, and we are really trying to unite people over solutions. But that being said, a lot of our solutions do have to do with, uh, human rights and equal representation, and a lot of things that do align with, uh, the changes that could potentially be coming based on these midterms. And maybe I’ll just leave it at that. Karissa: Yeah, exactly. I mean, it takes all of us to make a difference, to make a change, and we’re more alike than we are different, and I think that kind of has prevailed in these US elections. One of my friends made a great TikTok that was just talking about how if you have American nationality, you have such a great tool to be able to vote for not only our country, but we influence so many things around the world. So it was good to see a lot of people turn out for these elections, and I’m just feeling optimistic about it. We’ll talk about that more in just a moment. But before we get to that, we want to remind you that all these solutions are available in our free daily and weekly newsletter. Arielle: You can also follow us on socials. We are @optimistdaily on everything except for X. There we are @OdeToOptimism, and we love it when you guys slide into our DMs or comment on our posts or share stories with friends and loved ones. Karissa: And of course, we want to welcome any comments, questions, or feedback on our social media channels if you want, or you can also email us at podcast@optimistdaily.com. Arielle: A huge thank you to anyone who participates and engages with us. Our Optimist community is what makes this work so meaningful and special, and we appreciate every single one of you. We especially appreciate our Emissaries who financially support The Optimist Daily and help keep this mission going forward. An Emissary is anyone who donates. It could just be a one-time donation or a regular monthly or annual donation. Every little bit helps. And this year we do have a little goal. We have already mentioned this to people who receive our newsletters. We would love to get 100 new Emissaries by the end of 2026. So we can start 2027 even stronger than we are right now. We have gotten to the halfway point, I think, Karissa. Is that correct? Karissa: Just about. So we really need this final push by the end of the year to get to our goal. This is definitely the time to give back in this giving season. And we’d really appreciate if you would help us out, if you haven’t already. And speaking of the giving season, the Local Changemaker Series is currently being published right now. And we’ll talk about this week’s Changemaker later on. We wanna, again, thank everybody who submitted a nomination for that. And it’s been such a great time giving back to The Optimist Daily community, and recognizing who makes you optimistic. Arielle: Can’t believe we only have two more features after this week, then it’s already Thanksgiving. Well, with all of that said and done, Karissa, did you want to lead us into this week’s solutions? Karissa: Yeah, I will take it from here, Arielle. 2026 midterms produced a record wave of historic governor firsts Karissa: The first solution we had this week, which we kinda were already talking about, is that “2026 midterms produced a record wave of historic governor firsts.” Last week, on November 3rd, election day, 10 states elected governors who were first. And the thing that makes this interesting is it crossed party lines completely. We’re talking a Republican first Black governor in Florida, a Democrat flipping Texas. The night didn’t tell just one story, it told 10 different ones. Just for the governors, but it told a lot of stories just across the board. One that stood out to me, and one that will definitely end up in the history books, is that Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia became the first Black woman ever elected governor of any US state. And in 200 years of gubernatorial elections, it had never happened. Her election was very inspirational. I believe her great-grandfather was a slave. We’ve made so much progress, so it’s still so closely… It’s not that far away, too, and we’re still— Arielle: Yeah, that past is not as far away as a lot of us like to think. Karissa: Yeah, exactly. Of course, Texas was the biggest upset of the night across the board, and that was very inspirational to see as well. Democrat Gina Hinojosa beat incumbent Greg Abbott, and it made her the first Latina governor and the first Democrat to win that race in over 30 years. It was just good to see so many different people be elected to these positions across the United States. And it just feels like we’re shaking things up a bit, and having some more accurate representation of what our country looks like. Dermatologists weigh in on the eat-your-skincare TikTok trend Karissa: Well, moving on to the next solution, we have “Dermatologists weigh in on the eat-your-skincare TikTok trend.” Before I go on, Arielle, have you heard about this trend? Arielle: I’ve seen little YouTube Shorts or my sisters will send me reels about, like, this special carrot salad that’s like you eating your retinol or something, ’cause I’m in my 30s now, so they’re just sending me all this stuff. But I, yeah, I wonder if it really does work. So this article definitely caught my attention. Karissa: If you’ve been on this eat-your-skincare side of TikTok or the internet, this is for you, but it’s also for anyone who’s been kind of skeptical about it. It turns out that dermatologists say it’s both real and over-hyped at the same time, but the nuance is actually pretty interesting. So the core thing is that food can fill the tank, but it can’t overfill it. So it means that eating more vitamin C doesn’t make your collagen-making work faster or anything. It just makes sure it’s not running low. And one aspect this article talked about is the eat your sunscreen angle of it all. It sounds kind of wild, but it actually has science behind it, which I did not know. Certain carotenoids and polyphenols have been studied for UV protection, but dermatologists are very clear that these are an extra layer and not a replacement for actual physical SPF. The foods that actually show up in dermatologists’ recommendations are ones that you would probably expect. It’s salmon, avocado, walnuts, eggs, dark chocolate. So this is kind of a vindicating solution if you’re already eating that way. It’s helping you out. It’s not gonna do a million things more for your skin, but it’ll definitely help you out. Arielle: Yeah. Okay, that’s kind of what I thought. I think food, in terms of skincare, will support the overall system, but there’s so many products. I try not to have too complicated of a skincare routine, ’cause I know that too many products is also not ideal for your skin. So if you can combine the serums, the moisturizers, the creams that work for you with a really good nutritious diet, then I think that’s gonna help you glow from the inside and the outside. Karissa: 100%. Took the words right out of my mouth. Electric ferries that fly above water are arriving in the US Karissa: The next solution is “Electric ferries that fly above water are arriving in the US.” We’ve talked about this a little bit before on The Optimist Daily. There’s these really cool electric ferries that fly. They’re kinda like skimming across the water a bit. And so the technology is that they use underwater wings to lift the hull out of the water, and that will cut the drag by 66%, makes it a lot faster, and it’s finally what makes long range electric boats practical. Over in Europe and Canada, I believe they’ve already been kinda using these for transportation. But San Francisco is about to spend half of a billion dollars converting their whole ferry fleet over to these electric ferries. The problem with electric boats has been that the drag has been bad, and so they haven’t been so quick. Water resists a vessel much more than air resists a car, so batteries couldn’t hold enough charge to make it very useful. Hydrofoils solve that by just getting the boat out of the water a bit. I’m excited to see these over in the US, and San Francisco is close to me, and though I don’t really use ferries when I’m visiting the cities, maybe I’ll have to check it out the next time I’m over. Fall activities for you and your dog: a trainer’s guide Karissa: Okay, well, this solution is another lifestyle one, and it’s “Fall activities for you and your dog: a trainer’s guide.” So this solution is a cute and fun one, but it’s essentially a permission slip to take your dog somewhere fun this fall, whether that’s the farmer’s market, pumpkin patches, corn mazes, hiking trails. We have tips from a dog trainer named Sassafras Patterdale who breaks down what to bring, what to watch for, and how to make these trips actually good for the dog and not just all about the photos. Arielle, I thought about you and Tink. Have you done anything autumn-like with her? Arielle: She’s usually off leash, and she loves sniffing around, so we do take her out on, I guess you can call them hikes or just, like, really long walks. I haven’t really taken her to farmer’s markets, which is one of the tips here. Tink is kind of… She doesn’t like kids. Karissa: So. Well, that could be a little— a little hard at the farmer’s market ’cause there usually tends to be a lot of families. And in this article, they’re kinda talking about taking your dog to the farmer’s market, aiming it at, like, younger dogs because it can be a really good training opportunity with all the people and the smells and foot traffic. So it’s kind of like a good place for younger dogs to just get more of that exposure and more practice for calm leash behavior, helping them get used to that. So maybe Tink is a little bit past that. Arielle: Yeah, she’s a bit too old for that, set in her ways. But your dog is also… Is your dog a senior dog? Karissa: Oh, yes, he is a very senior dog now, so he’s not really out on the leash in public anymore, unfortunately. But we used to take him to the farmer’s market, and I think we took him to some kind of, like, fall pumpkin patch thing at some point, and we definitely have a lot of good photos over the years of him with a cute pumpkin. So yeah, it’s just a good time of year to get your pup out there. One consistent thread and important reminder for all the activities that are mentioned in this article is to call ahead or research ahead to make sure dogs are allowed to be wherever you’re going if it’s somewhere, uh, out in public. Brazil releases the world’s first fossil fuel phaseout roadmap Karissa: “Brazil releases the world’s first fossil fuel phaseout roadmap.” This first global roadmap is all about phasing out coal, oil, and gas. It’s a voluntary roadmap, and it has no legal teeth, and it came out during COP30 last year, which notably ended without mentioning fossil fuels in the final text at all. The roadmap exists because Brazil decided to just do it anyways, and it’s being brought back up now that COP31 is happening as we speak. Just kind of jumping back to last year, what happened at COP30, Saudi Arabia and Russia killed the fossil fuel language, and Brazil’s response was to publish this independently and bring it into COP31 this year, which opened, uh, this week. The plan is a three-phase plan through 2033, and it explicitly says there’s no universal solution. Countries are supposed to tailor it to their own situation, which makes it harder to dismiss, but also harder to hold anyone to. Arielle: I think it is encouraging that countries are creating plans, or at least Brazil is creating a plan even though it’s not legally required of them. There’s no external motivation other than the fact that they want to help our environment survive uh, and thrive. And I think that shift from asking or requesting people to commit to the change to just giving them an example of how they can actually make the change is a good kind of reframe. Karissa: 100%. Prince Bashangezi turned personal loss into peer tutoring for refugee students Arielle: The next solution is a Local Changemakers feature. It’s titled “Prince Bashangezi turned personal loss into peer tutoring for refugee students.” This Local Changemaker story is really quite moving. Prince grew up at Tongogara Refugee Camp in Zimbabwe, a camp of more than 17,000 people near the Mozambique border, home to families displaced by conflict across Central and Eastern Africa. He lost his own family to war before ending up there, and he was 17 or 18-ish when COVID hit. While that was happening, he was trying to finish his A-Levels, and when schools closed, he and a small group of fellow students just started teaching the younger kids themselves, ’cause, of course, there was a lack of schooling during that time. And this eventually turned into a program called TWEENS, which stands for Together We Educationally Empower Non-privileged Students. He’s now at Pomona College in California, studying computer science and economics, and the program he built in that camp is actually still running, so it’s now been, uh, over half a decade. The Optimist who nominated Prince for the Local Changemaker series said, “Prince’s work is a reaction to his incredible loss,” and that he turned his personal tragedy into loving service for others. And that framing says everything about what TWEENS is. This peer model works in a refugee context in a way outside volunteers can’t really replicate. These tutors live in the camp. They went through the same disruptions. They understand what it means to build a future from inside a displaced population, so their credibility comes from proximity and not credentials. TWEENS has expanded to include an A-level program, a girls’ book club, and ongoing homework support alongside the original peer tutoring. If you’re interested in helping out, then the GlobalGiving campaign is still active, and I can put a link to where you can donate to this project, uh, in the show notes. This is a great story that Optimists can actually do something about right now, so if you feel compelled to learn more or to give, then I would highly recommend just checking out the article. The dermatologist guide to a skin-friendly shower routine Arielle: The next solution is another skin solution. It’s titled “The dermatologist guide to a skin-friendly shower routine.” Three dermatologists are out here saying that showering every day might be working against your skin. They’re not saying it in, like, a soft, “Well, maybe,” kind of way. They’re actually pretty direct about it. This piece breaks down who actually needs daily showers, who doesn’t, and what the signs are that you’ve overdone it, because that squeaky clean feeling after a hot shower, you might think, “Oh, yeah, I got everything. I’m, like, completely clean.” But that’s not necessarily a good sign. Karissa, are you a shower every day type of person? Karissa: I mean, I definitely am, and I do a lot of heated workouts where I’m sweating a lot, so I definitely need my daily shower, but I’m so intrigued of the argument against it. What about you, Arielle? Arielle: I used to be a shower every day when I was living under my mom’s, uh, watchful eye, and definitely whenever I live in a tropical place, that’s, like, multiple showers a day ’cause I’m sweating, and it’s, like, kind of grimy, and you get sand and everything everywhere. But now I have to say I don’t shower every single day. If I don’t work out that day, and I don’t really do anything strenuous, then chances are, I’m probably gonna skip the shower. Karissa: Yeah. Arielle: Okay, so this article makes a key distinction. Hygiene and skin health are not the same thing. So daily washing serves hygiene, but when you think about it, if you’re not super active, then only your underarms, your groin, your feet, and the skin folds that, like, trap a lot of, I guess, like, perspiration and stuff, that’s what needs soap every day. The rest of your body, you can usually skip. The signs that your skin is asking for a break are quite specific. So if your skin feels super tight after the shower or if you’re experiencing persistent nighttime itchiness or ashiness or flaking on your shins, that’s what a stripped skin barrier looks like. All the listeners out there, you guys should just check those things out and see if any of that applies to you. There’s something about age here as well, ’cause age actually changes the whole game when it comes to showering. Babies, like, they can’t be showered all the time. Their skin is too sensitive, so twice a week is good for babies, whereas teens, on the other hand, they’re going through a lot of hormonal fluctuations. They’re going through puberty. They need more showers, for sure. And then older adults often need less showers because the skin produces fewer surface oils over time, and you just have to kind of use your own judgment. Uh, this is not a one-size-fits-all solution. There are some key tips that I’m glazing over right now, but you can find everything in the article. After a decade of community pressure, LA bans oil drilling for good Arielle: The next solution is titled “After a decade of community pressure, LA bans oil drilling for good.” Los Angeles just became the first major US city to ban oil extraction entirely, and what makes this story different from most environmental news is the decade of community advocacy that actually got it done. This wasn’t a top-down policy decision. People who are actually living next to oil wells pushed for this for more than 10 years. The neighborhoods where these wells sit are working-class communities of color. Residents have been living with benzene and hydrogen sulfide and higher rates of respiratory illness for generations. Wendy Miranda, one of the lead advocates, has asthma, and so does her mother. The city actually tried this back in 2022, but they just passed an ordinance. Oil companies challenged it in court, and they won. So California then passed legislation giving local governments more power, and this vote is what came out the other side. Environmental justice has shifted from an advocacy framework to a legal one, and these days, communities have better tools than they did 10 years ago. And then I also noticed that in the article, the communities expressed that they’re not necessarily anti-oil. They’re anti-drilling next to our kids’ school. And this framing could resonate more broadly than just the pure climate messaging, so they’re also positioning themselves in a much more strategic way. This isn’t just an environmental issue. It’s a health issue, and it’s a human rights issue. Karissa: I’m glad to see this pass in LA because, yeah, I don’t think anyone should have to live right next to a oil drilling well. The next challenge is going to be removing these oil wells because I don’t think there’s, like, a great legal framework for holding oil companies accountable for either paying for that cleanup or removing them. They’ve had a couple of oil wells in the area that have just, like, sat there for years, and getting those out of the way is also the next step here. Why spiders show up in your home every fall, and what to do about it Arielle: The next solution is very seasonal. It’s titled “Why spiders show up in your home every fall, and what to do about it.” Karissa: Oh, I need this solution. I think I have, like, two spider bites on my ankles, so. Arielle: Oh, you have actual bites? I just have so many spiders, like up in the corners of my… Well, basically all the rooms in my house. So yeah, this article gets into it, and if you are like me and Karissa and you’ve been seeing more spiders lately, there’s a simple biological reason. Fall is mating season for spiders, and a lot of them are coming inside to find mates and somewhere quiet to lay their eggs. And the reassuring thing an entomologist from Oregon State said is that most of them are minding their own business. They’re also eating your gnats and all those other insects that might be bothering you in your home. I found it unexpected that of the 3,700 spider species in the United States, only 0.3% are dangerous to humans. The ones showing up in your house are almost certainly not in that category, thankfully. The entry points are pretty mundane. You could probably guess. Your worn garage door weather strip, cracks in your foundation, gaps around window frames are all entry points for spiders and other critters. And if your house already has like a lot of gnats or flies, then the spiders are just following the food. Karissa: Yeah. That makes sense. Arielle: The most effective seasonal fix is clearing wood piles or compost heaps and old boards from around the perimeter of your house because that’s where spiders can shelter before they come into your home. There’s fall decluttering content everywhere right now, and this article gives it a practical reason beyond just aesthetics. But there’s also a maybe just leave them kind of framing at the end of this article, and it’s part of a broader shift towards coexisting with nature rather than trying to eliminate it. Because the spiders are cold, they just wanna get cozy, they wanna find a mate. It’s cuffing season for them as well, I guess. I used to be super scared of spiders, but I think they’ve… I don’t know. We don’t have like really juicy-looking spiders here in the Netherlands. They’re all kind of like spindly, and they look really fragile. Ah. I don’t know, maybe in Northern California it’s a bit of a different story. Karissa: Yeah. They’re pretty small. Like, obviously you won’t ever want one around. I did see a pretty juicy one though the other day on the wall, and it was a little bit scary. But usually the ones that end up in my house here are not too bad. But yeah, I think there’s some kind of one that like bites, ’cause every once in a while I’ll just have like this giant, like welt from… That’s what I’ve heard, read. I never see the spider doing it, but yeah, my ankle currently has a bite, so it’s a little bit annoying, but it’s nothing like poisonous of course. I guess I’ll take this advice and this solution to let them coexist. How two Princeton graduates built the world’s first microplastics removal system Arielle: All right. The last solution that I’m going to be sharing with all you Optimists this week is titled “How two Princeton graduates built the world’s first microplastics removal system.” There is now a wastewater treatment plant in Atlantic City, New Jersey, that removes microplastics before they reach the ocean, and it’s the first one in the entire world. The two people who built the technology are architects who basically looked at how certain wetland plants trap microplastics naturally, and then scaled it up. There’s, again, no law that’s requiring this, but they just did it anyway. The design philosophy is explicitly about simplicity. The founders wanted something like an iPhone approach to a complex problem. Minimal material, low energy, but big results. It’s a pretty big problem, these microplastics. They’ve already turned up in human bloodstream, in brain tissue and other organs. And the Atlantic County plant manager said it pretty plainly, “We’re discharging to the ocean. If we’re not removing the plastic, we’re putting it back in.” And yeah, it’s just like the, the Brazil, uh, phase out fossil fuels roadmap. There’s no law that’s requiring this. It’s the municipality doing it because it’s the right thing to do, not because they have to. Karissa: Yeah. This is so awesome, and it’s very intriguing that it’s the first in the world to do this. I know we’ve written on The Optimist Daily about a lot of solutions that can filter out microplastics and being developed, but I guess we haven’t really seen them deployed so much. So this is a great, uh, article describing how this is actually being put into action now. And the fact that they don’t have to, they’re doing it to better their municipality is, uh, is great news. Arielle: All right. Well, those were all the solutions that we had to share with everyone this week. But as usual, we leave you off with a positive quote. Karissa: This week we have, “If they don’t give you a seat at the table, bring a folding chair.” And that’s from Shirley Chisholm. I really like this one, and I was inspired to add it just from all the great progress in the United States we saw in this past week of people getting a seat at the table. So I’m excited to see what those seats will produce. Arielle: Well, Karissa and I wish everyone a wonderful, restful weekend. Uh, we will be back next week with more solutions. But in the meantime, stay positive and optimistic. Karissa: Absolutely. Have a great weekend, everyone. Bye! The post Podcast Transcript November 13th, 2026— This midterm’s historic governor firsts, flying electric ferries, and eat-your-skincare first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.title: Το "Frozen" animator λανσάρει μια διαδραστική εφαρμογή εκμάθησης ASL και υπόσχεται να την κρατήσει δωρεάν για πάντα
items.titleOriginal: ‘Frozen’ animator launches an interactive ASL learning app and vows to keep it free forever
items.description: Ο Τζος Στάουμπ είχε μια μεγάλη καριέρα. Ο διάσημος animator και καλλιτέχνης οπτικών εφέ της Disney έχει δουλέψει σε μερικές από τις μεγαλύτερες επιτυχίες της σύγχρονης εποχής, όπως το Wreck-It Ralph, το Tangled και το εμβληματικό Frozen, το οποίο είναι περισσότερο φαινόμενο παρά απλή ταινία. Όμως, παρά τις διακρίσεις, ήταν έτοιμος για μια νέα πρόκληση. Πριν από μερικά χρόνια, ξεκίνησε την ανάπτυξη…
items.descriptionOriginal: Josh Staub has had quite a career. The renowned Disney animator and visual effects artist has worked on some of the biggest hits of the modern era, including Wreck-It Ralph , Tangled , and the iconic Frozen , which is more of a phenomenon than just a film. But despite the accolades, he was ready for a new challenge. A few years ago, he began developing a script for a new animated series , a project that would take him on an incredible and unexpected journey. New project sparks a deep connection with the Deaf community Staub began developing an idea for an animated series that would tackle big themes of family, empathy, and the ways we communicate with one another. There was just one complication: the animated family at the core of the series would include characters who are deaf. Staub knew that if he wanted to pursue this idea, called Small Talk , he couldn’t simply translate parts of his script into American Sign Language for the animation. As a hearing person, he needed to really learn much more about Deaf culture and the community behind it. He began learning ASL from a Deaf teacher, which he says is the absolute best way to learn. Staub took to the lessons immediately, writing in a LinkedIn post , “I began learning about Deaf culture and fell in love with the Deaf community, forging deep friendships.” The people he met as he forged friendships within the Deaf community became collaborators on the series, helping shape the animation, filmmaking, story, and art behind the show. But as Staub got further along on his journey, he began using ASL learning apps to supplement his in-person instruction. That’s when he saw another opportunity to take the world, characters, and message of Small Talk even further. An opportunity bigger than the series The Small Talk ASL app was born. “I want it to be very clear that learning from a Deaf ASL teacher is by far the best way to learn the language,” Staub told Upworthy . Apps are a useful supplement, but Staub found the existing ones had some frustrating limitations: most notably, they weren’t very engaging, typically featuring bland photos or short video loops of people signing with little zexpression. That’s where the lively design of one of Staub’s characters, Oscar, comes into play. In the app, Oscar isn’t your teacher. He’s your friend. Oscar is your new Deaf friend. Photo credit:: Jubilee Studios “[The app] helps hearing and Deaf of all ages learn the rich and expressive ASL language in an innovative and engaging way like only animation can,” the Small Talk website states. Because Oscar is fully animated as he signs and fingerspells, users can rotate him to view his signs from different angles, making it easier to see how his hands and fingers move. They can also adjust the playback speed, slowing it down as they learn or speeding it up to test their fluency and handshape recognition. Crucially, they can experience Oscar’s larger-than-life facial expressions (unsurprisingly reminiscent of Disney and Pixar characters), which are an essential part of communication in ASL. “Facial expressions are supremely important with ASL and that is where the whole ‘character’ or ‘friend’ part comes in. Pre-recorded videos of teachers tend to be pretty stern,” Staub said. “Deaf folks in general are extremely outgoing and ‘animated’ when they communicate, so why not express that in the character?” But perhaps the most important thing about the app is that it doesn’t cost a penny. And it never will. “It’s completely free, and because there should never be an obstacle to learning ASL, we’re committed to keeping it that way, forever,” Staub said. It’s all backed by a world-class team of Deaf, hard-of-hearing, and hearing animators, consultants, engineers, and producers. App doesn’t replace anyone or anything Staub doesn’t really view other ASL learning apps as competition. He sees Small Talk ASL as just another tool in the world, admittedly a pretty fun one, to help more people learn ASL and overcome barriers to human communication. “There are 48 million Deaf and hard-of-hearing people in America, yet the… community is, in many ways, an isolated community. There is a hidden barrier which impedes a hearing person and a deaf person from building deep relationships. ASL overcomes that barrier,” the website states. It adds that about 70% of parents of deaf children don’t learn ASL. Further research shows that parents are often discouraged from learning ASL because they’re told it will be difficult, and some are led to believe it will interfere with their child’s ability to learn spoken language, which isn’t true. An app like Small Talk ASL could help make it a little easier, and a little more fun, for anyone who wants to communicate with Deaf and hard-of-hearing people. Small Talk ASL is a fun tool to help more people communicate. Photo credit: Jubilee Studios Making a friend, not just a lesson Learning from an actual Deaf teacher is the best way to learn the language. Apps and videos can help. Small Talk ASL brings a special flavor to the table: a friendly character you’ll grow to love and free access forever. Anyone can download the app from the Apple App Store or the Microsoft Store right now. Instead of asking for payment, Staub asks just one thing: “For some of you, Oscar is your first Deaf friend. Don’t make him your last. Learn about Deaf culture. Seek opportunities to immerse yourself and communicate with the Deaf community. Make mistakes. Keep trying. The Deaf community is diverse and inviting and will embrace you as they have me. It might just change your life. It changed mine.” This article originally appeared in July. It has been updated. The post ‘Frozen’ animator launches an interactive ASL learning app and vows to keep it free forever appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Τέλος, κάποιος εξηγεί γιατί όλοι χρειάζονται υπότιτλους όταν παρακολουθούν τηλεόραση
items.titleOriginal: Finally, someone explains why everyone needs subtitles when watching TV
items.description: Φαίνεται ότι όλοι χρειάζονται υπότιτλους στις μέρες μας για να «ακούνε» την τηλεόραση. Αυτό είναι κάτι που έχει γίνει πιο συνηθισμένο την τελευταία δεκαετία και έχει κάνει τους ανθρώπους να αναρωτιούνται εάν η ακοή τους δεν πάει καλά ή αν οι ηθοποιοί έχουν τεμπελιάσει με την εκφώνηση . Μια δημοσκόπηση του AP-NORC του 2025 βρήκε ότι περίπου το ένα τρίτο των ενηλίκων στις ΗΠΑ παρακολουθούν πάντα ή συχνά…
items.descriptionOriginal: It seems everyone needs subtitles nowadays in order to “hear” the television. This is something that has become more common over the past decade, and it’s caused people to question whether their hearing is going bad or whether actors have gotten lazy with enunciation . A 2025 AP-NORC poll found about one-third of U.S. adults always or often watch with subtitles, and adults under 45 are especially likely to do so. So if you’ve been wondering if it’s just you who needs subtitles in order to watch the latest marathon-worthy show, worry no more. Vox video producer Edward Vega interviewed dialogue editor Austin Olivia Kendrick to get to the bottom of why we can’t seem to make out what the actors are saying anymore. It turns out it’s technology’s fault, and to get to how we got here, Vega and Kendrick took us back in time. Why modern mics actually made things worse They first explained that way back when movies were first moving from silent film to spoken dialogue, actors had to enunciate and project loudly while speaking directly into a large microphone. If they spoke and moved like actors do today , it would sound almost as if someone were giving a drive-by soliloquy while circling the block. You’d only hear every other sentence or two. But with today’s technology, microphones are so small they can be strapped just about anywhere on an actor. This allows the actor to move about the set freely and speak at a normal volume without worrying that their words won’t be picked up. “A lot of people will ask, ‘Why don’t you just turn the dialogue up?’ Like, ‘Just turn it up.’ And… if only it were that simple,” Kendrick said before explaining, “If you have your dialogue that’s going to be at the same volume as an explosion that immediately follows it, the explosion is not going to feel as big. You need that contrast in volume in order to give your ear a sense of scale.” So why does the music drown everything out? Sure, you may be thinking, well, that kinda explains it, but why do the music and other cinematic noises sound like they’re beating on your eardrum while the dialogue sounds like the actors are whispering every line? That doesn’t seem very balanced. There’s more to it, and again, it falls back on technology. In the video, they explain how our televisions are too thin to hold large speakers facing in the correct direction, and until this video, it didn’t dawn on me that the speakers on my television are indeed in the back. No wonder we can’t hear. The actors are quite literally talking to our walls. Here is a another video explaining steps to take to potentially remedy the problem of inconsistent-sounding dialog. Do subtitles actually help kids read? While it may be a confusing trend, there’s a reason for it, as Kendrick explains. And some experts, like the World Literacy Foundation note that watching television and movies with subtitles is especially beneficial for children. Research has suggested that putting on subtitles can help improve literacy for kids, and many actors support the practice. This is good news for those worried about the literacy crisis in America. If subtitles help us “hear,” then I’m all for them. This article originally appeared three years ago. It has been updated. The post Finally, someone explains why everyone needs subtitles when watching TV appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Κάτω ή πάνω; Υπάρχει πραγματικά ένας «σωστός» τρόπος να κρεμάσετε ένα ρολό χαρτιού υγείας.
items.titleOriginal: Under or over? There actually is a ‘right’ way to hang a toilet paper roll.
items.description: Οι άνθρωποι έχουν συζητήσει μεγάλα και μικρά πράγματα κατά τη διάρκεια χιλιετιών, από τη δημοκρατία μέχρι τον θηλασμό δημόσια και πόσο συχνά πρέπει να πλένουν τα σεντόνια τους. Αλλά ίσως η πιο ανόητη, αλλά και εκπληκτικά καυτή συζήτηση στο νοικοκυριό είναι αυτή κατά την οποία μαλώνουμε για το πώς να κρεμάσουμε το ρολό χαρτιού υγείας. Το ερώτημα «πάνω ή κάτω» έχει ταλαιπωρήσει τους γάμους…
items.descriptionOriginal: Humans have debated things large and small over the millennia, from democracy to breastfeeding in public to how often people ought to wash their sheets . But perhaps the most silly-yet-surprisingly heated household debate is the one in which we argue over which way to hang the toilet paper roll. The “over or under” question has plagued marriages and casual acquaintances alike for over 100 years, with both sides convinced they have the soundest reasoning for putting their toilet paper loose end over or loose end under. Some people feel so strongly about right vs. wrong TP hanging that they will even flip the roll over when they go to the bathroom in the homes of strangers. Contrary to popular belief, it’s not merely an inconsequential preference. According to health experts and the inventor of the modern toilet paper roll, there is actually a “correct” way to hang toilet paper. What is the correct way to hang a roll of toilet paper? First, let’s be clear about what we’re even talking about here with a visual. In the image below, left is “over” and right is “under.” Toilet paper rolls hanging. Photo credit: Elya/Wikimedia Commons So which one is the right way? According to health experts, “over” is the way to go. “One key to maintaining a hygienic washroom is minimizing contact between people and surfaces,” Dr. Christian Moro, associate professor of health sciences and medicine at Bond University on Australia’s Gold Coast, told the Australian Broadcasting Corporation . “Depending on the type of roll holder, [hanging the toilet paper ‘over’] often lowers the chance that a user will touch the wall behind when fishing for paper, leaving germs behind on that surface which can be spread to the next user.” Picture it: Grabbing the end of the toilet paper when it’s hung “over” means you only touch the part of the toilet paper you’re going to use. When it’s “under,” you sometimes have to fish for it or scrape your fingers on the wall in order to grab the loose end. In addition to whatever might be on people’s hands already, think about all the people who wipe twice, potentially transferring fresh fecal matter or other bacteria to the wall on the second pass, which then get picked up by other people who inadvertently touch that wall when trying to grab their TP. Theoretically, we all should have become better hand washers during the pandemic, scrubbing with soap for the full 20 seconds it takes to remove bacteria. But I wouldn’t be willing to bet on it. And touching any surface in a bathroom is pretty nasty, according to a study from the University of Colorado. As Inc. reported : “Using a high-tech genetic sequencing tool, researchers identified 19 groups of bacteria on the doors, floors, faucet handles, soap dispensers, and toilets of 12 public restrooms in Colorado: six men’s restrooms and six women’s restrooms. Many of the bacteria strains identified could be transmitted by touching contaminated surfaces.” Those germs can include bacteria like E. coli, a common source of food poisoning. If you’ve ever had a bout of food poisoning, I’m sure you’ll agree that a toilet paper roll hanging preference isn’t worth risking it. What the patent tells us But sanitary health concerns aren’t the only argument for the “over” camp. After all, an 1891 patent for the perforated toilet paper roll shows the TP in the “over” position. Thank you for the clarity right from the get-go, Mr. Wheeler. The toilet paper roll was patented by Seth Wheeler in 1891. Public Domain In Wheeler’s patent drawing, the perforated toilet paper hangs on a roll in the “over” position, though the patent text doesn’t say how the roll should be mounted. In the words of Wheeler’s September 1891 patent, the sheets of TP are “partially separated, having their points of attachment arranged in a novel manner, whereby each sheet will easily separate from the series as it is drawn from the roll, there being no litter occasioned, and any waste of paper is thereby prevented.” Now, before the “under” folks come running with their pitchforks, there are some understandable exceptions to the “over” rule. Namely: cats and kids. If you have a furry friend or a tiny toddler who likes to unroll the toilet paper roll, “over” makes it super fun for them, while “under” stops them in their tracks. For many people, cats and kids are the primary motivator of their TP hanging habits. That doesn’t change the fact that “over” is actually the “correct” way to hang toilet paper according to health science and the patent drawing, of course, but “under” is certainly preferable to having a pile of TP on the floor. Now go forth do that with information as you will, and try to make peace with your over vs. under rivals. This article originally appeared two years ago. It has been updated. The post Under or over? There actually is a ‘right’ way to hang a toilet paper roll. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Ο Αμερικανός παραγγέλνει κοτόπουλα τύπου Olive Garden στην Ιταλία και η ανταπόκριση του σερβιτόρου είναι τέλεια
items.titleOriginal: American orders Olive Garden-style chicken parm in Italy and the waiter’s response is perfect
items.description: Ένα από τα σπουδαία πράγματα για την Αμερική είναι ότι έχουμε μια σχετικά νέα κουλτούρα, τόσο πολλά από τα τρόφιμα που τρώμε προέρχονται από άλλες χώρες. Αυτό κάνει την Αμερική ένα εξαιρετικό μέρος για να δοκιμάσετε όλα τα διαφορετικά είδη φαγητού από όλο τον κόσμο. Ωστόσο, μας αρέσει επίσης να βάζουμε τη δική μας σφραγίδα σε συνδετήρες από όλο τον κόσμο που δίνουν το Ameri…
items.descriptionOriginal: One of the great things about America is that we have a relatively young culture, so many of the foods that we eat were brought over from other countries . That makes America a great place to try out all the different types of food from around the world. However, we also like to put our own stamp on staples from around the globe that give the American version its own unique flair. Some foods that we claim originated overseas were actually first made right here in the U.S. of A. For example, chimichangas, which can be found in many Mexican restaurants, most likely originated in the state of Arizona. Crab Rangoon, a popular “Chinese” dish, is believed to have been created in the San Francisco Bay area, and spaghetti and meatballs is largely an Italian-American creation. The video that broke the internet TikTok creator Gabby Donahue posted a video that’s the perfect example of how some ethnic foods get remixed once they become popular in the States. In a video with over 7 million views, her father shows a waiter in Italy a photo of chicken parmesan from Olive Garden so he can order it at the restaurant. The waiter’s reaction is an excellent example of someone trying to be polite while he cannot believe what he is seeing. “My Boston Irish father trying to order a Google image of the Olive Garden chicken parm in Italy ,” Donahue wrote in the text overlay. When the father showed the picture to the waiter, he seemed a bit confused about the image. “Only in the States,” he said. “It doesn’t exist in Italy.” The father couldn’t believe what he was hearing: “It doesn’t exist in Italy?” “I don’t know what it is… on the pasta?” the waiter said, trying to make sense of the chicken breast smothered in cheese and sauce. The waiter gave his final verdict while holding his chin: “No. That’s horrible.” “Horrible? Wow. Look at that. That doesn’t,” the father laughed. “That looks good… but,” the waiter shrugged off the father. “It does look good,” the father continued. “It tastes good. I’ll tell you what, I’m gonna mail you some. I’ll send it to you.” “Okay? Olive Garden chicken, I’m gonna search,” the waiter said, walking away from the table. The commenters had a field day analyzing the waiter’s body language. “‘No, that looks good’ while looking completely disgusted was the most Italian reaction ever,” one commenter wrote. “Bro remembered halfway through his disgust that he’s at work,” another added. So where did chicken parm actually come from? It’s not crazy that an American would think that chicken parmesan is an Italian dish; after all, it’s served in most Italian-American restaurants. However, according to Paesana , it was created in America by the Italian diaspora. “In the Old World, that’s Italy prior to the Italian diaspora (the large-scale emigration of Italians from Italy to America), proteins like chicken were not widely available,” according to an article on the site. “As such, the prototypical chicken parmigiana was actually made with breaded, fried slices of eggplant in place of chicken for a dish called melanzane alla Parmigiana.” Even though chicken parmesan didn’t originate in the old country, Pasquale Sciarappa , a popular Italian-born food influencer living in America, has no problem cooking the dish. “‘That’s not Italian!’ I hear this every time I share a dish like Chicken Parmigiana. And you know what? They’re right. It’s not something you’d traditionally find in Italy. But you know what else is true? It’s Italian-American. It was born in immigrant kitchens from people who left Italy, landed in the U.S., and made do with what they had. They took inspiration from dishes like melanzane alla parmigiana and recreated comfort from memory using what was available,” he wrote. Watch Pasquale make his chicken parmesan: America’s food is a beautiful remix It’s understandable that an American could go to Italy without knowing that something he’d had in Italian restaurants wasn’t actually from Italy. It’s understandable for an Italian server to balk at a photo of a dish served in an American restaurant that you’d find in a shopping mall. But we should all agree that one of the wonderful things about American culture is that it’s an amalgamation of different cultures stirred around in the same pot, and if that means we get a fresh variation on the burrito, a new way to eat Chinese crab, or a tasty piece of chicken where eggplant used to be, the more the better. This article originally appeared last year. It has been updated. The post American orders Olive Garden-style chicken parm in Italy and the waiter’s response is perfect appeared first on Upworthy .

items.titleOriginal: The IITian Who Quit Coding to Make Ramayana! 🔥

Αντί να συνεχίσει με μια συμβατική καριέρα λογισμικού, επέλεξε την αφήγηση και συνέχισε να δημιουργεί ταινίες που συνέδεαν το πνεύμα…
items.descriptionOriginal: He graduated from IIT Bombay, landed a software job and quit just four months later to follow his passion for filmmaking! 🎬 Meet Nitesh Tiwari, the filmmaker behind popular films like Dangal, Chhichhore and Chillar Party. Instead of continuing with a conventional software career, he chose storytelling and went on to create films that connected with audiences across India.
