items.title: Αυτό το 17-YO βοήθησε να μετατραπεί η αίθουσα αποθήκευσης ενός σχολείου της Bengaluru σε μια βιβλιοθήκη βιβλίων του 2000 για παιδιά
items.titleOriginal: This 17-YO Helped Turn a Bengaluru School’s Storage Room Into a 2000-Book Library for Children
items.description: Το πρωί του Σαββάτου σε ένα κρατικό σχολείο στην αποικία Mullur της Μπανγκαλόρ, η 17χρονη Asavari Agrawal μόλις και μετά βίας περνάει από την πύλη πριν την περικυκλώσουν τα παιδιά. Κάποιοι τρέχουν να την αγκαλιάσουν. Άλλοι τραβούν τα χέρια της, πρόθυμοι να της δείξουν κάτι ή να την τραβήξουν σε ένα παιχνίδι. Οι νεότεροι συχνά προσκολλώνται πάνω της, αρνούμενοι να την αφήσουν ακόμα και όταν προσπαθεί να ξεκινήσει…
items.descriptionOriginal: On a Saturday morning at a government school in Bengaluru's Mullur Colony, 17-year-old Asavari Agrawal barely gets through the gate before the children surround her. Some run up to hug her. Others tug at her hands, eager to show her something or pull her into a game. The younger ones often cling to her, refusing to let go even as she tries to begin the day's activities. By now, the scene is familiar. Asavari greets the teachers and children, gets everyone moving and settles into whatever the morning calls for. There may be table tennis, an art activity, a lesson, a fitness session or simply time spent talking and playing. "When she enters the gate, they run to her," says Victoria, headmistress of the school. "In the beginning they were shy. But because she came every week, they became comfortable very quickly." At 17, Asavari is balancing Class 12 , college applications, national-level table tennis, Bharatanatyam and Grade 8 piano. Yet for nearly five years, she has also made space for spending her weekends with children at government schools and residential homes across Bengaluru. For the children at Mullur Colony Government School, Saturday mornings mean games, activities and time with their favourite Didi. That commitment began when she was a child herself and eventually grew into Shape the Future, the youth-led initiative she founded at 13. Today, around 50 student volunteers are part of the wider network, reaching roughly 250 children. There have been sports sessions, health and eye camps, menstrual hygiene drives, book collections and learning activities. But when Asavari talks about what matters most, she does not begin with those numbers. "I think the idea of showing up is what matters most to my NGO," she says. "No matter how many drives or fundraisers or events that I hold, I feel like being there for the kids, emotionally and physically, matters the most." It started with playdates Asavari's connection with children from underserved communities began long before Shape the Future. When she was young, her mother began volunteering at Karuna Shreya hospice after experiencing several personal losses. Asavari would accompany her and, over time, also began visiting Thayi Mane, a government-recognised home for orphaned and destitute children. Back then, she did not think of herself as a volunteer. "I was really small when I started going there," she recalls. "Honestly, initially it was like playdates for me. It was so fun going there and playing with the kids." From table tennis and fitness sessions to art and learning activities, Asavari and her volunteers create opportunities for children to explore new interests. As she grew older, those visits began to look different. She started noticing the opportunities she had access to, from learning sports and dancing to playing the piano, and how different that access could be for the children she was meeting. In 2021, that realisation took a more concrete form. Asavari had started her own table tennis academy and decided to take the sport to the children she had been visiting. She brought tables, rackets, balls, shoes, clothes, jackets and fitness equipment and conducted a session for around 100 children. For many, table tennis was unfamiliar. "I think they were really excited to learn a new sport that they probably hadn't heard of yet," she says. The first session was not easy. Asavari was around the same age as many of the children and had to introduce a completely new sport to a large group. But some children took to it quickly, and the experience made her think about what else she could bring to them. Asavari believes that showing up consistently and building relationships with children matters more than organising one-off donation drives. A year later, in 2022, she started Shape the Future. What began with one sport slowly expanded into a broader effort to give children access to learning, play and experiences that might otherwise remain outside their everyday lives. What a Saturday looks like Today, a typical weekend begins with Asavari and her volunteers packing supplies for the day's session. Depending on the activity, that could mean sports equipment, stationery, educational material or art supplies. Around 10 to 15 volunteers may join her, although the group changes because they are all school students managing their own academic schedules. There is usually a warm-up, the main activity and plenty of time for games before everyone heads home. The session may last only a couple of hours, but it has become a regular part of Asavari's week. "I have a lot of exams and applications and personal work," she says. "But setting aside one or two hours every weekend doesn't do any harm. It's not like work to me. It's more of a hobby going there." With around 50 student volunteers, Shape the Future now reaches nearly 250 children across Bengaluru. At Mullur Colony, Victoria has seen that commitment first-hand. "Most Saturdays she comes herself. On some Saturdays when she cannot come, her team comes, but someone is always here every Saturday without fail," she says. That consistency has changed the relationship between Asavari and the children. "When she first came, they would just silently follow what she said," Victoria recalls. "Now they talk back, they argue, they pull her, they sit close to her. This closeness takes time. It comes only because she has been here every week." Aparna, in-charge and principal at Thayi Mane and Lakshya Residential School, has witnessed the same bond. "They know each one by name," she says. "They wait for her on Saturday. When she comes, they run to her." Why a missed Saturday matters to the children There are two kindergarten girls at Mullur Colony, Aarohi and Anjali, whom Asavari has grown particularly close to. When she arrives, they often run towards her and refuse to let go. "They keep calling me Didi, they keep calling me Amma," Asavari says. "We've built such a close connection with these kids that it just hurts me to not end up going there." For Asavari, the most meaningful part of volunteering is the trust she has built with children who now look forward to seeing her every Saturday. Then there is Sumit, a boy who recently lost both his parents. One day, he told Asavari, "You're the only family I have left now." For a teenager who is still learning how to understand grief, moments like this can be difficult to process. "I think I'm still too young to understand each and every kid's emotion," she says. "But I try." At Thayi Mane, Aparna remembers another moment. When Asavari had surgery on her appendix, she could not visit for several weeks. When she finally returned, a boy named Partha told her that one night his "heart pained" because he thought she might not come back. "She did not say anything. She just held him," Aparna recalls. These experiences have shaped Asavari's understanding of volunteering . She has seen people arrive for one-off activities, donate something, take photographs and leave. For children who have experienced people coming and going, that can make it difficult to trust that someone will stay. Sumit, who recently lost both his parents, found a sense of belonging in Asavari. "The best and worst part is getting attached to these kids," she says. The children have even told her that when she does not come, they worry she might leave like others have. "They don't look for money. They don't look for items," Asavari says. "They look for someone who isn't going to give up on them." For her, that means treating the children as equals rather than beneficiaries. "It's about not treating them like a project. Treating them as equals and constantly building that relationship." When the children asked for books The library at Mullur Colony grew out of these everyday conversations. Asavari would ask the children what they wanted to learn about, what they dreamed of becoming and what they wished they could read. Their answers revealed a simple gap: they wanted to explore beyond their school textbooks, but there were very few books available to them. So Asavari and her team began collecting them. Over nearly two years, five student volunteers took charge of the collection, reaching out to schools and communities and bringing in donated books. Slowly, the collection grew to more than 2,000. Asavari and her team transformed an unused room at the government school into a library, complete with bookshelves, furniture and reading material. The school also had a room that had essentially become a storage space. Turning it into a library meant redoing the flooring, repainting the walls, cleaning the room, adding shelves and furniture, and finally sorting and arranging the books. "It went from being an absolute rag of a room," Asavari says. "We had to uproot the entire flooring, repaint the walls, clean the entire room and then bring in the furniture and the books." For Victoria, who has watched the school change since Shape the Future first arrived in 2024, the library represents something the children simply did not have before. "Before this we had nothing. Only textbooks. No library, nothing like that," she says. "She collected more than two thousand books and arranged the room also with shelves and light. For our school this is a very big thing ." The idea has also been about understanding what individual children want to read rather than simply filling a room with books. At Thayi Mane, one girl wanted more advanced reading material, so Asavari sourced a set of 25 encyclopaedias specifically for her. "That kind of attention is rare," Aparna says. "The children feel seen when someone notices what they individually need." Preparing for the Saturdays she may miss Shape the Future has remained entirely bootstrapped. Asavari has funded its work through earnings from her Bharatanatyam Arangetram, table tennis prize money and even by selling her own piano and table tennis table. But she does not see those decisions as sacrifices. "I wouldn't call myself selfless," she says. "I think the kids needed it more than I did." If anything, the harder thing to give has been time. And now, time is precisely what Asavari is preparing to have less of. She is in Class 12 and hopes to study at university in the US or UK. For the first time since she began visiting these children regularly, she may soon be unable to walk through the school gates every Saturday. "I'm absolutely terrified as to how these kids are going to feel once I leave," she says. "When I'm in college, I'm not going to be able to come for months." So she is preparing Shape the Future to continue without her. Responsibilities have been divided among heads of fundraising, volunteering, social media and operations, while younger students are being given more responsibility. Asavari is deliberately preparing a team that can continue the work even when she is away. Her mother, who first introduced her to volunteering, remains part of that support system too. "This is not just Asavari's work," Aparna says. "Her mother has always been part of this. This is their family's commitment." Asavari describes what she hopes to build in a different way. "I think of it like generational wealth," she says. "You build it, you pass it on, you make sure it outlasts you." As she prepares to leave for university, Asavari is training younger volunteers to ensure Shape the Future continues even in her absence. What began as playdates now includes dozens of young volunteers, hundreds of children and a library built from thousands of donated books. Yet what Asavari values most cannot be measured in numbers. It is the familiarity of a Saturday morning, the children knowing she will walk through the gate, and the trust that has grown because she has kept returning. "I've just done it consistently," she says. "And I've grown it into something big. These little changes, being consistent with these little changes, is what matters most." Her advice to other young people is just as simple. "You don't need to build the world's biggest NGO. Start with 10 children, but stay." All images courtesy of Asavari Agrawal

items.descriptionOriginal: What if your biggest worry in old age is not who will look after you, but who will look after the person you love when you’re gone? This is the moving story behind Pyre, filmmaker Vinod Kapri’s award-winning film set in an almost-deserted Himalayan village. In 2018, Vinod met an elderly couple in Munsiyari, Uttarakhand, whose livelihood depended on their goats. The husband said their income helped him arrange for people to carry his ailing wife downhill for medical care. As long as he had his goats, he said, his wife would survive. But his biggest fear was who would care for her if he died first. His wife’s worry was just as moving: who would cook for him, since he didn’t know how? These simple yet profound answers stayed with Vinod for years, inspiring him to tell a story about love, ageing, loneliness and an elderly couple’s arduous wait for their estranged son. Starring first-time actors Padam Singh Kapri, a retired Army serviceman, and Heera Devi, Pyre was made with limited resources. With no big studio backing, Vinod exhausted his savings and even sold his car and a plot of land to finance the film. After winning 18 international awards, including multiple Best Film honours, Pyre finally made its way to Indian theatres on 30 October. Have you caught it on the big screen yet? #VinodKapri #PyreFilm #IndianCinema #IndependentCinema #Uttarakhand

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News A Year In, Networks for Nature is Reconnecting Cheshire’s Wild Spaces Reading Time: 3 minutes Chester Zoo’s Networks for Nature community project planted 14,000 trees and restored and created 13 ponds in its first year, putting it well on its way to its five-year goals. Networks for Nature started with a simple idea. Wildlife does better when habitats connect, and so do communities. One year in, about 8,700 people across northwest Cheshire, England, have put that idea to work. Chester Zoo launched the project with a £4.4 million grant from The National Lottery Heritage Fund. It covers about 60 square miles, from Ellesmere Port to Chester, and runs through 2028. The Westminster Foundation and individual supporters also help fund it. The project builds on the zoo’s earlier Nature Recovery Corridor. That effort improved more than 62 hectares for wildlife and engaged over 12,000 people. Connection is the core of the approach. Small, isolated habitat patches leave plants and animals stranded. Hedgerows, ponds, and green corridors help them move, feed, and breed across a wider area. Hannah Brooks leads the project as Chester Zoo’s Senior Community Participation and Engagement Manager. She says connectivity is how species grow and thrive. In her view, the project works the same way, relying on landowners, community groups, and individuals working together. Networks for Nature’s first-year numbers show that cooperation in action. Volunteers and partners planted 14,000 trees and created or restored 13 ponds. They also established or restored 1.6 kilometers of hedgerow. Those figures put the project well on track. Over the full five years, it aims for 20 ponds and nearly 3,000 meters of hedgerow. In year one, it reached about two-thirds of the pond target and more than half of the hedgerow goal. Woodland work added nearly 7 hectares of new or improved habitat, roughly the size of 10 soccer fields. Teams also removed 269 tonnes of invasive plants and animals from the water. These species crowd out native wildlife and can choke waterways. One cleanup stands out. The project cleared 500 cubic meters of illegally dumped rubbish from a single community green space. That is enough to fill about seven large shipping containers. Each site has its own focus. At Gowy Meadows Nature Reserve near Ellesmere Port, work has improved public access. In Lache, a neglected space called The Backies has reopened as an enhanced community green space. Along the Shropshire Union Canal, teams have cleared invasive species. The Canal and River Trust is also monitoring water quality there. Meanwhile, The Land Trust is creating a wetland at Countess of Chester Country Park. Getting people to nature matters as much as restoring it. The project built 1,090 meters of new pathways so residents can reach green spaces more easily. Cheshire West and Chester Council is also planting wildflower meadows and improving five public parks for wildlife. Local participants did much of the hands-on work, from planting and clearing to laying footpaths. Others joined bug hunts, bird box building, and garden makeovers that brought wildlife closer to home. Some participants have gone further and trained as Wildlife Champions. They learn practical skills to keep improving outdoor spaces in their own neighborhoods. Brooks sees this long-term local leadership as central to the project’s value. Young people have played a central role. In year one, 83 young people joined hedgehog awareness campaigns, built bird and bat boxes, and improved allotments. They also completed leadership skills courses, nearly reaching the project’s five-year goal of 90. Schools are the next big focus for Networks for Nature. The project aims to reach 4,500 students through a year-long program to improve school grounds for wildlife. Local pupils have already joined in through wildlife clubs. Through Networks for Nature, Sutton Green Primary pupils joined the City Nature Challenge, using tablets to log the plants and animals they found outdoors. Photo courtesy of Chester Zoo . The project also links nature with health. Through green social prescribing, doctors can refer patients to outdoor, nature-based activities instead of, or alongside, medicine. Western Avenue Medical Centre in Blacon and Great Sutton Medical Centre in Ellesmere Port take part. Research suggests that time in green spaces can boost mental and physical wellbeing. Restoring parks and ponds close to home makes that benefit easier for residents to reach. Helen Featherstone, Director, England, North at The National Lottery Heritage Fund, praised the project’s community-led approach. She says it shows how communities and conservation groups can protect natural heritage together for the long term. Year one has focused on completed work, such as planting trees and restoring ponds. The bigger test will be whether wildlife responds. Ongoing monitoring, including water quality checks on the canal, will help show those results over time. The first year shows what community involvement adds. Thousands of residents turned a funded plan into trees in the ground, cleaner green spaces, and new local leaders. With four years still to go, Networks for Nature is only beginning to grow. Schools, community groups, landowners, and volunteers can learn more on Chester Zoo’s Networks for Nature page. Opportunities to train and take part continue to expand. The post A Year In, Networks for Nature is Reconnecting Cheshire’s Wild Spaces appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Your height is one number. Your weight is another. Put them together and you get your BMI. But is that enough to understand your weight and health? Not by itself. BMI is a useful screening measure. But it doesn’t directly tell us how much of your weight is muscle or fat, or where that fat is stored. That is where your waist adds context, giving us a view of abdominal fat distribution that can be relevant to cardiometabolic risk. So should you trust your waist more than your BMI? Not really. They give different information, and neither is a diagnosis on its own. If they seem to tell different stories, don’t try to diagnose yourself. Bring both to a qualified doctor. Use them as a reason to have a conversation, not to judge yourself. Keep up balanced meals, regular movement, strength activity and good sleep. BMI and waist are starting points, not verdicts. Talk to a qualified doctor about your weight-management needs. This is general information, not a diagnosis or medical advice. #CountWhatMatters #BMI #WaistMeasurement #KnowYourNumbers #MetabolicHealth [BMI vs waist measurement, what does BMI tell you, is BMI enough, waist size and health risk, body composition India]

items.descriptionOriginal: Every winter, Delhi struggles with worsening air pollution . As smog settles over the city, efforts to clear the air raise an unusual possibility. What if it rained? Could artificial rain wash away pollutants and make the air easier to breathe? The idea gained attention after the United Arab Emirates (UAE) invested in cloud seeding, a technique that encourages existing clouds to produce rainfall. Research in the region has also highlighted how rain can reduce airborne dust and particulate matter. This raised hopes that the same technology could help Delhi tackle its pollution. In October 2025, the Delhi government partnered with the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Kanpur to conduct a cloud-seeding experiment. However, the operation failed to produce meaningful rainfall in the capital. So, why did a technique associated with improved air quality in Dubai fail in Delhi? The answer lies in differences in weather conditions, cloud formation, and the limitations of cloud seeding. What happened in Dubai? The UAE has invested in cloud seeding for decades to increase rainfall in a country that receives very little natural precipitation. Its programme primarily aims to improve water security and replenish groundwater. Every winter, Delhi struggles with worsening air pollution. Photograph: (Image generated by AI) Researchers have also examined whether rainfall could help reduce air pollution in the region. A study published in the journal Environmental Pollution examined atmospheric dust and particulate matter around Dubai and Abu Dhabi. It found that dust storms contributed to higher concentrations of suspended particles, while rainfall helped bring these levels down. A January 2021 report by The National highlighted these findings. When raindrops fall through the atmosphere, they collect suspended particles and carry them towards the ground. This process, known as wet deposition, helps remove some pollutants from the air. However, the research established the benefits of rainfall in reducing airborne dust. It did not conclusively prove that cloud seeding alone was responsible for improving Dubai's air quality. How does cloud seeding work? Cloud seeding does not create clouds or produce rain from a clear sky. It works by introducing tiny particles into existing clouds to encourage water droplets or ice crystals to grow. Depending on the cloud type and atmospheric conditions, scientists use materials such as silver iodide or salts, including sodium chloride and potassium chloride. These particles act as nuclei around which water droplets or ice crystals form . As the droplets grow heavier, they may eventually fall as rain. The UAE uses specially equipped aircraft to release seeding materials into suitable clouds. However, the technique needs naturally occurring clouds with sufficient moisture. According to the World Meteorological Organization , cloud seeding cannot create rain clouds or bring moisture into an otherwise dry atmosphere. Cloud seeding does not create clouds or produce rain from a clear sky. Photograph: (Reuters) Why did the experiment fail in Delhi? On 28 October 2025, aircraft carrying cloud-seeding flares conducted two sorties over parts of Delhi, including Burari, Karol Bagh, and Mayur Vihar. The experiment was part of a pilot project undertaken by the Delhi government in collaboration with IIT Kanpur. However, it did not produce rainfall in Delhi. Only negligible precipitation was recorded in neighbouring Noida and Greater Noida, at 0.1 mm and 0.2 mm respectively. The biggest obstacle was insufficient moisture in the clouds. According to NDTV's report on the experiment , IIT Kanpur director Manindra Agarwal explained that the clouds had moisture levels of around 15 to 20 percent, which were insufficient to trigger the desired rainfall. A second attempt scheduled for 29 October was also put on hold because atmospheric conditions were unsuitable. The problem was not simply the technology or the material released by the aircraft. The clouds themselves lacked the conditions needed to produce rain. Delhi's winter weather adds to the challenge Delhi's weather makes cloud seeding particularly difficult during the months when pollution is at its worst. During winter, the city frequently experiences low wind speeds, temperature inversions, and limited atmospheric mixing. These conditions trap pollutants close to the ground instead of allowing them to disperse. At the same time, the atmosphere often lacks the moisture and suitable cloud formations required for artificial rainfall. A study by IIT Delhi researchers titled 'Can Cloud Seeding Help Tackle Delhi's Air Pollution?' examined weather and pollution data collected between 2011 and 2021. The researchers found that suitable conditions for cloud seeding are relatively uncommon during Delhi's winter pollution season. Western disturbances, which bring moisture and precipitation to north-western India, can occasionally create favourable conditions. However, these opportunities are limited. The researchers concluded that cloud seeding could be considered an emergency measure when suitable weather conditions exist, but it cannot serve as a dependable pollution-control strategy. Can artificial rain really clear the air? Rainfall can help remove suspended particles, but the relief is generally temporary. Depending on the cloud type and atmospheric conditions, scientists use materials such as silver iodide or salts, including sodium chloride and potassium chloride. Photograph: (Newsonair) The IIT Delhi research found that heavy rainfall can wash out PM2.5 and PM10 more effectively than light rainfall. However, pollutant concentrations can return to earlier levels within one to five days as vehicles, industries, and other sources continue releasing emissions. Delhi's pollution comes from several sources, including vehicular exhaust, construction dust, industrial emissions, waste burning, and agricultural residue burning. Even if cloud seeding successfully produces rain, it cannot stop these sources from adding fresh pollutants to the atmosphere. There is also no conclusive evidence that cloud seeding consistently improves air quality in every region. A 2022 study published in the International Journal of Environmental Science and Technology examined particulate matter during cloud-seeding operations in the UAE and raised questions about the possible contribution of seeding materials to airborne particles. What does this mean for Delhi? Dubai's experience shows how rainfall can help remove airborne dust, but it does not establish cloud seeding as a reliable way to reduce AQI. Delhi's failed experiment highlights an important limitation. Technology can encourage clouds to produce rain, but it cannot compensate for unsuitable weather conditions. On 28 October 2025, aircraft carrying cloud-seeding flares conducted two sorties over parts of Delhi, including Burari, Karol Bagh, and Mayur Vihar. Photograph: (India Weekly) Cloud seeding may offer temporary relief when sufficient moisture and suitable clouds are available. For Delhi, cleaner air will depend less on waiting for artificial rain and more on preventing pollutants from entering the atmosphere in the first place. Better control of vehicle emissions, construction dust, industrial pollution, and agricultural burning will do far more for long-term air quality than waiting for the right clouds to arrive.

items.descriptionOriginal: O n August 8, 2023, fast-moving wildfires swept through several parts of West Maui. The town of Lahaina, which holds a deep place in Hawaiian history and once served as the capital of the Hawaiian Kingdom, suffered the greatest devastation: Most of its buildings were destroyed, and thousands of residents were displaced. The disaster exposed vulnerabilities that had been building long before the flames, from a shortage of affordable housing and dependence on tourism to questions around land use, water access and food security. items.descriptionOriginal: Grief has a way of ambushing us in ordinary places. It was in the middle of an Ikea store, surrounded by display of sofas and couples building lives together, that a recently widowed woman sat down and wept. A passing stranger stopped, pressed a packet of tissues into her hands, rested a palm on her shoulder, and waited in silence until a nod signaled she was steadier. Then, she simply walked on. That wordless exchange, offered without expectation or introduction, cracked something open: "I knew then that a relationship was possible, because there are good people in the world." What followed, over the next decade, was a new love, a rebuilt life, and a quiet personal ritual -- the widow now carries tissues wherever she goes and has pressed them into the hands of four strangers crying in restaurants and bars. Kindness, it turns out, doesn't just comfort; it teaches, and those who receive it often become its most faithful carriers.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Living with the Wild Documentary Confronts What Coexistence Actually Looks Like Reading Time: 3 minutes A five-part Living with the Wild documentary series explores what coexistence really looks like as elephants, lions, and rural communities increasingly compete for the same shrinking landscapes. Living with the Wild documentary from the International Fund for Animal Welfare (IFAW) arrives at a moment when human-wildlife conflict has become one of conservation’s most pressing and least resolved challenges. Across Africa’s great ecosystems, growing human populations, expanding agriculture, and shifting climate patterns push people and wildlife into ever-closer proximity, often with deadly consequences for both. Nowhere is this tension more visible than in Kenya’s Amboseli ecosystem, a landscape spanning the shadow of Mount Kilimanjaro where more than a thousand elephants roam alongside tens of thousands of Maasai pastoralists and their livestock. The documentary draws heavily on landscapes like this, where elephants raiding crops can destroy an entire family’s harvest overnight, and where retaliatory killings of wildlife remain a persistent, painful reality. IFAW has worked in Amboseli for years, partnering with the Amboseli Ecosystem Trust and Kenya Wildlife Service to mitigate conflict and secure migratory corridors elephants depend on. The organization’s multi-year commitment to securing tens of thousands of acres as wildlife dispersal land reflects a core premise underlying the Living with the Wild documentary: coexistence requires physical space, not just goodwill. That space-based approach extends well beyond Amboseli through IFAW’s broader Room to Roam initiative, which works to secure safe migratory corridors for African elephants across multiple countries. In Zimbabwe, the initiative has leased tens of thousands of acres between Victoria Falls and Hwange National Park, creating no-poaching territory that benefits elephants and more than a dozen other migratory species sharing the landscape. The Living with the Wild documentary connects to IFAW’s Room to Roam initiative, which secures tens of thousands of acres of safe migratory territory for elephants and other species across Southern Africa, demonstrating how physical space underpins genuine coexistence. Photo by Gil DAIX on Pexels. The Living with the Wild documentary captures a central truth about modern conservation: protecting iconic species increasingly means addressing the needs of the people living alongside them, not treating human and wildlife welfare as competing priorities. Communities bordering protected areas often bear disproportionate costs from wildlife presence, losing crops, livestock, and sometimes lives, while receiving comparatively little benefit from the tourism revenue wildlife generates elsewhere. Addressing this imbalance requires solutions extending beyond fences and patrols. IFAW’s work supporting human-wildlife conflict mitigation has included deploying tracking collars on elephants to better predict and prevent dangerous encounters, funding infrastructure improvements benefiting local communities, and developing early warning systems that help people and elephants avoid confrontations before they escalate into tragedy. The Living with the Wild documentary arrives as momentum builds to treat coexistence as an achievable policy rather than a distant aspiration. Organizations including the Elephant Protection Initiative increasingly bring communities, governments, and conservation groups to the same table, recognizing that sustainable solutions require buy-in from everyone sharing a landscape, not interventions imposed from outside. This shift matters because conventional conservation approaches, focused narrowly on anti-poaching enforcement or protected-area boundaries, often fail to address why conflict happens in the first place. When communities lose half their crops to wildlife and receive no compensation or support for alternative livelihoods, tolerance for coexistence erodes, no matter how much international attention a species receives. The Living with the Wild documentary suggests that genuine coexistence depends on reframing wildlife not as a burden communities must endure, but as a shared resource whose benefits and costs are distributed more equitably. Corridors that allow elephants to migrate safely also reduce crop-raiding incidents. Conflict mitigation infrastructure protects both human livelihoods and animal lives. Community-based conservation models increasingly demonstrate that when local people have genuine stakes in wildlife survival, coexistence becomes self-reinforcing rather than externally enforced. As climate change intensifies pressure on already-strained landscapes and pushes wildlife and communities into more frequent contact, the questions raised throughout the Living with the Wild documentary will only grow more urgent. The series offers no simple resolution, because none exists. Instead, it offers a clear-eyed look at what sharing a planet with megafauna requires: space, compromise, and sustained investment in solutions that work for both the elephants crossing ancient migratory routes and the families whose homes and farms lie along the way. The post Living with the Wild Documentary Confronts What Coexistence Actually Looks Like appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: This story is part of The Better India's new wildlife series, Species in Focus: 52 species. 52 stories. 52 reasons to protect India's wildlife. One species at a time, the series explores India's rare, endangered and lesser-known wildlife, their habitats, behaviour, ecological roles and conservation status. A lime-green ring marked '2K' has helped birdwatchers in Bengal identify a visitor whose journey began thousands of kilometres away. The bird, a spoon-billed sandpiper, was photographed at Kargil Beach in Bakkhali, South 24 Parganas, on October 24, 2026. The following day, it was spotted again at nearby Patibunia Beach. According to The Times of India , the bird was tagged in Russia's Chukotka region on July 6, 2025. Its appearance on the Bengal coast, around 8,000 km from its tagging location, offers a glimpse into the movements of one of the world's most threatened migratory shorebirds. For birdwatchers, identifying the same individual across different locations is an important record. The spoon-billed sandpiper's survival is tied to a chain of coastal habitats stretching from the Russian Far East to South and Southeast Asia. Bengal is one part of this journey, and protecting its mudflats matters far beyond the state's coastline. A tag that connects two coastlines The bird's movements along the Bengal coast have been documented over several months. On March 29, 2026, birdwatcher Sandip Das, a founding member of the Bengal-based Birdwatchers' Society, photographed a spoon-billed sandpiper at Patibunia Beach. Birdwatchers Soumya Aon and Kaustav Khan were also present. Two days later, another individual was photographed by Jayanta Manna. This second bird carried a lime-green tag on its right leg . The tagged bird continued to be sighted at Patibunia until June 1. When it reappeared at Kargil Beach in October, the tag marked '2K' helped birdwatchers establish that it was the same individual. The bird may be only a few centimetres long, but its journey links conservation decisions across continents. Photograph: (Facebook/BirdCount India) According to Das, the bird may have travelled to feeding grounds in Bangladesh before returning to Bengal. He also told The Times of India that a return to its Russian breeding site was unlikely, as the territory was already occupied by breeding pairs , potentially leading to conflict. With these sightings, three individual spoon-billed sandpipers have now been photographically recorded in Bengal: one in 2018 and two in 2026. But what makes this record important is not simply that a rare bird has visited the state. It offers evidence of how individual birds move between habitats, helping researchers understand which coastal stretches they depend on. Why a spoon-shaped bill matters Unlike most sandpipers, which have relatively straight, narrow bills, this species has a distinctive spatula-shaped tip that helps it pick small food items from wet mud. These birds feed on small invertebrates and other organisms found in intertidal mudflats. Such habitats provide food and resting places during migration, helping them build the energy needed to continue their journey. The species is classified as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List. Its global wild population is estimated at fewer than 500 individuals. The challenge is that its feeding grounds are not interchangeable. A bird that loses access to one important stopover may not find another suitable habitat in time. When a wetland disappears, the journey is interrupted The spoon-billed sandpiper's migration takes it across the East Asian–Australasian Flyway, a network of routes connecting breeding grounds in the north with wintering areas further south. One of its most important ecological bottlenecks is the Yellow Sea, between China and the Korean Peninsula. Its tidal flats provide feeding and resting grounds for migratory shorebirds. 🏁It's time for the birds' annual migration marathon 🕊️ 🐧 🦅 Watch this video to follow a remarkable spoon-billed sandpiper's incredible journey over thousands of kilometres. Will he be able to cross the finish line? #SaveSpoonie #wetlands #WMBD2023 #wwfindia #wwf https://t.co/eyY4devKST — WWF-India (@WWFINDIA) May 13, 2023 However, coastal reclamation, infrastructure development, hunting and disturbance have reduced or degraded several of these habitats. In June 2026, Sixth Tone , a Chinese news daily, reported how public pressure helped halt a proposed highway in China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region. The 47-km project, estimated to cost 5.1 billion yuan (approximately $710 million), threatened mudflats used by nearly 20,000 waterbirds belonging to 46 species. An environmental assessment identified more than 24 hectares of important spoon-billed sandpiper habitat, including mangrove wetlands . Following citizen campaigns and complaints to authorities, China's central environmental authorities suspended the project on May 25, finding that its environmental assessment lacked a sufficient scientific basis. Alternative routes were subsequently proposed for evaluation. Can conservation give the species a head start? One conservation intervention being used in Russia is called headstarting. Under this method, eggs are collected from the wild, incubated and hatched under human care. The chicks are raised until they are old enough to be released into their natural habitat. According to the Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust (WWT), 236 headstarted spoon-billed sandpipers have been released so far, with 19 subsequently returning to breed in Russia. Illustrated by @mitul987 and Asif Kureshi. The Spoon-billed Sandpiper is listed as critically #endangered by @IUCNRedList. Fewer than 200 estimated in the #wild, It's never been recorded breeding over 5 km from the shore. Destruction of #wetlands is a huge threat to this #bird. https://t.co/WnYMtpAU4r — Sanctuary Asia (@SanctuaryAsia) December 10, 2019 The technique addresses one of the species' biggest challenges: the low survival rate of chicks in the wild. WWT estimates that only around three out of every 20 eggs laid naturally produce chicks that survive to adulthood, compared with 15 out of every 20 among headstarted chicks. However, breeding interventions cannot replace the need to protect the wetlands these birds depend on. What Bengal's sightings mean Back in Bakkhali, conservation efforts are also taking place at the local level. Birdwatchers have been conducting monthly surveys at Patibunia and Kargil beaches to monitor waders and other shorebirds. The South 24 Parganas Forest Department has installed signboards asking visitors and local residents not to disturb birdlife and has increased patrolling. The appearance of bird '2K' does not, by itself, indicate that the spoon-billed sandpiper population is recovering. But it provides another record of the connections between Bengal's coastline and distant breeding and feeding grounds. The bird may be only a few centimetres long, but its journey links conservation decisions across continents. Whether it can make that journey again will depend, in part, on whether places like Bakkhali remain safe enough for it to stop, feed and move on. Sources: 'Critically endangered Spoon-billed Sandpiper, tagged in Russia, sighted again on Bengal beach' : By TOI, Published on 26 October 2026 'Critically endangered spoon-billed sandpiper clicked on beach near Bakkhali, 2nd photo record from Bengal' : Krishnendu Mukherjee, Published on 30 March 2026 'How a Rare Bird Stopped a Highway Project in South China' : By Jiang Xinyi and Yang Yang, Published on 2 June 2026

items.descriptionOriginal: Imagine spending years watching films and wondering how they’re made, only to find your own name in the end credits of one! That’s the surreal moment for Mani Kantesh Allapuram, whose creative journey began with a few video edits and a lot of curiosity. His father introduced him to video editing in Class 11. Soon, Mani was making edits, designing graphics, and putting his ideas online, simply because he loved creating. During the lockdown, he took that passion further, spending hours experimenting with creative tools. Even while pursuing Computer Science, he kept finding ways to explore visual storytelling. And those experiments eventually opened a door he hadn’t imagined. His work caught the attention of DNEG, one of the world’s leading visual effects studios. He joined the team in early 2026 as a Creative Technology Artist and got the opportunity to contribute to Ramayana. For someone who once watched films dreaming about the magic behind them, being credited alongside some of the industry’s finest artists, including A. R. Rahman and Hans Zimmer, is a full-circle moment. As Mani says, “Your boy made it to the big screen.” A reminder that the things you create just for the love of it might one day take you somewhere extraordinary. #Ramayana #BehindTheScenes #RamayanaVFX #VisualEffects #IndianCinema #RamayanaMovie #7yearsforramayan #makingoframayan

items.description: Για κάποιον που βιώνει πόνο στο στήθος ή δύσπνοια σε ένα απομακρυσμένο χωριό, η λήψη ΗΚΓ μπορεί να σημαίνει ότι θα ταξιδέψει αρκετά χιλιόμετρα στο πλησιέστερο νοσοκομείο. Μέχρι να γίνει η δοκιμή, πολύτιμα λεπτά μπορεί να έχουν ήδη χαθεί. Αυτό το κενό ήταν που οδήγησε τον Rajat Jain και τους συνιδρυτές του να δημιουργήσουν τη Sunfox Technologies, μια εταιρεία τεχνολογίας υγείας στο Dehradun,…
items.descriptionOriginal: For someone experiencing chest pain or breathlessness in a remote village, getting an ECG can mean travelling several kilometres to the nearest hospital. By the time the test is done, precious minutes may already have been lost. It was this gap that led Rajat Jain and his co-founders to build Sunfox Technologies, a health-tech company in Dehradun, Uttarakhand. They launched Spandan, a pocket-sized ECG device that connects to a smartphone. The device can record a medical-grade ECG and generate a report within minutes, without needing a conventional ECG machine, an external battery or an internet connection. Today, more than 60,000 Spandan devices have been deployed across India, reaching over 20,000 villages across 28 states. The technology has been used to screen around five million patients, and over 2,00,000 lives have been saved. The journey to making cardiac testing more accessible, however, began with a personal tragedy that changed the course of Rajat's life. The personal loss that started it For Rajat, the idea for Sunfox began with a loss that was difficult to make sense of. At 21, he lost a close friend to a heart attack. The experience made him realise that cardiac emergencies can strike without warning and that, even when help is available, the first few minutes can make a crucial difference. At the time, Rajat was a mechanical engineer working in the automotive field. But the loss made him look towards a problem that felt far more urgent: "How could technology make basic cardiac diagnosis available when a hospital or specialist was not close by?" Bill Gates listening to Rajat Jain demonstrate Spandan's prowess at ICMR HQ in Delhi. Spandan was selected among India's best healthcare innovations supported by ICMR. That question led him and his co-founders — Arpit Jain, Saurabh Badola, Nitin Chandola and Sabit Rawat — to start Sunfox Technologies in Dehradun in 2016. They began working on ways to make an ECG, one of the first tests doctors use when a patient shows signs of a heart problem, smaller, more affordable and easier to use. The prototype was developed in 2017, laying the groundwork for the company's effort to take cardiac screening into places where access to specialised care is limited. How a smartphone became an ECG machine An ECG, or electrocardiogram, records the tiny electrical signals the heart produces with every beat. Doctors use it to identify a heart attack, a blocked artery or an irregular heartbeat. Traditionally, it requires a large machine, a trained technician and a hospital room. Spandan changes that. It is a portable 12-lead ECG device that connects to a smartphone, records the heart's signals and produces a report in about two minutes. "The advantage of using Spandan is that anyone with or without medical education can use it," says Jain. "Spandan devices use ECG sensors, smartphone integration, and software to record and display ECGs. It uses AI and analytics for report generation," he explains. "Also, it does not need an external battery to work; it uses power from your smartphone to work." That design was a deliberate choice, made with rural India in mind. "These features were very important for us as the device had to work in remote locations in the country without a regular source of electricity or internet connection," says Rajat. While the devices range in price from Rs 6,900 to Rs 75,000, depending on the model, Sunfox says a significant share of its users come from smaller towns and rural areas. Around 60 per cent of its users are from rural or semi-urban locations, with more than 20,000 devices currently active in these regions. Co-founders of Sunfox Technologies. Small clinics are among the buyers, as they see value in the device even at the Rs 16,000–17,000 price point, says the company. For healthcare facilities with limited access to conventional ECG machines, a portable device that can generate reports within minutes offers another way to conduct cardiac screening. For Sunfox, the goal was to make a heart test as routine as other everyday health checks, without hurting the wallet. Making cardiac monitoring accessible at home The device is also being used by individuals who want to monitor their heart health between doctor visits. Sandip Deodhar, 52, an accountant assistant from Kolhapur, has been using Spandan for the past month. He is hypertensive and diabetic, and says he would often spend Rs 200–300 every other week on ECG tests recommended during his consultations. After discovering Spandan online, he discussed it with his doctor, who agreed that he could use the device to record ECGs at home. "For the first three-four days, I ran multiple tests to review the reports and become accustomed to the device. Now, he tells me to notify him only if there is an abnormal test; otherwise, he says there's no need to even show him the report," says Sandip. The pilot: Testing in a hospital Before Spandan could go to villages, it had to prove itself inside a hospital. "We did the pilot in Fortis Hospital in Uttarakhand in 2018-19 along with SELCO Foundation," shares Rajat. The team wanted answers to two questions. "We were trying to prove the validity and accuracy of our devices and wanted to know how user-friendly our devices are so that frontline health workers with minimal trainin g could operate them." Then, in 2021, a study was conducted at Fortis Escorts Hospital in Dehradun under the supervision of cardiologists. The patients were first tested on the hospital's standard ECG machine. Within five minutes, the same patients were tested on Spandan, and a cardiologist reviewed the readings independently. Of the 153 patients enrolled, 110 were counted in the final results, and Spandan's reading matched that of the standard machine in 108 of those 110 cases. It was a small study, but it provided a base for what followed. Larger hospital studies came next, including a study of 2,799 patients, published in 2025 in the Anatolian Journal of Cardiology , and one in Meerut involving 184 patients with chest pain. The company says the count is now 30 studies. "We have compared the performance of Spandan with standard ECG devices in more than 30,000 patients and have achieved a 99.7% accuracy," says Rajat. How Sunfox found its footing Proving Spandan in a hospital was one step. Getting it into the field brought a different set of challenges. The first problem was money. "The biggest challenge for us was overcoming a funding crunch while developing a health device, which conventionally requires a large investment," says Rajat. In the early days, the founders paid for the work themselves. "When we first started, there was no funding or grant. We self-sponsored in most part and also did side-gigs to support the research and development of our devices," he recalls. The second problem was testing the device where it was meant to be used. A hospital in Dehradun is very different from a village clinic, and a device built for villages had to be tried in villages. "Secondly, we had difficulty in validating the results of our device in low-resource and rural areas because we couldn't get too many patients there," says Jain. There was also the matter of trust. Sunfox was entering India's medical device sector, which is known for high entry barriers, strict rules, heavy investment and a market crowded with imported products. Rajat says, "We faced constant doubts about whether medical technology built in India could be trusted." Help arrived in stages. In 2017, the first prototype was ready, and the team moved into its first office at a technology incubator at Graphic Era University in Dehradun. Government funding followed. "Later, we received funding from the state government of Uttarakhand, from our university, and also from the Department of Science and Technology (DST), Government of India, to conduct the pilot tests," says Jain. Private money came next. "In 2022, Sunfox appeared on Shark Tank India, where we got funding of Rs 1 crore," adds Rajat. Larger funding has followed since. In August 2024, Sunfox raised Rs 15 crore in a round led by Venture Catalysts. Inc42 also reports that the company had earlier received Rs 5 crore from USAID through its SAMRIDH Health programme and LetsVenture. Now the product had to be tested in real-life settings. Government partnerships gave Sunfox access to rural clinics. In September 2026, Sunfox raised $7 million (INR 66 crore) in a Series A funding round led by renowned investor Ashish Kacholia, Lashit Sanghvi, Alchemy Capital and 3one4 Capital. The real-life challenge Now the product had to be tested in real-life settings. Government partnerships gave Sunfox access to rural clinics. In December 2020, the Government of India's biotech agency BIRAC and the industry body Nasscom launched JanCare, a challenge offering health-tech startups pilot test beds at rural health centres in partnership with state governments. Sunfox took part, deploying eight devices across six CHCs and PHCs in Nagaland and two CHCs in Uttar Pradesh. In July 2022, Sunfox also worked with the Uttarakhand government to set up a free screening camp at Sonprayag, where the Kedarnath trek begins. Trained local volunteers screened pilgrims with Spandan and sent abnormal readings over WhatsApp to a cardiologist in Dehradun. In the first month, the camp screened nearly 1,500 people and referred 59 to a local doctor. These pilots showed that health workers without specialist training could operate the device, and larger deployments followed. SAMRIDH, the USAID-backed programme, says its support helped place 1,551 Spandan units in public and private clinics across Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Jammu and Kashmir, and Delhi, screening 63,486 people. From a prototype to 60,000 devices What began as a self-funded lab in Dehradun has since grown into a nationwide deployment. More than 60,000 Spandan devices are now in use, covering over 20,000 villages. "We have deployed over 60,000 devices in the country, from Himalayan states like Uttarakhand to Nagaland in the North-east and heavily forested and remote areas in Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand," says Rajat. State governments have come on board. "We are working with the state governments of Uttarakhand and Haryana so that any patient with symptoms of heart ailments can get access to quick diagnosis and treatment," he says. The two-minute turnaround is particularly significant in these settings. "The healthcare worker, whether a nurse, technician or even doctor, puts the leads on the patient and receives an ECG within 3 minutes, with a clinician-reviewed diagnosis and prescription," Jain explains. The results show up in the numbers. Until October 2026, "In Uttarakhand, we have worked in CHCs and PHCs on the Char Dham Yatra route and have screened more than 13100 pilgrims and identified 463 critical patients who could receive treatment on time," he says. In Haryana, "We have deployed our devices in more than 597 PHCs and CHCs and conducted ECGs for 60,000 people and detected 2000 critical cases since June." The device can also flag the most dangerous kind of heart attack early. "We can detect the deadliest kind of heart attack, called STEMI, in less than an hour of it first occurring, saving thousands of lives," says Jain. The road ahead In August 2026, Sunfox marked 10 years with the opening of an innovation hub in Dehradun. Its next goal is to take Spandan beyond India. "We plan to expand in low- and middle-income countries, especially in Africa and South Asia, and we have already started." According to SAMRIDH, more than 400 Spandan devices are in use across Africa. The mission has not changed since the day Jain lost his friend. "Most heart attacks in India are preventable if diagnosed early," he says. "Our vision is to take this portable ECG technology and make it so ubiquitous that everyone has access to it, just as they do for thermometers and BP machines." And if the numbers are anything to go by, Sunfox is surely on its way to success.

Πέρασε περίπου μισή ώρα σε κάθε στάση δ…
items.descriptionOriginal: Daniel Te, an American artist living in London, has set his sights on sketching distinctive landmarks at the city’s 272 active Tube stations. The 27-year-old recently completed all 16 stops on the Victoria Line in a 10-hour sketching marathon, beginning with Brixton and concluding with Walthamstow Central. He spent about half an hour at each stop drawing something near the station. Daniel Te / SWNS “I think drawing landmarks helps create a more distinctive sense of what a place is exactly,” he told SWNS. “Seven Sisters was the most memorable, and I really like the origin story — it’s the symbol of the place, just seven trees in a circle.” Te said he was surprised by what he discovered, not having researched the stations in advance. For example, at Highbury & Islington, he spotted a green plaque marking where George Orwell used to live. “And that’s something that I never knew,” he remarked. Daniel Te / SWNS When he got to the final stop at Walthamstow Central, it was getting dark and hard to see what he was sketching. “I felt relieved, hungry, tired, and satisfied,” Te said. “It was fulfilling, and I really liked the journey.” And despite increasing costs of transport, his day of traveling cost him less than $10. Daniel Te / SWNS Te moved to London from Portland, Oregon, in July, inspired to explore European city planning. “One of the reasons why I started doing Tube sketching is that I wanted to see more of London and have an excuse to go out and about,” he explained, adding, “I really do love the process of just exploring every single destination.” He has visited many cities, including Amsterdam, Vienna, and Prague, and has completed drawings of Berlin’s S7 S-Bahn and the Palace of Culture and Science in Warsaw. Whenever he sketches, he likes that people come and talk to him, share their own art, or simply watch him in action. Daniel Te / SWNS Next up? Te is inviting fellow Londoners to join him at Farringdon Station at 11 a.m. tomorrow to begin sketching the Circle Line. And further down the line (pun intended), he plans to turn the sketches into a book or expand his work to cover other locations. This article was originally written by Tahira Amini for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets.

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM For decades, wastewater treatment plants have been filtering out bacteria, chemicals, and biological waste before discharging treated water back into the environment. Microplastics have been going straight through. This week, a plant in Atlantic City, New Jersey, became the first in the world to do something about that, installing a system built specifically to capture microplastics before they reach the ocean. As of this moment, no law requires this. PolyGone Systems , a startup founded by two former Princeton University graduate students, built it anyway. Why microplastics are hard to remove Plastics don’t biodegrade; they break down into tinier and tinier fragments called microplastics, which don’t go away and build up in living organisms over time. Standard wastewater treatment removes a lot, but it wasn’t designed for particles this small or this plentiful. They get into the water from industrial discharge, stormwater picking up particles shed from car tires, and washing machines releasing microfibers from synthetic clothes. By the time water arrives at a treatment plant, the microplastics are already in it. “We’re discharging to the ocean,” said Matt DeNafo, president of the Atlantic County Utilities Authority. “So, if we’re not removing the plastic that’s in our wastewater, we’re putting it back into the environment. It’s getting into the fish that we’re eating, even the water that we’re bathing. So, it really becomes an issue for human health.” Microplastics and nanoplastics have already turned up in human bloodstream, brain tissue , and other organs. Some researchers have linked exposure to a higher risk of heart attack or stroke, though scientists are still working out exactly what harm these particles cause at different levels of exposure. How the technology works PolyGone’s founders, Nathaniel Banks and Yidian Liu , trained as architects, and the technology they built shows it. Their system, called Polypods, doesn’t try to filter microplastics out of water the conventional way. Instead, it replicates the surface of ultrahydrophobic plants found in wetlands, which microplastics cling to naturally. Scale that up, and you can pull microplastics out of a water stream with very little material and minimal energy. The lab numbers are strong: more than 98 percent of microplastics removed. There’s no commercial data yet, but Banks and Liu say the Polypods work best on the smallest particles, which are also the hardest to catch by other means and the ones most easily absorbed by living tissue. Liu on the design philosophy: “We really like how some sleek products such as the iPhone were able to resolve very complex problems with very simple but sleek-looking designs. And we want to really emphasize that in how we design the Polypods.” “I think this really marks a new era for treatment innovation, where we’re able to build very large, scalable systems that use a very small amount of material and very low energy to treat very challenging contaminants,” Banks said. “And, having the first system in the world for that in Atlantic County, it’s quite unusual.” Where PolyGone goes from here A similar installation is already running at a wastewater plant in California, and PolyGone is developing a residential version. The Atlantic City system was fully funded by a federal grant, and both the technology and the funding route could give other municipalities a path to act without waiting on a mandate. items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM If you’ve noticed more spiders lately, near window frames, behind boxes in the garage, lurking in basement corners, you’re not imagining it. Fall is mating season for spiders , which makes them more active than usual, and when temperatures drop, many of them make the same call you would and head inside. Of the roughly 3,700 spider species in the United States, only about 0.3 percent are dangerous to humans. The rest are, in the words of Oregon State University Extension horticulturist Brooke Edmunds , “minding their own business.” Two things converging in the spiderverse It’s not only the cold driving these arachnids indoors. Spiders like cellar spiders, wolf spiders, and hobo spiders move indoors as temperatures fall, and once inside, many are also looking for mates and somewhere quiet to leave their eggs . “Just like us, they’re coming inside to get warm,” Edmunds explains. “They aren’t aggressive toward people, not even the spiders.” Some females carry egg sacs on their bodies; others are hunting for corners, furniture undersides, the back of a closet, anywhere spider silk can hold a sac in place. That’s part of why fall can feel like a sudden invasion when it’s really just two instincts running in parallel. What makes your home The Destination Some of it is biology, and some of it is a gap in the garage door seal. If the weather strip at the bottom is worn or the door doesn’t sit flush, that’s an open invitation. Same goes for cracks along the foundation and gaps around window frames. And if your house already has gnats, flies, aphids, or termites, spiders will follow, because those critters happen to make up a great menu for our eight-legged friends. Outside, what’s close to the house does a lot of the inviting. Colorado State University’s entomology experts recommend clearing away rock piles, wood stacks, old boards, and compost heaps from around the perimeter. Spiders go for dark, damp, undisturbed spots. Tree limbs that touch or hang near windows are another way in, and crawl spaces packed with boxes are definitely attractive to them. How to keep them out Caulking cracks in your foundation and making sure screens and door seals are intact does a lot. Fall is also a good time to go through basements, garages, and closets, not for tidiness, but because those neglected corners are exactly what spiders are looking for. If you’re digging into old cardboard boxes or boots that haven’t moved since last winter, wear gloves. Spiders have sometimes made a cozy home inside them. If you’d rather not evict the ones already there, that’s fine too. They’re eating the insects you’d otherwise be swatting at, and most will move on once the season turns anyway. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Can Today’s Construction Firms Make Their Operations More Sustainable? Reading Time: 5 minutes How Can Today’s Construction Firms Make Their Operations More Sustainable? When you envision a typical construction site, you likely picture roaring diesel engines, towering waste bins and clouds of dust. However, forward-thinking builders are proving that heavy-duty work doesn’t have to create heavy pollution. While traditional operations take a massive toll on the planet through emissions and discarded scrap, you can drive real change on the ground. By embracing thoughtful equipment care, cleaner energy and circular material sourcing, your crews can build a greener world from the ground up. 1. Prioritizing Low-Emissions and Salvaged Materials Every major construction project begins with a blueprint, but the materials you specify in those early drawings dictate your build’s lifetime environmental footprint. Traditional supplies like standard Portland cement and virgin structural steel carry staggering amounts of embodied carbon—the hidden greenhouse gas emissions generated during raw material extraction, manufacturing, and transport. Many firms are swapping out carbon-intensive staples for lower-impact alternatives that still perform reliably. Mass timber, sustainably harvested from certified forests, sequesters atmospheric carbon right inside a building’s frame. Meanwhile, opting for supplementary materials, such as ground granulated blast-furnace slag — a recycled industrial by-product that can replace part of the cement in concrete — can significantly undercut the carbon emissions of traditional concrete mixes. Sustainability also means keeping things local and circular. By sourcing reclaimed lumber, crushed stone and recycled structural steel from regional deconstruction projects, you eliminate the fuel burned shipping heavy freight across the country. Salvaging high-quality elements prevents unnecessary virgin extraction, reduces procurement costs and gives historic materials a useful second life. 2. Adopting Proactive Machinery Maintenance to Reduce Waste and Boost Efficiency A truly sustainable jobsite isn’t just about what’s being built, but also about how efficiently machines run while building it. Proactive heavy equipment care is an essential pillar of low-impact construction. When diesel-powered machinery operates at peak mechanical efficiency, engines encounter less drag, burn significantly less fuel and prevent harmful oil leaks from threatening surrounding soil and local waterways. Routine inspections and precision adjustments prevent premature component breakdowns, keeping bulky metal and synthetic assemblies out of scrap heaps. Daily cleanings with a pressure washer clear away packed dirt and rocks that strain the undercarriage rollers, while maintaining proper track sag prevents engine strain and reduces excess fuel consumption. For example, checking the rubber tracks on skid steers to avoid wear and tear while encouraging optimal performance through proper tension reduces engine strain from overly tight tracks. Doing so means saving fuel and protecting components, leading to fewer emissions and a longer lifespan, which reduces manufacturing footprints. Prioritizing consistent preventive maintenance across excavators and loaders also curbs project delays and saves expenses. 3. Cutting Site Waste Through Circular Construction Practices Traditional construction projects generate mountains of debris, but progressive firms are more often viewing discarded materials as valuable future commodities. Moving toward a circular model begins with systematic on-site sorting, so instead of commingling off-cuts and packaging into generic roll-off dumpster bins, crews establish clearly labeled recovery stations for clean timber, scrap metal, cardboard and masonry. Processing materials directly where the work occurs can save significant hauling fuel and slash disposal tipping fees. Contractors often deploy portable rock crushers to break down clean demo concrete and masonry rubble on-site, producing quality sub-base aggregate to use for access roads, staging areas and sturdy foundation pads. When structures must come down, intentional deconstruction is replacing wrecking balls. Instead of demolishing older framing, crews carefully deconstruct timber and fixtures for repurposing in community projects or donation. Through active partnerships with local salvage yards and regional architectural reclaimers, firms keep large volumes of solid waste out of municipal landfills and help nearby communities access sturdy, character-rich, reusable materials. 4. Cleaning Up Fleet Power Heavy diesel machinery is a core part of commercial construction, but powering an entire fleet on fossil fuels carries a steep environmental and human price tag. Construction vehicles can emit substantial particulate matter and greenhouse gases, worsening local air quality while driving up fuel costs. Consequently, modern contractors are investigating ways to make fleet operations cleaner, quieter and more efficient. Electrification is leading this charge, especially among compact utility machinery. Battery-powered mini-excavators, electric wheel loaders and cordless hand tools deliver instant torque without generating smelly exhaust fumes or extreme noise levels. The shift to electric dramatically improves jobsite air quality, safeguards the respiratory health of on-site crews and earns goodwill from neighboring residential communities. Many larger diesel rigs cannot yet fully transition to electric powertrains, so operational discipline must bridge the sustainability gap. Establishing an automatic five-minute engine shut-off rule for loaders and haul trucks will reduce the exhaust fumes in the air while shaving gallons off daily diesel usage. Routine fuel tracking can ensure every engine runs at peak efficiency. 5. Leveraging Smart Planning and Modular Prefabrication Careful planning can make modern jobsites more efficient, with organized factory processes replacing crowded material storage areas. Modular prefabrication shifts significant building processes off-site into climate-controlled manufacturing facilities. In these organized plant environments, automated cutting systems reduce raw material scrap while optimizing usage down to the millimeter. Assembling wall panels off-site allows workers to recycle off-cuts and minimize on-site construction noise and dust. Simultaneously, modular construction eases neighborhood strain by slashing repetitive truck traffic. Instead of individual supply trucks trickling through local residential streets each day, preassembled building modules arrive in consolidated shipments. Digital project management platforms take this operational efficiency even further with advanced scheduling software accurately tracking incoming deliveries to ensure high-value lumber, drywall and delicate insulation arrive exactly when crews are ready to install them. As a result, there are fewer chaotic staging yards and likely a large reduction in expensive, weather-related material damage from heavy rain or exposure to damp ground. 6. Building a Jobsite Culture Around Everyday Sustainability Advanced equipment and green certifications certainly help, but authentic sustainability ultimately begins with people. Creating an eco-conscious jobsite means fostering a crew culture with daily habits that make resource conservation feel simple and worthwhile. The small decisions made throughout an ordinary shift quickly multiply across multi-month commercial developments. Simple operational swaps, like eliminating disposable water bottles in favor of refillable hydration stations and ditching single-use plastic wrap, drastically curb daily jobsite litter and establish an environmental mindset on the ground. Switching to energy-efficient LED lightbulbs in temporary site offices and encouraging shared crew transit foster an office and field culture in which eco-friendly choices become second nature. Sustainability-minded firms actively show their teams how these practical habits mirror broader everyday eco-friendly lifestyles. Incorporating simple sustainable living ideas into workers’ routines inspires tradespeople to make mindful, low-waste choices at home and at work. When crew members see company leadership genuinely backing these principles, green building becomes a shared source of pride instead of just a compliance task. Lay the Groundwork for a Cleaner Industry You can transform your construction operation into a more sustainable operation without overhauling everything overnight. True sustainability is an ongoing journey built on practical, everyday choices. By making each project cleaner, less wasteful and more efficient, you will make a tangible difference with every build. You hold the power to reshape the building landscape, proving that with each structure, you can construct a stronger, cleaner and more resilient tomorrow. The post How Can Today’s Construction Firms Make Their Operations More Sustainable? appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: In Kerala, your father’s property could belong to your aunt’s children! Just like in the new series AKKA, for centuries, many Nair families followed a unique matrilineal system called Marumakkathayam, where family identity and inheritance passed through the mother’s side. Even a king’s son could not inherit the throne. It went to his sister’s son! But here’s the twist: women passed down the family name, while men, especially the eldest maternal uncle, held the power. The system was abolished in 1975, but matrilineal traditions continue in parts of India.
