items.title: Επιστροφή στο σπίτι με κάθε τόξο
items.titleOriginal: Returning Home with Every Bow
items.description: Ένας Πολωνός μοναχός ξεκινούσε κάθε μέρα με επτά τόξα -- μια χειρονομία συγγνώμης προς έναν πατέρα που δεν μπορούσε να αντιμετωπίσει. Η ιστορία του Bhikshu Jin Wei δεν είναι ένα τακτοποιημένο τόξο πνευματικής προόδου. Είναι μια ειλικρινής περιγραφή του πώς η πείνα για μεταμόρφωση μπορεί να γίνει η δική της παγίδα και η ήπια διαδικασία συντονισμού με κάθε στιγμή. Η στροφή ήρθε αθόρυβα, μέσα από ένα μόνο χτύπημα…
items.descriptionOriginal: A Polish monk began each day with seven bows -- a gesture of apology toward a father he couldn't face. Bhikshu Jin Wei's story is not a tidy arc of spiritual progress; it's an honest account of how the hunger for transformation can become its own trap, and the gentle process of attuning to each moment. The turning came quietly, through a single word: a Thai Forest monk suggested a one-word loving-kindness mantra, and Jin Wei sat in the meditation hall asking himself what his word was. Immediately, it came: "safe". What followed was the discovery that the compassion he had been excavating through discipline had been waiting in his body all along -- "our body remembers our trauma," he reflects, "but the body also keeps the love." While on a trip back to Poland earlier this year, he experienced profound, full-circle moments along a softening journey: giving a talk at his own university and sitting down to a vegetarian lunch lovingly offered by his meat-eating family. The monastery, he suggests, is not only a physical place but a quality of listening, available to anyone willing to stop and ask what word is waiting to open their heart.

items.title: "A Labor of Love": Οι επιστήμονες ξαναδημιουργούν το γυαλί που αλλάζει χρώμα που χρησιμοποιείται για να φτιάξει ένα ρωμαϊκό αριστούργημα 1.600 ετών
items.titleOriginal: “A Labor of Love”: Scientists Re-Create the Color-Changing Glass Used to Make a 1,600-Year-Old Roman Masterpiece
items.description: Οι επισκέπτες του Βρετανικού Μουσείου του Λονδίνου μπορούν να θαυμάσουν ένα αξιοσημείωτο παράδειγμα ρωμαϊκής ευρηματικότητας που θεωρείται ένα από τα επτά γυάλινα θαύματα του κόσμου. Χρονολογείται στον τέταρτο αιώνα, το περίτεχνο Lycurgus Cup είναι ένα απαλό πράσινο νεφρίτη — ή ένα εντυπωσιακό ρουμπινί κόκκινο, ανάλογα με το πού βρίσκεται η πηγή φωτός. Η ικανότητα αλλαγής χρώματος του κύλικα έχει μακρύ p…
items.descriptionOriginal: Visitors to London’s British Museum can admire a remarkable example of Roman ingenuity that’s considered one of the seven glass wonders of the world. Dated to the fourth century, the ornate Lycurgus Cup is a soft jade green — or a striking ruby red, depending on where the light source is positioned. The goblet’s color-changing capability has long perplexed scientists. No one is sure exactly how it was created, but the consensus is that Romans added tiny bits of gold and silver to their glass mixture, forming layers of nanoparticles that interact with light differently depending on their size and shape. Experts had struggled to devise a reliable method of re-creating the material in quantity, but now, for the first time, the mystery appears to have been solved. Melding an ancient recipe with modern science, a glass specialist from the University of Sheffield has reproduced the effect, and commissioned a sculpture that pays homage to the original. Lisa Hollands, with the institution’s School of Chemical, Materials, and Biological Engineering, took on the challenge, which was “very much a labor of love,” per a news release from the university. She worked with a Roman glass expert to develop a base that mimicked those used nearly two millennia ago, then set about experimenting with different furnace types, oxygen levels, and more. She said she knew it would be a much more complicated task than simply sprinkling some gold and silver nanoparticles into a mixture, but did think at one point, “If the Romans could have seen me experimenting, they’d probably laugh and ask: ‘Why does she not know how to make this?’” Finally, Hollands landed on a recipe for glass that looked opaque green under reflected light but red when a light was shone directly on it. “To me, it’s magic,” she told The Guardian . So how exactly does it work? “White light is made up of many different colors and you see this when there is a rainbow in the sky. Nanoparticles are much smaller than the wavelengths of light and in certain conditions they block certain colors due to the light affecting the electrons in the atoms,” she explained to the outlet. “So, for this glass, if light is shone through it, the gold and silver particles block blue and green light, only allowing reds and oranges to pass through. If light is reflected off the surface, the particles have the effect of scattering the light, giving the opaque green color we see,” she continued. Hollands and her project manager approached U.K. glass artist Elliot Walker, who won Season 2 of Netflix’s Blown Away , to create a finished piece that could be exhibited at Sheffield’s upcoming Festival of the Mind, which runs Nov. 6-15. It will then go on permanent display at the university’s Turner Museum of Glass . “You can really get an idea of how the glass makers of the past would have adapted to this sort of glass; it’s like shaking their hands,” Walker said in the release. The Lycurgus Cup depicts the legend of King Lycurgus from Homer’s Iliad , showing the triumph of the Greek god Dionysus over the lawgiver Lycurgus . The 2026 homage bridges the time between the Roman artwork and now. “I wanted to keep the sculpture quite classical in form and to carry through the original story of Lycurgus shown on the cup, but we needed a blown element within this to really show the dichroic glass ,” said Walker. “The piece is a blend of the Lycurgus story and the Farnese Atlas sculpture , with the globe replaced by a cup.” RELATED: Researchers Re-Create 5,000-Year-Old Egyptian Blue, the World’s Oldest Synthetic Pigment Once Lost to Science

items.title: The Spark: Όταν οι κοινότητες κατέχουν τη γη, η στέγαση παραμένει προσιτή
items.titleOriginal: The Spark: When Communities Own the Land, Housing Stays Affordable
items.description: Καλώς ήρθατε πίσω στο The Spark, τη μηνιαία γιορτή μας για το πώς άνθρωποι σαν εσάς δημιουργούν θετικές αλλαγές, ένα σημαντικό βήμα τη φορά. Το Spark υποστηρίζεται γενναιόδωρα από τη Laura Rice. Εγγραφείτε στο Reasons to be το εβδομαδιαίο ενημερωτικό δελτίο του Cheerful εδώ και θα λαμβάνετε το The Spark στα εισερχόμενά σας στην αρχή κάθε μήνα. Σε αυτό το τεύχος The power of communit…
items.descriptionOriginal: Welcome back to The Spark, our monthly celebration of how people just like you are creating positive change, one meaningful step at a time. The Spark is generously supported by Laura Rice. Sign up to Reasons to be Cheerful’s weekly newsletter here and you’ll get The Spark in your inbox at the start of each month. In this issue The power of community land trusts Cool roofs, cooler homes The perks of intergenerational roommates A community takes back its land In 2019, Nachand Trabue began noticing investors’ “We buy houses” signs all over her corner of Louisville, Kentucky. A historically Black neighborhood since the Civil War, Smoketown has deep roots and a long, proud past — including the city’s first Black library and first Black dentist, and as the birthplace of Muhammed Ali. But increasingly, long-term residents were getting priced out of their own community. For those like Trabue, a fourth-generation resident who remembered Smoketown in its thriving heyday, the change in their community was especially galling. “Because they’re taking away everything that made Smoketown great. They’re buying up the parks, the vacant lots, and putting in houses. There’s nothing for the kids. There’s no enrichment, no activity,” says Theresa Boyd, executive director of Smoketown Community Land Trust. A mural in Smoketown by The Art of Kacy. Credit: Don Sniegowski Trabue had had enough — she started pulling out the investors’ signs, reached out to the city’s land bank to figure out which vacant lots in the neighborhood were held by the city and connected with River City Housing , a local nonprofit home developer, to see how they could work together. At the same time, “the Smoketown Originals started to come together,” says Boyd, referring to a community organization of older residents with deep roots in the neighborhood. “They went to the churches, the community centers, the youth centers.” They started pushing the city to do a housing needs assessment and got in touch with Grounded Solutions , a national nonprofit for affordable housing, to decide whether a community land trust would be a viable option. Community land trusts (CLTs) are grassroots nonprofits that provide long-term affordable housing by buying and developing land on behalf of the community. When selling or renting homes, the CLT retains ownership of the land they’re built on, which makes the homes cheaper and keeps the land itself under community control. Crucially, CLTs also preserve affordability long-term by requiring owners to sell at an affordable price. The first CLTs grew out of the civil rights movement to secure land ownership for Black farmers. Today, they are an increasingly popular way of protecting land from speculators and creating long-term affordable housing, with over 300 CLTs in the US . The CLT’s first houses were recently completed, and more plots have already been chosen. Courtesy of Smoketown CLT In Smoketown, a lot of the initial work focused on explaining what a CLT is and getting the broader community on board. “Communities that have been divested [from] and have been talked to and at versus with, they lose their voice,” says Boyd. “We really had to rally the troops here in the community to be like, ‘You actually have a say in what goes on in your community.’” In 2020 the community and its partner organizations won the city’s Request for Proposals, securing $2.1 million to create a CLT. By 2023 the CLT was formalized and Boyd was brought onboard as the executive director. “I really whipped us into shape administratively and organizationally,” she says. “But most importantly, I went back out into the community and I was like, ‘Okay, this is what you wanted. Now what are we going to do with this land?’” Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Based on a series of surveys, Smoketown CLT built its first seven houses right across the street from where Muhammed Ali threw his first punches under the watchful eye of trainer Fred Stoner, the grandfather of the CLT board president. These houses were recently completed, and the next seven plots have already been chosen. Before starting new developments, the CLT approaches the people living around the plots, says Boyd. “We invite them to the table: Okay, what are your concerns? What are your comments? This is what we are thinking. Is it a viable housing option for your street?” CLTs come in many different shapes, sizes and funding arrangements. In Smoketown, the CLT is funding the construction of the houses, but received the plots of land for free from the city. The land bank has earmarked around 70 plots in the neighborhood for the trust, says Boyd: “We were fortunate that those that came before me had enough gall to go to the city and be like, “Y’all holding all this land and you are absolutely not going to give it to investors. You are going to earmark it for the Community Land Trust.’ And we made them put it in writing.” Mayor Craig Greenberg joined Smoketown CLT to celebrate the completion of the CLT’s first seven homes. Courtesy of Smoketown CLT The city government has been supportive of the CLT, says Boyd, but it would not have happened without the community putting years of work into it. “Louisville’s been around for a really long time, and the people in our community absolutely will hold them to task, and that’s absolutely what they did. They started showing up at the council meetings, the reallocation of funds.” Partnering with experts, like Grounded Solutions, is key to getting a CLT off the ground, as is ensuring that community members see themselves represented in the CLT leadership, says Boyd. “[And] you have to be willing to change and really meet people where they are and not be afraid to make good trouble.” Learn more about Smoketown Community Land Trust here , or get additional information from Grounded Solutions here . Keeping it cool one roof at a time When Tony Chaves noticed how extreme heat and rising air-conditioning costs were affecting his Las Vegas neighborhood, he decided to help solve the problem with a ladder and a bucket of ultra-reflective white paint. As part of the two-person nonprofit Alchemical Opus, Chavez started painting the roofs of Arts District businesses for free, significantly decreasing their indoor temperatures, with one business owner reporting saving $60 to $70 a month on electricity. Coating roofs in white paint is an easy way to lower the temperatures of homes and public buildings. In recent years homeowners across India, Burkina Faso, Mexico and South Pacific have painted their roofs white as part of a global scientific study, with early results indicating substantial cooling. In the U.S., Philadelphia gave 62 households free cool-roof coatings in a 2025 pilot project, while the New York City CoolRoofs program has painted over 12 million square feet of roofs with reflective white paint since 2007. A number of U.S. cities also require cool roofs on new and re-roofed buildings. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime The science behind the idea is straightforward: White and reflective roofs absorb less solar heat, and applying reflective coatings is the easiest way to transform a roof into a so-called “cool roof,” while also prolonging the life of the roof . The U.S. Department of Energy says cool roofs can reduce annual air-conditioning energy use in single-story buildings by up to 15 percent, while other studies show that painted roofs can lower maximum indoor temperatures by 2.2 to 5.9°F in residential buildings that are not air conditioned. Learn more about cool roofs here . Housing across generations After moving from the countryside to Vienna for university, Lukas Hecke, Manuel Schuler and Marlene Welzl experienced first-hand how difficult it could be to find good housing on a student budget. At the same time, they knew the city was full of elderly people with small pensions and large apartments, who often felt lonely after their children grew up and moved out. In 2015 they started connecting older people with spare rooms to younger people looking for a place to live. It began organically, by word of mouth, and soon grew into the housing platform Wohnbuddy that has carefully matched over 400 people based on their interests and communications over the years. The impact goes beyond private homes. Since 2017, Wohnbuddy has also partnered with senior residences, where students bring new energy through activities, music and social interaction. Learn more about Wohnbuddy here . The post The Spark: When Communities Own the Land, Housing Stays Affordable appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.title: Πώς οι καθηγητές και οι φοιτητές του Κολλεγίου αναβιώνουν τις τοπικές ειδήσεις
items.titleOriginal: How College Faculty and Students are Reviving Local News
items.description: Το Πανεπιστήμιο Northwestern αναφέρει ότι «πάνω από 3.000 εφημερίδες έκλεισαν στις ΗΠΑ τα τελευταία 20 χρόνια». Δεν σημαίνει μόνο περιορισμένη πρόσβαση στις τοπικές ειδήσεις, αλλά απώλεια εργασίας για το προσωπικό που ζει και έχει μακροχρόνιες σχέσεις με την κοινότητα. Ακαδημαϊκά ιδρύματα όπως το Northwestern συνεργάζονται με φοιτητές είτε για να διασώσουν κληρονομικές εφημερίδες είτε…
items.descriptionOriginal: Northwestern University reports that "over 3,000 newspapers have closed in the U.S. in the past 20 years." It not only means limited access to local news, but job loss for staff who live in and have long-term relationships with the community. Academic institutions such as Northwestern are working with students to either rescue legacy newspapers or start new publications focused on serving the community over profit. Students and academic staff work together to provide the journalism for the community while students earn credits or internships. "While the student newspaper office is inside the journalism school's building, it operates independently." One journalism school director said, "They know these communities. So that was really important just from a moral and ethical imperative, but also from a news perspective," she said. "They're trusted in their communities. They know what's going on."

Η μοναδική εμπειρία στο Λονδίνο σχεδιάστηκε για να ενθαρρύνει τους ανθρώπους να σκέφτονται διαφορετικά για τα λουλούδια, δείχνοντας πώς μπορούν να διαδραματίσουν ρόλο στην καθημερινή ευημερία και όχι απλώς να δεσμεύονται για γενέθλια, anniv…
items.descriptionOriginal: The U.K.’s first “Flower Pharmacy” opened its doors last month — prescribing bouquets instead of medicine to those in need of a mood boost. The one-off experience in London was designed to encourage people to think differently about flowers, showing how they can play a role in everyday well-being rather than just being reserved for birthdays, anniversaries, and other special occasions. It was created in partnership with Plants and Flowers Foundation Holland and chartered horticulturist, TV gardener, and author David Domoney. Guests were matched with blooms tailored to their mood before leaving with a bouquet recommended to lift, calm, or energize them. For example, yellow flowers, including sunflowers, roses, freesias, and snapdragons, were prescribed to boost happiness, while calming bouquets featured blue and green blooms like hydrangeas, delphiniums, and chrysanthemums. For those who needed a dose of energy, there were also vibrant orange, red, and pink flowers. Courtesy of SWNS The event came as a poll of 2,000 British adults found 37% struggle when daylight saving time ends, with 29% admitting the time change leaves them feeling glum. Discussing the partnership with Plants and Flowers Foundation Holland, which commissioned the research and the pop-up, Domoney said: “There’s something incredibly uplifting about flowers, and research has shown that they can have a positive effect on our mood and emotional well-being. From the cheerful yellows of sunflowers and freesias to the calming tones of blues and greens, color can influence how we experience the spaces around us.” “We often associate flowers with special occasions, but there’s no reason we shouldn’t enjoy their beauty and the benefits of having them around us in everyday life,” he continued. “Sometimes, it’s the simplest connections with nature that can make a real difference to how we feel.” Courtesy of SWNS The survey also found that around a third of respondents spend more time indoors following the clock change, while 28% find the darker evenings difficult and 22% experience lower energy levels. The good news? There are plenty of ways to lift that low mood, like listening to music, reading a book, exercising, spending time in nature and, yes, buying flowers. While just 9% of people said they regularly treat themselves to blooms, the emotional response to receiving them is clear — half said they feel happy after being presented with a bouquet, 45% grateful, 34% joyful, and 24% comforted. Courtesy of SWNS Monique Kemperman, horticulture expert for Plants and Flowers Foundation Holland, said: “As the days become shorter and darker, small acts of self-care can make a real difference, and flowers are a simple way to bring color, joy, and positivity into everyday life.” “Our research shows just how much of an emotional impact they can have, yet many people still reserve them for somebody else or a special occasion,” she added. “The Flower Pharmacy is about encouraging people to see flowers as an everyday well-being boost rather than a treat.” This article was originally written by Jasmine Lenthall for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets.

items.title: Το ράντσο της Μοντάνα όπου οι αυτιστικοί άνθρωποι είναι καυγάδες και οδηγοί
items.titleOriginal: The Montana Ranch Where Autistic People Are Wranglers and Guides
items.description: Το προσωπικό στο Erik’s Ranch & Retreats λέει ένα ρητό: Σεντόνια, πετσέτες και ζωή άλλαζαν καθημερινά. Το Erik's Ranch είναι ένα καταφύγιο επισκεπτών, όπου τα αυτιστικά άτομα είναι θυρωροί, οδηγοί, τσακωτοί, μάγειρες και πολλά άλλα. Βρίσκεται σε 230 στρέμματα παρθένου βοσκοτόπου και άγριας φύσης κοντά στο Livingston της Μοντάνα, το ράντσο απέχει λιγότερο από μία ώρα από το Εθνικό Πάρκο Yellowstone. Προσφέρει…
items.descriptionOriginal: T he staff at Erik’s Ranch & Retreats has a saying: Sheets, towels and lives changed daily . Erik’s Ranch is a guest retreat where autistic people are concierges, guides, wranglers, cooks and more. Located on 230 acres of pristine pasture and wilderness near Livingston, Montana, the ranch is less than an hour from Yellowstone National Park. It offers horseback riding, fly fishing, nature hikes, history walks and experiences with ranch animals and wildlife — most led or assisted by paid neurodivergent “members,” most of whom also live on the property. The inspiration for Erik’s Ranch dates back to 2008, when founder Kathryn Nordberg was pondering how her son, Erik, whom she described as “a moderately functioning teenager with autism,” would live as an adult — and particularly what would happen when she was no longer around. Ranch manager Cameron Porter (in black hat) and member John Rekedal help a visitor from New Jersey mount her steed for a trail ride. Credit: Jodi Hausen “As someone challenged with expressive language, there weren’t very many opportunities for kids like him,” she said, sitting in the well-appointed kitchen of the ranch’s six-bedroom lodge. So she established a nonprofit with a boutique-style hotel in Edina, Minnesota, where, even after she’s gone, Erik and others like him can live, work and thrive. There, adults on the autism spectrum work and live independently and are guided by life coaches toward achieving personal goals like interviewing, equine or cooking skills; or setting up an Etsy page to sell their artwork. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Using a similar model, in 2014 Nordberg opened the Montana ranch, where not only employees on the spectrum benefit: She designed most of the cabins specifically for neurodivergent guests. Though anyone can appreciate the soothing atmosphere, it’s particularly accommodating for those on the spectrum, who sometimes experience sensory overload. The calmingly simple cabins provide awe-inspiring vistas of the surrounding mountains with little to no sign of human activity. Hardware was selected to close drawers, cabinets and doors with hardly a sound. Walls, furnishings and bedding are muted earth tones and lights have dimmers. Credit: Jodi Hausen Erik’s Ranch is run primarily by young autistic people, some of whom also live on the property. The ranch has unparalleled views of the Absaroka-Beartooth Mountains. Autistic and other neurodivergent people are often misunderstood and feel out-of-place, experiencing discrimination, social exclusion, bullying and other situations that can lead to low self-esteem. That — and an inexorable need to mask their differences — often results in depression and anxiety. Some studies indicate that people on the spectrum are four times more likely to experience major depression compared with the general population. “Depression, loneliness, lack of confidence, feeling isolated, rejected, and a lack of community and people who care is what Erik’s Ranch is working to minimize and eliminate,” Nordberg said. And it’s working. John Rekedal, 21, lives in Minnesota but just spent his first summer working at the Montana ranch. When he’s home, he works in a large production greenhouse. And though his coworkers there are understanding, he prefers the camaraderie of working with the ranch’s small staff amid the hush of the surrounding mountains. Jacob Thoresen fetches horses from a pasture in preparation for a trail ride. Thoresen has been working for Erik’s Ranch and Retreats for 10 years. Credit: Jodi Hausen “I’m a whole lot more inclined to work outside,” he said. “And I know everyone’s name. It’s more relaxed.” Cornell University autism researcher Leslie Shaw analyzed a national sample of autistic adults who could answer a survey unassisted and found that only about 53 percent were working in 2023. Furthermore, in 2024, people with cognitive disabilities (of which neurodivergence is a subset) were employed at less than half the rate of people without any disability, according to Cornell’s Northeast ADA Center . These low employment rates may be due to neurotypical employers’ lack of experience with and understanding of neurodivergent people leading to misaligned work assignments, confusion and a fraught or untenable work environment. On a recent late summer day in Montana, Jacob Thoresen, 33, was gearing up to lead a small group of guests on a trail ride. He has been working with the nonprofit for 10 years and splits his time between its two locations. In black cowboy hat and jeans, he walked back and forth across the dirt-floored indoor arena to a tack room, gathering saddles and bridles. He saddled horses while other members dutifully scooped and cleaned areas around the animals. Credit: Jodi Hausen Erik’s Ranch & Retreats is part of a growing trend of workplaces designed to integrate people with autism or other disabilities. Thoresen had other jobs before coming to Erik’s. He was a baggage handler at the Minneapolis-Saint Paul Airport and worked in retail and manufacturing. He even tried a desk job. “But,” he said with a smile, “that isn’t me.” Thoresen said he’s gained confidence working with Erik’s Ranch & Retreats. “If you would have met me 10 years ago, I would have been, like, I couldn’t be able to do anything independent and be trusted to actually get the work done,” he said. “This place is teaching me how to be independent. In this last year, I’ve grown more.” He still gets support, but staff, recognizing his achievements, have loosened the reins. “I’m having to rely more on myself to work on those independent skills,” he added. Hannah Jacobs (left) helps Zoe Markman put fresh linens on a bed in one of the guest cabins at Erik’s Ranch. Credit: Jodi Hausen When asked what he finds challenging about working at Erik’s Ranch, Thoresen said workdays can be inconsistent. At the Minnesota retreat, he completes the same tasks daily. On the ranch, daily schedules shift and sometimes he gets overwhelmed. “But I can move through it,” he said. “I attribute that to the staff that I work with and just practice. They do a good job of seeing [my overwhelm] and being like, okay. And that helps, you know. I’ve had too many employers in the past that have been like, ‘Oh, you’re not having a good day? Well, just go home.’” Over the years, Erik’s Ranch & Retreats has employed 27 autistic young adults — 19 in the last year. The goal, Nordberg said, is to serve 30 members regularly. The organization is part of a growing trend of workplaces designed to integrate people with autism or other disabilities. John Rekedal helps clean around the horses in the indoor arena before a trail ride. Credit: Jodi Hausen Not far from Erik’s Ranch, Special K Ranch in Columbus, Montana, provides living quarters and jobs in farming, ranching and gardening and contracts with area businesses to employ adults with developmental disabilities. Over in Jackson, Wyoming, Vertical Harvest integrates people with a wide array of disabilities into their operations growing lettuces, microgreens, tomatoes and basil. In a fully accessible greenhouse, Vertical Harvest operates on what’s known as the “Grow Well” model of employment : providing opportunities for workers to pursue passions by creating or placing them in positions that correspond to their strengths and aspirations, their likes and dislikes. In other words, adapting the workplace to the employee rather than the other way around. Although she hadn’t heard of Grow Well, Nordberg embraces its philosophy. It doesn’t always work out as planned, though. “Not everyone wants to learn hospitality,” she said. In fact, one autistic young man told her he wanted to be a “white hat hacker,” using his computer skills for good. But she didn’t have a role that fit his skills and aspirations. In other instances, however, a member’s passions can be integrated into ranch operations. Part-time member Zoe Markman shows off a colorful collection of eggs gathered from the hens in the coop behind her. Credit: Jodi Hausen Zoe Markman, a 21-year-old autistic woman from Bozeman, loves animals — particularly chickens. So when Markman started working part-time at the ranch, Nordberg built a chicken coop and populated it with more than a dozen hens whom Markman gave punny names: Chiquille O’Neal, Princess Layer and Hen Solo. On a recent workday, Markman gathered more than a dozen colorful eggs. Nordberg also helped Erik start a baking business making cookies, brownies, scones and banana bread. Erik is a visual learner and communicator, so Nordberg created a pictorial cookbook with step-by-step instructions. She marked bins of flour, sugar and other ingredients with pictures so Erik can do most of the work independently. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime The ranch can currently house five members and has five cabins and the lodge for guests on its expansive property. So Nordberg has room to expand, and she’d like to. But finances and land-use regulations present barriers. It’s expensive running a guest ranch, though the costs are partly covered by guest fees and philanthropy. And area permitting will only allow for seven more cabins. “This will never be a huge operation,” Nordberg said. But she’s gratified knowing there are places for Erik and others like him to live, belong and find meaningful work. This story was supported in part by the Solutions Journalism Network’s HEAL Fellowship. items.titleOriginal: The Birds Planted the Grove
items.description: Για αιώνες, τα ιερά άλση του Ρατζαστάν θεωρούνταν ανθρώπινα δώρα στη φύση -- μέρη όπου η πίστη έθεσε ένα όριο και το δάσος αφέθηκε να αναπνεύσει. Αλλά όπως υποστηρίζει σιωπηλά αυτό το δοκίμιο, η σειρά αυτής της ιστορίας είναι λάθος: οι άνθρωποι προστάτευαν μια χούφτα συκιές και τα πουλιά έκαναν όλα τα άλλα. Το peepal, το banyan, το guular -- thre…
items.descriptionOriginal: For centuries, the sacred groves of Rajasthan were understood as human gifts to nature -- places where belief drew a boundary and the forest was allowed to breathe. But as this essay quietly argues, the order of that story is wrong: people protected a handful of fig trees, and the birds did everything else. The peepal, the banyan, the gular -- three figs that tradition placed beyond the reach of the axe - fed birds through every lean season, and those birds, carrying seeds from across the landscape, built the grove outward from that protected center, generation after generation. "What belief really preserved was a process," the author writes, "a place where the planting could go on undisturbed for centuries." There is something worth sitting with in that realization: that the deepest acts of protection are often for something we cannot fully see, and that what looks like a tree standing alone is, if the birds still come, a forest in the making.

items.titleOriginal: The Election That Transcended Tribalism
items.description: Οι P undits περιγράφουν τη χθεσινή βραδιά ως φασαρία για τους Δημοκρατικούς, μια επίπληξη των Ρεπουμπλικανών, ένα μπλε τσουνάμι, μια καταστροφή στις κόκκινες πολιτείες. Αλλά κάτω από αυτούς τους τίτλους υπάρχει μια πιο ήσυχη, παράλληλη ιστορία για τους ψηφοφόρους που επιλέγουν να εγκαταλείψουν τη φυλετική πίστη και να λάβουν αποφάσεις για τους εαυτούς τους. Για μήνες, ακούμε για την πιθανότητα ενός μπλε κύματος — και το…
items.descriptionOriginal: P undits are describing last night as a romp for Democrats, a rebuke of Republicans, a blue tsunami, a rout in the red states. But underneath these headlines is a quieter, parallel story about voters choosing to abandon tribal allegiance and make decisions for themselves. For months, we’ve been hearing about the possibility of a blue wave — and then, in the same breath, the caveat: Is a wave even possible in today’s hyper-polarized America? And yet, in Texas, Florida, Kansas and beyond, the electorate refused to let party loyalty make their choice for them. Young, Latino and red-state voters moved, sometimes dramatically, in just two years. The composition of the two sides turned out to be less fixed than we imagined, with a meaningful number of voters willing to cast ballots across party lines when a candidate, issue or circumstance spoke to them. In Texas, where Democrats had historic wins, people of all parties have recently united to fight against a border wall through Big Bend National Park. Credit: Sam Karas Part of the story was turnout, said New York Times Chief Political Analyst Nate Cohn on The Daily . But, he added, “Many people who are registered as Republicans and voted for Donald Trump voted for the Democratic candidate.” This feels like a fitting conclusion to The Depolarization Project , our special series about how political polarization works and what we can do about it. The premise of that series was that depolarization isn’t about meeting in the middle. It’s about choosing to remain open and curious, rather than blindly clinging to arbitrary affiliations. In the end, many voters showed that their party label doesn’t have the final say. Data center opposition is proving to be a bipartisan, or even nonpartisan, issue across the U.S. Credit: Here Now / Shutterstock Wednesdays are normally “What We’re Reading” day here at Reasons to be Cheerful, so in that spirit, here’s a post-Election Day list of stories from our own depolarization series and from elsewhere around the web. items.title: Ο εμπειρογνώμονας του αντιεξτρεμισμού χτίζει την ικανότητά μας για συμπόνια
items.titleOriginal: The Counter-Extremism Expert Building Our Capacity for Compassion
items.description: Ένα πρώην μέλος συμμορίας του Λος Άντζελες, ένας πρώην σκίνχεντ και ένας πρώην ριζοσπαστικός ισλαμιστής μπαίνουν σε ένα κέντρο νεολαίας. Αυτό που ακούγεται σαν το στήσιμο για ένα ανήσυχο αστείο είναι ο πυρήνας της δουλειάς του Farah Pandith: Βάλτε ανθρώπους που διαφορετικά δεν θα μοιράζονταν ποτέ ένα δωμάτιο μπροστά σε νέους. αφήστε τους να εξηγήσουν τι τους τράβηξε στον εξτρεμισμό και πώς βρήκαν το δρόμο τους.…
items.descriptionOriginal: A former Los Angeles gang member, a former skinhead and a former radical Islamist walk into a youth center. What sounds like the setup for an uneasy joke is at the core of Farah Pandith’s work: Put people who might otherwise never share a room in front of young people; let them explain what drew them into extremism and how they found their way out. “They’re the most authentic and credible voices there are,” Pandith says. More than once she has observed that their stories reach an audience that official warnings cannot. For decades, including while working for the U.S. government under the Obama, George W. Bush and George H.W. Bush administrations, Pandith researched why people embrace ideologies that divide the world into “us versus them.” Before people can be persuaded away from hatred, she argues, one has to understand what they are looking for: recognition, certainty or a place in the world. “You don’t suddenly explode and become an extremist overnight. You’re having some self-doubt, you’re asking questions about who you are,” she says from her light-filled living room in Arlington, Virginia. Preventing someone from becoming an extremist has been her lifelong goal, because it’s “infinitely easier than dealing with the fallout.” Farah Pandith visits the Indonesian city of Bekasi during her time as the U.S. special representative to Muslim communities. Credit: U.S. Embassy, Jakarta / Wikimedia Commons While working for the government, she traveled to nearly 100 countries, from Belgium to Bangladesh, to understand how extremists’ descent into violence can be interrupted. Today she applies what she learned to a broader problem: how to make compassion more than an admirable sentiment and help communities put it into practice. Last year Pandith received the ADL Daniel Pearl Award , which is given annually to a person who has had a positive impact on understanding between Jews and the Muslim world, and is sponsored by the parents of the journalist who was kidnapped and killed in Pakistan in 2002. “It is hard to think of anyone more knowledgeable than Farah Pandith when it comes to countering violent extremism,” Joseph Nye, the late chair of the National Intelligence Council, said about her. On September 11, 2001, Pandith watched on television like millions of others as two planes struck the World Trade Center. “It felt very heavy,” she recalls, putting a hand to her heart. “The world kind of went still for a moment, like, ‘What do we do about this?’” She felt compelled to act, to help prevent such violence from happening again. She especially rejected the way extremists attempted to define her religion on the airwaves. “Who are they to dictate what Islam is?” she remembers thinking. “For me, Islam means humility, compassion, to treat others with respect.” Initially, when she worked for the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), cooperating with local organizations showed her that effective policy depends on understanding the people on the ground. “You have to listen really well to find a solution that matches with the local community,” she says. “That’s tricky and complex. Trust has to be built first.” The same principle, she realized, applied to preventing violent extremism. Government officials could not design effective strategies from Washington alone. They needed to hear from the people they hoped to reach, including those whose voices had been overlooked. After joining the National Security Council in 2004, Pandith helped develop the “soft power” side of the Global War on Terror through a new approach called Countering Violent Extremism. Military action might disrupt extremist organizations, but it could not prevent them from recruiting new members. Nor were public relations campaigns successful in overcoming the distrust of Muslims worldwide. Even in her own government, distrust was impossible to ignore. One congressman called the White House to complain a “jihadist” was sitting in the Council. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Pandith was briefly living in Afghanistan’s capital, Kabul, in 2004 when photographs of abuse at Abu Ghraib surfaced showing American soldiers humiliating Muslim prisoners. “In an instant, all our efforts on the ground were harmed irreparably,” she says. Locals asked how she could represent a government that treated Muslim prisoners that way. The experience reinforced a lesson: Building trust also meant receiving criticism, sitting through uncomfortable conversations. Pandith carried that approach into her work at the State Department, where Hillary Clinton appointed her the first U.S. special representative to Muslim communities in 2009. Instead of treating Muslim populations as a single audience for American messages, she traveled widely, meeting people in homes, mosques and community settings to learn what mattered to them. “You have to go to the rural areas,” she says, aiming to support credible local voices that could offer alternatives to extremist narratives. Pandith herself has been shaped by a background that made her an ideal diplomat. She came to the U.S. from Kashmir as a baby with her mother, a pulmonologist and the medical director of a hospital. Pandith describes growing up in a highly educated Muslim family without experiencing discrimination. She remembers an America in which people of different faiths could live alongside one another, “with a synagogue, a church, a mosque and a temple in the same part of town.” Today, she admits, that harmonious coexistence feels nearly impossible. Her parents separated when she was 10, and her mother raised Pandith and her brother on her own. One of her greatest influences was her uncle, a heart surgeon. “I’ve held the hearts of different people in my hands,” he would tell her. “Always remember: There is no difference between the heart of a Muslim, a Jew, a Hindu or a Christian.” Pandith feels she carries “many identities” — an American, a woman, a Muslim and a foreign policy professional, among others. While traveling as Special Representative to Muslim Communities in the Obama administration, she said she had a “superpower” when speaking with Muslims. When she told them she was born in Srinagar in Kashmir, India, the atmosphere often changed. “Suddenly I’m like a sister to them.” Farah Pandith on a panel at the Milken Institute Asia Summit. Courtesy of Farah Pandith Her ability to forge connections would become one of her greatest professional assets. By chance, Barbara Bush, the wife of President George H.W. Bush, visited Smith College during Farah’s senior year. She was so impressed by a speech Pandith gave as student body president that she helped her secure her job at USAID after graduation. That was how the young woman began traveling around the world. Pandith’s work challenged conventional explanations of radicalization. Poverty and lack of education, she argued, could not explain why people embraced violent ideologies. Some of the 9/11 terrorists were well educated. Pandith pointed to a different cause she observed in Muslim communities: deep identity crises among young people who struggled to find their place in a rapidly changing world. She thinks of a young woman in Denmark whose Imam told her she wasn’t a Muslim if she didn’t cover her head. Or Mubin Shaikh in Canada, who went to Pakistan and Syria as a 19-year-old to fight alongside the jihadists and who now teaches security politics at the University of Ottawa. Pandith has seen firsthand that dialogue can change minds. ““It’s less interesting for the media than an extremist’s video, but the conversations we had affected people.” Her initiatives have sought to make dialogue a shared responsibility. Against Violent Extremism became the world’s first and only network of former extremists, launched by the U.S. Department of State, the Institute for Strategic Dialogue and Google. The “Hours Against Hate” campaign encouraged teenagers to spend an hour doing something for someone different from themselves. Millions participated. Sisters Against Violent Extremism connected mothers concerned about their children’s vulnerability to extremist recruitment. In a citizen-dialogue program, Pandith traveled through Europe with other Muslim Americans to share experiences and listen to local concerns. People had the chance to meet someone they might otherwise see only through stereotypes and to develop a relationship that complicated those assumptions. In her book How We Win , recently reissued, Pandith remains stubbornly optimistic: The fight against extremism can be won. Preventing people from being drawn into extremist movements requires intervening early and bringing together the people who can reach them — not just government officials, but business leaders, teachers, local communities and influencers whose networks, knowledge and credibility government agencies lack. “The fight against violent extremism is not going to be won solely by the efforts of government,” she argues. “We need businesses to step up as never before, for the public interest as well as their own.” She insists that this work cannot be dismissed as idealism or do-goodery but is “a matter of national security” — as important as the hard power of military force. Pandith emphasizes that the underlying lessons can be relevant for many communities. The same dynamics of exclusion and dehumanization can fuel hostility toward religious minorities, LGBTQ+ people and Asian communities, among others. Still, she admits that the strategies for countering violent extremism never fully came to fruition, often mired in bureaucracy. “Congress provided just 0.0138 percent of funding compared to the funding for the military,” she calculates. “We know what we need to do. We spent 25 years researching and exchanging strategies. But we left the field to the extremists.” Pandith sees the reality as a call to action: “We cannot just wring our hands and keep saying things are bad and things are difficult and somebody else’s problem. We need everybody.” Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime She now works outside government to advance another part of this agenda, as senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations , teaching countering violent extremism at Georgetown University, and as a Global Peace Laureate for the Muhammad Ali Center. She has been developing the Muhammad Ali Index on compassion . For Pandith, compassion is the capacity to recognize another person’s humanity even amid disagreement, and to resist the impulse to turn differences into a reason for contempt. “There isn’t a faith on planet Earth that doesn’t have compassion in it. And even if you are not religious you understand what it means, right?” As part of the Muhammed Ali Index, more than 5,400 people in 12 American cities responded to the 2025 State of Compassion survey . Sixty-one percent said they felt compassion has declined in the last four years, but 43 percent were optimistic about the future of compassion in America. A second index, planned for 2027, will cover 20 U.S. cities and 12 cities around the world. The ambition is practical. Pandith hopes the data will help mayors, school leaders, faith groups and local organizations identify opportunities to build stronger connections and design efforts suited to their own communities. The point is not to prescribe a universal program, but to create a framework that can be adapted. “We want to see people taking inspiration from the data to actually do something over time so we can measure and see what takes place,” she says passionately, insisting that compassion can be trained: “Compassion is a muscle that can be exercised.” Yet the starting point is personal: “Self-compassion is essential.” Building the capacity for compassion, Pandith argues, begins with recognizing what is happening inside oneself. She is particularly interested in reaching young people early. “The world that they are growing up in is so polarized and so difficult and so different from the one that we have grown up in,” she says, “that they don’t have a memory of people who are different from them speaking to each other with dignity regularly.” As Pandith sees it, waiting for polarization to disappear on its own is not a strategy. The task is to build relationships and connections that open up hearts and minds — and to keep investing in them long enough to learn what works. She repeats her favorite sentence: “Solutions are available and affordable.” UPDATE — November 3, 2026: This story has been updated to clarify facts about Pandith’s work and background.
